# Decision log

> **IDs are slugs, not numbers.** Entries are identified by a content-derived slug
> (`D_surrogate_first`) with an explicit `<a id="…"></a>` anchor, so numbering never has to be
> allocated — and never clashes across worktrees. Old numeric IDs map at
> [DECISION-ID-MAP.md](../DECISION-ID-MAP.md).

> **Licence.** This log is Apache-2.0, like every doc in the repository — the module it sits in is
> not ([`PROVENANCE.md` § Lanes](../PROVENANCE.md#lanes)). JDK source, javadoc and Oracle notices
> quoted here remain under their own terms; quoting them relicenses nothing.


ADR-lite. Entries carry stable IDs (`D_import_swap_target`, `D_peer_terminology`, …) that never renumber or reuse — cross-references from code, commits, and sibling docs must stay resolvable. Content is edited in place as the project's understanding evolves; when a decision is fully superseded, its entry shrinks to a one-line pointer at the superseding ID rather than being deleted. Each entry: **Decision**, **Rationale**, **Alternatives** considered, **Accepted limitation**.

---

<a id="D_import_swap_target"></a>
## D_import_swap_target. Target is import-swap drop-in, not binary-drop-in

**Decision.** Users port apps by rewriting `javax.swing.*` imports to `vaadinx.swing.*` and recompiling. We do not shadow the JDK's `javax.swing` module.

**Rationale.** `javax.swing` lives in the `java.desktop` module and cannot be replaced at runtime without JDK-level hacks. Import rewrite + recompile is a tractable migration step.

**What `vaadinx` means.** The root mirrors **`javax`**: `javax.swing.X` → `vaadinx.swing.X`, and `java.awt.X` → `vaadinx.awt.X`, so one root stands in for both JDK roots and the swap stays a token substitution. It does **not** mean "Vaadin, extended" — reading the `x` that way inverts the architecture, because the layer that literally extends Vaadin components is `:surrogates` ([D_emulator_surrogate_split](#D_emulator_surrogate_split)), while `vaadinx` is the has-a emulation layer that holds a peer. Stated explicitly because both readings are available to someone meeting `vaadinx.awt.Label` cold, and only one is right.

The root is also deliberately **not** the project's own name, and that is load-bearing rather than incidental: it is the identifier a migrator types most, and it names the package's *job* (the mirror of the JDK namespace) instead of its vendor. Vendor names churn — this project has been renamed once already — and JDK namespaces do not.

**Alternatives.** Bytecode rewriting of compiled jars (a build-time plugin rewriting `javax.swing` references post-compile) — rejected: extra toolchain complexity for marginal benefit, it slows iteration, and it breaks IDE tooling, which sees the pre-rewrite types. Plugging a custom `java.awt.Toolkit` and peer set was considered separately and rejected in [D_awt_peer_hooking_rejected](#D_awt_peer_hooking_rejected).

Renaming the root onto the project's own token (`sbemul.swing.JFrame`) was proposed and rejected in 2026-09, when the project was renamed to SwingBridge Emulators. The rename is the evidence for keeping it: `vaadinx` needed no change, which is the vendor-independence above doing its job. Two distinct roots also carry a lifetime split that one root erases — `vaadinx.*` is scaffolding the migrator removes at stage 4, while the project's other packages hold `IntentionallyStatic` and the guardrails, which are permanent in the migrated app by design. Those are `com.vaadin.swingbridge.*` — reverse-domain, because nothing about them is mechanically swapped and so nothing about them claims `vaadinx`'s brevity ([D_naming_scheme](#D_naming_scheme)). The split also gives the migrator two independent progress meters: an empty `grep vaadinx` means no view is still at stage 2, an empty `grep com.vaadin.swingbridge.surrogates` means none is still at stage 3.

**Accepted limitation.** Users must have source access for all Swing code they depend on, including third-party libraries — a jar that cannot be rebuilt is a blocker, not a rough edge. Common Swing libraries are covered by the add-on model instead ([M1D_addon_packaging](../migration/1-swing-to-emulators/decisions.md#M1D_addon_packaging)); JCalendar 1.4 and JGoodies Forms 1.2.1 ship today.

<a id="D_naming_scheme"></a>
## D_naming_scheme. Three name tokens, one job each: `vaadinx`, `com.vaadin.swingbridge`, `emul`

**Decision.** The project is **SwingBridge Emulators** — feature 2 of the five under Vaadin's *SwingBridge* umbrella — and its identifiers are partitioned across exactly three tokens by one principle: **`vaadinx` holds everything that leaves the migrated app at stage 4 together with the emulators; every other Java package takes a reverse-domain root; and where reverse-domain is absurd — the DOM — a short project token.**

| token | job |
|---|---|
| `vaadinx.*` | the emulator runtime's whole API, unchanged: `:emulators`, `:emulators-printing`, the add-ons' swap targets (`vaadinx.jgoodies.*`, `vaadinx.toedter.*`), and the hand-wired corners that leave with them — `vaadinx.swing.app` (`SwingBridgeEmulatorsBootstrap`, `MainWindowRoute`), `vaadinx.EHelper` |
| `com.vaadin.swingbridge.*` | every other Java package, and the Maven `groupId`: `:surrogates`, `:migration-annotations`, `:migration-guardrails`, `:migration-tool`, `:sampler`, `:generator`, test fixtures, the hand-built testapps |
| `emul` | the DOM / resource layer only, **never a Java package**: CSS classes, `data-*` attributes, custom DOM events, the JS globals, `META-INF/` directories, the system property, style-element keys |

ArtifactIds are `swingbridge-<module>`; the add-ons keep `M1D_addon_packaging`'s `<prefix>-<lib>-<upstream version>` shape (`swingbridge-emulators-jcalendar-1.4`), with `swingbridge-emulators` as the prefix because an add-on extends SB-Emulators, not the SwingBridge umbrella — a bare `swingbridge-jcalendar` reads as a sibling of SwingBridge Streamer. In prose: full name on first use per document, then **SB-Emulators** for the whole project and module notation (`:emulators`) for a module — never bare "the emulators" for the project, which also reads as the product.

**Rationale, token by token — each is what an alternative arrangement would have broken.**

- **`vaadinx` stays, and the rename is the evidence for it.** It sat untouched while the project went from `sov` to SwingBridge Emulators — vendor-independence working. It is the identifier a migrator's tree contains most, machine-written by `ImportSwap` and human-read constantly, and it names the package's *job* (the mirror of `javax` / `java`) rather than its vendor; vendor names have changed twice in a year here, JDK namespaces have not. Full etymology and the case against retiring it: [D_import_swap_target](#D_import_swap_target).
- **What is *in* `vaadinx` is decided by lifetime, not by mechanism.** `vaadinx.swing.app` is hand-wired, not swapped; read as "the mechanically swapped surface" it would move out, and that would break the grep meter — an empty `grep vaadinx` would stop meaning *the emulator runtime is unwired*. The same test moves `:generator`'s own class the other way: a maintainer tool is never in a migrated app, so `vaadinx.internal.Generator` became `com.vaadin.swingbridge.generator.Generator`.
- **Two roots give two independent progress meters.** `grep vaadinx` empty → no view is still at stage 2; `grep com.vaadin.swingbridge.surrogates` empty → none is still at stage 3. `:migration-guardrails` is already specified against *"at stage 4 `vaadinx` is gone"*, so the meter is load-bearing. `vaadinx.surrogates` — the strongest rival, since a surrogate literally subclasses a Vaadin component — was rejected for collapsing the two meters into one ambiguous one.
- **Everything else takes reverse-domain because nothing about it is mechanical.** The short-root argument was always about volume: thousands of tool-written import lines. Stage 2→3 is a per-view *rewrite* by construction ([R_vaadin_first](../CLAUDE.md) makes surrogates functionally complete but API-narrow), so there is no swap tool and the imports are hand-written with autocomplete; the same holds for `IntentionallyStatic` and the guardrails in the migrator's own source and tests. Reverse-domain is also what a published Vaadin OSS artifact looks like — `com.vaadin.flow.*` is the neighbourhood. One shape was rejected outright: **`vaadinx` for everything** fails at `vaadinx.migration.IntentionallyStatic`, since that annotation is carried by UI-free service modules, where a `vaadinx` import would undo the very Step-0 classification `:migration-annotations`' zero-dependency contract protects ([M1D_static_taxonomy](../migration/1-swing-to-emulators/decisions.md#M1D_static_taxonomy)).
- **ArtifactIds are `swingbridge-<module>`, not bare `<module>`.** A jar filename stands alone in a `lib/` directory and a build log: `emulators-0.1.jar` is anonymous, `swingbridge-emulators-0.1.jar` is not, and Vaadin's own artifactIds are self-describing without their groupId (`vaadin-core`, `flow-server`). Not `vaadin-swingbridge-*`, which is redundant with the groupId.
- **The version property we tell a migrator to declare is `${swingbridge-emulators.version}`, not `${swingbridge.version}`** — the same collision reasoning as [`M1D_bootstrap_canonical`](../migration/1-swing-to-emulators/decisions.md#M1D_bootstrap_canonical)'s, applied to a build property. A bare `swingbridge` names the *umbrella*, and where the two routes compose (Streamer first, then port view-by-view) a migrated pom holds **both** `com.vaadin:vaadin-swing-bridge` and our artifacts on independent release trains, so one property named for the umbrella cannot serve them and picking which feature gets the short name is arbitrary. The qualified form also mirrors its artifactId exactly, which is what Maven property convention already does — this repo's own parent pom carries `${maven-compiler-plugin.version}`, `${maven-surefire-plugin.version}`. It is longer, but it is declared once per pom and copy-pasted from the guide, never typed. **Not the `emul` token:** that one is DOM-and-resource-layer only, and this name is coordinate-adjacent — it exists to say *"the version of the artifact called `swingbridge-emulators`"*. Note this is a *documented convention for the migrator's own pom*, not a property any pom here defines; the reactor uses `${project.version}`.
- **The DOM token is `emul`, and it only became possible once the token left Java.** Every collision argument against the candidates was about how a *package root* reads in a stranger's source tree; a CSS prefix, a JS global, a `META-INF/` directory and a system property share their namespaces with parties we do not control, but in practice with nobody who would plausibly also say `emul-`. `.emul-rootpane` is the most self-explaining form the DOM can carry, and the brand is already on the coordinates and the Java packages.

**Alternatives.** `sbe` — **SBE is Simple Binary Encoding**, and the positioning doc's named targets are disproportionately trading firms. `sbemu` — **SBEMU is taken** ([crazii/SBEMU](https://github.com/crazii/SBEMU), Sound Blaster emulation for DOS), and the clash is semantically exact: it already expands to "SB emulator". `sbemul` — the answer while the token was still a Java root, and the runner-up; six characters, and an abbreviation of an abbreviation. `swingbridge` as the DOM prefix — **claims the umbrella**, one of whose other features (Streamer) emits DOM into a page the interop story says may also be running us. Keeping `sov` — the name is *official*; a codebase whose every identifier says `sov` while its README says SwingBridge Emulators is exactly the drift the doc rules exist to prevent.

**Accepted limitation.** `emul`'s one real cost is **searchability from devtools**: a migrator meeting `.emul-rootpane` with no import line to say whose it is can search it and find nothing, where `.sbemul-rootpane` would have found us. Judged not to outweigh brevity and self-description once the DOM was the token's whole job; the mitigation shipped with the sweep — every stylesheet and script under `META-INF/resources/emul/` opens with a comment naming the project and its repo, so the file a devtools reader lands in says where it came from. Revisit this if it ever bites.

<a id="D_peer_terminology"></a>
## D_peer_terminology. Terminology: "peer" for the underlying Vaadin component

**Decision.** The Vaadin `Component` backing a `vaadinx.awt.Component` is its *peer*. Field: `protected final Component peer`.

**Rationale.** AWT already uses "peer" for the native widget behind a Java widget (`java.awt.peer.ButtonPeer`). Vaadin plays the same role here. Reusing an established term avoids inventing jargon.

**Alternatives.** `backing`, `delegate`, `adaptee`, `counterpart` — rejected as overloaded, awkward, or non-directional.

**Accepted limitation.** The relationship is not literally identical to classical AWT peering (AWT peers were platform-specific; ours is cross-platform by construction). Terminology is close enough.

---

<a id="D_own_awt_package"></a>
## D_own_awt_package. Emulate down to `java.awt.Component` in our own `vaadinx.awt` package

**Decision.** Re-implement AWT base classes (`Component`, `Container`, events, `Color`, `Font`, …) under `vaadinx.awt` rather than extending real `java.awt` classes.

**Rationale.** Extending the real AWT classes drags in peer/headless/toolkit internals we don't want. Re-implementing keeps the hierarchy clean and decoupled from `java.desktop`.

**Alternatives.** Extend real `java.awt.*` — rejected for coupling and headless baggage.

**Accepted limitation.** More scope. Worth it for the clean architecture.

---

<a id="D_peer_ctor_injection"></a>
## D_peer_ctor_injection. Peer instantiation via constructor injection

**Decision.** Each leaf class passes its chosen Vaadin peer up the constructor chain. Base `vaadinx.awt.Component` stores it in a `protected final` field.

**Rationale.** Avoids calling overridable methods from constructors (fragile in Java), keeps `peer` final, makes the peer choice explicit per class.

**Alternatives.**
- Protected `createPeer()` factory called from base ctor — unsafe (runs before subclass fields initialise).
- Lazy creation on first access — viable backup but adds state.
- Registry keyed on `getClass()` — indirection with no upside.

**Accepted limitation.** A `vaadinx.swing` subclass that needs richer capabilities than the default peer (e.g. JGoodies-style extensions of `JButton`) must expose a constructor taking a different peer — possibly forcing API additions. Refactor when encountered.

---

<a id="D_never_fail_on_gaps"></a>
## D_never_fail_on_gaps. Never fail due to incomplete emulation; still match Swing's own failure modes

**Decision.** Incomplete or unimplemented API calls `EHelper.onUnimplemented(className, method, args)` — logs WARN via slf4j and returns a sensible default. **But** when real Swing/AWT throws under the same inputs (bad index into `getComponent(int)`, orphan `getLocale`, adding a component to its own ancestor, …), we throw too, using the same exception type where practical.

**Rationale.** A missing `setEnabled` should not crash a customer's app mid-migration — "do something silly and log" produces a working-if-imperfect app. Conversely, a call that Swing itself rejects as a programming error *should* fail here too; swallowing it masks real bugs behind log lines that users rarely read, and diverges from Swing's contract where matching is cheap. Centralising the incompleteness case in `onUnimplemented` lets us later add dedup, usage tracking, or coverage reports without touching call sites.

**Alternatives.**
- Throw `UnsupportedOperationException` on everything unimplemented — too aggressive for a migration bridge; apps wouldn't boot.
- Never throw, not even on programming errors Swing would have rejected — hides real bugs and lets invalid state propagate silently.
- Silent no-op with no log — hides incompleteness problems.

**Accepted limitation.** Apps may exhibit subtle behavioural bugs from incompleteness with no visible error. Users must read logs to discover missing support.

---

<a id="D_best_effort_behaviour"></a>
## D_best_effort_behaviour. Behaviour compatibility is best-effort

**Decision.** Behaviour fidelity is capped at "close enough to run a typical Swing app" rather than bug-for-bug Swing semantics — [R_best_effort_behaviour](../CLAUDE.md#R_best_effort_behaviour) states the cap. This entry holds why it is set there.

**Rationale.**
- Matching 25+ years of Swing event ordering, focus traversal, model timing, etc. is unbounded work. The product is a migration bridge, not a permanent home.
- **The cap is on observable behaviour, not on the call graph.** A method whose body does nothing must still be *called* where the JDK calls it, and must still recurse to children where the JDK recurses — `Container.removeNotify()` is the specimen: user code overrides it and depends on being reached, so an emulator that skips the walk because the body is empty breaks an override that compiles and looks wired. "Best-effort" licenses falling short of Swing's *effect*; it never licenses a hook that is never reached. The general form is [R_no_vaadin_in_api](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_vaadin_in_api) limb 2, with [R_decline_effect_only](../CLAUDE.md#R_decline_effect_only) for what a declined method still owes.

**Alternatives.** Exhaustive compatibility — rejected: prohibitive cost for a tool meant to be temporary.

**Accepted limitation.** Some apps will behave subtly differently and require code changes. Expected — this is a stepping stone to a proper Vaadin rewrite.

---

<a id="D_pixel_layout_not_planned"></a>
## D_pixel_layout_not_planned. Pixel-accurate layout is not built here and not planned

**Decision.** SB-Emulators does not implement pixel-accurate layout, and no external library is coming to supply it. Close-enough is the permanent answer, not a placeholder — bounded by [R_layouts_close_enough](../CLAUDE.md#R_layouts_close_enough), which is where the line between accepted cosmetic divergence and required structural correctness lives.

**Rationale.** Pixel fidelity in a browser is unbounded work against a layout model that is not Swing's, for a migration bridge whose value is that the app *runs*. Structural correctness is what decides whether a migrated view is usable; the last pixel is not.

**Alternatives.**
- **Build a pixel-accurate layout engine here** — rejected: unbounded cost, and the wrong place to spend it for a stepping-stone product.
- ~~**Depend on a separate pixel-accurate layout library in flight outside this project.**~~ **This library does not exist and is not planned.** The claim stood in this entry, in `R_layouts_close_enough`, in `emulators/architecture.md` and in four javadoc blocks, where the definite article ("*the* external library") read as a thing that exists. It is struck everywhere; a migrator reading `GroupLayout`'s javadoc was being told to wait for something that was never coming.

**Accepted limitation.** Apps with hand-tuned pixel layouts (`setBounds`, complex `GridBagLayout`) will look different. Permanently.

---

<a id="D_single_ui_per_session"></a>
## D_single_ui_per_session. Single `UI` per `VaadinSession` for now

**Decision.** Assume one Vaadin `UI` per session. Static Swing registries (`JFrame.getFrames()`, etc.) scope to that UI.

**Amended by [D_window_registry](#D_window_registry): the window registries moved from UI scope to *tab* scope**, so they survive an F5 `@PreserveOnRefresh` teleport (UI scope does not), and they *retain* — the "no retained list, hence no leak" gloss this entry used to carry is replaced by AWT's own leak, deliberately reproduced and bounded to the browser tab. Tab scope is the `AppContext` analogue: AWT's public registry is itself an attribute map on a scope narrower than the JVM. That amendment does not weaken this entry — the two answer orthogonal axes (`Q_registry_multi_tab`, closed 2026-08-31): tab scope is *where app-instance state lives* (`AppInstance`), while this entry is a *cardinality* rule — at most one app instance per session, enforced by `MainWindowRoute`'s curtain and `EHelper.onSessionLiveUI`'s throw. The single-UI-per-session assumption below is otherwise unchanged.

**Rationale.** Swing apps assume single-user, single-JVM globals. Multi-UI multiplexing per session is a rabbit hole not needed for the first slice.

**Alternatives.** Full multi-UI support from day one — rejected (premature scope).

**Accepted limitation.** Apps that open multiple top-level windows mapping to multiple Vaadin UIs won't work correctly. Revisit once the single-UI case is stable.

---

<a id="D_blocking_dialogs_deferred"></a>
## D_blocking_dialogs_deferred. Blocking dialogs deferred to vaadin-loom approach (closed by D_callswing_loom)

✅ Closed by [D_callswing_loom](#D_callswing_loom). `vaadinx.EHelper.callSwing` runs every peer→Swing event as a UI fiber of vaadin-blocking-dialogs ([D_blocking_dialogs_library](#D_blocking_dialogs_library)).

**Original decision.** `JOptionPane.showMessageDialog` and other blocking modal API initially do not block. They display and return immediately (or `onUnimplemented`). Real blocking semantics will come via the virtual-thread approach from https://github.com/mvysny/vaadin-loom.

**Rationale.** Blocking a server thread on user input is the central hard problem of the migration. Solving it deserves its own focused work — not the first slice.

**Alternatives.** Solve blocking dialogs up front — rejected (too much scope to take on first).

**Accepted limitation (historical, closed by D_callswing_loom).** Apps that rely on `showMessageDialog`-style blocking calls from inside listeners will not work correctly until vaadin-loom integration lands.

<a id="D_pure_java_artifact"></a>
## D_pure_java_artifact. Published artifacts carry no language runtime but Java's

**Decision.** `src/main` is pure Java in every published module — [R_pure_java_library](../CLAUDE.md#R_pure_java_library).

**Rationale.** Not "a Kotlin consumer would suffer" — SB-Emulators' consumers are legacy Swing apps, and a legacy Swing app is Java by construction. The cost lands on *Java* consumers instead: in the enterprise shops SB-Emulators targets, a **language runtime** in the dependency tree is a different conversation from a library — dependency approval, security scanning, "no new languages on the platform" — and it quietly contradicts the pitch that the migrated app is still Swing-shaped Java you recompile. Kotlin also buys little here: `src/main` reproduces a Java API whose signatures the JDK dictates, so the conveniences that make Kotlin worth a runtime never get to apply. The same classpath-minimalism argument later carved the PDF engine out into `:emulators-printing` (D_printing_optional_module).

**Alternatives.** Kotlin throughout — rejected: spends the argument above to buy conveniences the JDK-dictated signatures block anyway.

**Scope note.** This entry says nothing about the *test* language. `kotlin-stdlib` is `test`-scoped and has never reached a consumer classpath, so the argument above never bore on `src/test` — see [D_tests_in_java](#D_tests_in_java), which is where that question actually lives.
