<a id="D_tests_in_java"></a>
## D_tests_in_java. New tests are Java; the Kotlin corpus shrinks by attrition

**Superseded in its decision, not its rationale, by [D_kotlin_retired](#D_kotlin_retired)** — the corpus was ported in a campaign rather than left to attrition. Everything below stands as the reasoning that made Java the default and made the eventual port affordable; only the *"the 185 existing files are not being rewritten"* half is no longer operative. Kept in full because D_kotlin_retired's argument is a delta on this one.

**Decision.** [R_java_karibu_tests](../CLAUDE.md#R_java_karibu_tests). This entry holds why the default flipped, and why the 185 existing Kotlin files were not rewritten *at the time*.

**Rationale.** Both reasons Kotlin was originally chosen for were re-checked on 2026-08-27, and both had decayed:

- *"Karibu-Testing is Kotlin-first."* `:sampler` runs 47 Karibu tests in Java through `LocatorJ`, with no Kotlin plugin in its pom at all — and those are the `WarnInventoryTest` exit gates, the most load-bearing tests in the repo. Only 65 of 185 Kotlin test files even import Karibu; for the other 65% Kotlin bought backtick names and `it`.
- *"Agents write Kotlin more easily than Java."* Agents wrote those same 47 Java files, `MockVirtualThreadAwareServlet` plumbing included.
- *"No Kotlin stdlib on consumer classpaths"* was never an argument about tests at all — see D_pure_java_artifact's scope note.

What replaced them is an asymmetry: **Java is the only language that could ever be this repo's sole test language; Kotlin structurally cannot.** Two Java lanes are permanent. `:sampler`'s exit gates are one. The other is sharper — a test whose claim is *"migrated Java source still compiles and resolves this way"* has to be written in Java, because Kotlin's resolution rules are not javac's. `HTMLEditorKitJavaCompatTest` exists for exactly that reason: Kotlin does not resolve a nested classifier inherited through a superclass, so `HTMLEditorKit.ParserCallback` was inexpressible there. SB-Emulators' product is a Java-***source***-level compatibility surface, and a green Kotlin suite exercises the *bytecode* surface — it is not evidence that a migrator's Java compiles.

So the two-language split is permanent whatever we do, and only a full port to Java could ever retire it. That makes the choice a ratchet: every new Kotlin test file makes an eventual unification more expensive, every new Java one makes it cheaper. Defaulting new tests to Java keeps that option open at no cost and without a rewrite campaign.

**Alternatives.**
- *Keep Kotlin as the default.* Rejected: after the premise check it had no surviving rationale beyond inertia and backtick test names, and `@DisplayName` recovers the latter at one line per test.
- *Rewrite all 185 files now.* Rejected here, and **later adopted** by [D_kotlin_retired](#D_kotlin_retired) on an argument this entry never weighed: 48.7k LOC of working tests, months of work, zero migrator-visible gain, and every ported assertion is a chance to weaken one silently. Attrition reaches the same place for free if it ever matters. What flipped it was not a cheaper port but a *cost this entry did not price* — the two-language tax falls on the agents that write this repo, not on its readers.
- *Convert opportunistically whenever a file is touched.* Rejected: it turns every unrelated edit into a port review, and produces diffs where the behaviour change hides under the language change.

**Accepted limitation.** Two test languages indefinitely; contributors still read both. The build cost is bounded but was **not** free, and is easy to get wrong: kotlinc must run before javac, so each Kotlin-bearing module binds `kotlin:test-compile` to `process-test-sources`, not to `test-compile`. Maven injects `compiler:testCompile` *before* a POM-declared execution in the same phase, so with the naive binding a Java test that references any Kotlin test class fails to compile on a clean build — and **passes on a stale `target/`**, because the previous run left the Kotlin classes on javac's classpath. That is precisely the misleading-failure shape CLAUDE.md's *Building* section warns about, arriving from a new direction.

**Measured cost of a port** (three files, 2026-08-27, chosen at the Karibu-heavy / plain-unit / idiom-heavy sample points): see the case note in [ideas/decision-log-consolidation.md](../ideas/decision-log-consolidation.md).

---

<a id="D_kotlin_retired"></a>
## D_kotlin_retired. The Kotlin test corpus is ported to Java and kotlinc is deleted

**Decision.** All 180 Kotlin test files are ported to Java and the Kotlin toolchain is removed from the build: no `kotlin-maven-plugin` in any pom, no `kotlin.version` property, no explicit `kotlin-stdlib` test dependency, no `.mvn/jvm.config`. Every test in the repo is Java. Supersedes [D_tests_in_java](#D_tests_in_java)'s *decision* — its rationale is what made this affordable and stands unchanged.

**Rationale.** D_tests_in_java priced the port correctly (48.7k LOC, months, zero migrator-visible gain) and left one cost unpriced: **who pays the two-language tax.** SB-Emulators is written almost entirely by agents, and an agent handed a phantom Kotlin diagnostic spends its turn deciding whether the compiler or the tool is wrong. That cost is invisible in the suite (green either way) and invisible in the diff — it shows up only as an agent that seems slow. It was already recorded in three places before anyone named it as a cost: the `sourceDirs` block existed *purely* so kotlinc could parse Java it does not compile; `ideas/awt-widgets.md` carries two Kotlin-only shadowing footguns (`vaadinx.awt.List` vs `kotlin.collections.List`; a package-private field shadowing its own accessor pair) that have no Java analogue; and D_tests_in_java's own accepted limitation is a build-order trap that *passes on a stale `target/`*.

The ratchet D_tests_in_java installed is what made the campaign cheap rather than heroic: by the time it ran, `:sampler`'s 47 Java tests had already proved Karibu-from-Java at scale, and `AbstractKaribuTest` was already in the Java lane.

**What the port cost, measured.** 24 shards of ~5 files, one commit each, 2026-08-28 → 2026-08-29. Line growth landed at the predicted 8–12%, almost all `@DisplayName`. **No test was dropped, merged or added: every module's test count is identical before and after** (`:emulators` 1,966, `:surrogates` 1,341) and every file's `@Test` count matched its Kotlin original — that pair of numbers is the whole safety net, and it is what made the per-file discipline checkable rather than aspirational.

**What it bought.** One test language; the `process-test-sources` phase-binding workaround and its stale-`target/` failure mode retired; the dual-lane `sourceDirs` hack gone; `.mvn/jvm.config` deleted and Surefire's `argLine` down to the `--add-opens` the loom runner needs; and no per-file question of which lane a new test belongs in. Nothing on a *migrator's* classpath changed — it was all test-scoped, and `karibu-testing-v10` still brings `kotlin-stdlib` transitively, which is fine: the goal was deleting the **compiler**, not the stdlib jar.

**Alternatives.**
- *Leave it to attrition* (D_tests_in_java's decision). Rejected: attrition never converges — the corpus only shrinks when a file is touched for another reason, and the tax is paid on every turn until the last file goes.
- *Convert opportunistically whenever a file is touched.* Rejected again, unchanged: it turns every unrelated edit into a port review and produces diffs where a behaviour change hides under a language change.

**Accepted limitation.** Three assertion-layer losses are real and permanent: `assertIs<T>` smart-casts where `assertInstanceOf` only *returns* the narrowed value (assign it), `val` → `var` unless every local is written `final var`, and `String?` → bare `String` turning compiler-required null guards into decorative ones. Two silent-behaviour-change hazards were hit and are worth knowing before any future port of this shape: **numeric literals crossing an overload set** (`SpinnerNumberModel(5L, …)` resolves to a `Double` model in Java and a `Long` model in Kotlin — box every argument), and **capture-after-super** (Java assigns an anonymous class's captured locals *after* the super constructor returns, so an override the super ctor calls sees `null`). The Karibu-from-Java audit those ports produced is in [emulators/architecture.md §"Reaching Karibu from Java"](./architecture.md#reaching-karibu-from-java); the per-shard findings are in the 24 `test(emulators): port batch N` commit bodies, which is where they are useful.

---

<a id="D_generated_stubs"></a>
## D_generated_stubs. Stubs generated by reflection helper; hand-finished as needed

**Decision.** A small throwaway Java program reflects over `javax.swing.*` classes and emits `vaadinx.*` skeletons with `onUnimplemented`-body methods. Real implementations are written by hand when the current scope needs them.

**Rationale.** Generating skeletons is mechanical; hand-writing each signature is waste. Generating complete implementations is not feasible — every class has unique semantics.

**Alternatives.**
- Hand-write every class from scratch — tedious.
- Generate full stubs plus attempted implementations — brittle, lossy.

**Accepted limitation.** Generator output is a starting point and may need manual cleanup (generic signatures, inner classes, protected members).

---

<a id="D_awt_peer_hooking_rejected"></a>
## D_awt_peer_hooking_rejected. Considered AWT peer hooking; rejected

**Decision.** Do not implement the emulation by plugging a custom `java.awt.Toolkit` and `java.awt.peer.*` implementations that route to Vaadin. Keep the `vaadinx.*` reimplementation approach.

**Rationale.**
- **Peers only cover heavyweight components.** `JFrame`, `Window`, `Dialog` have peers; `JButton`, `JLabel`, `JTextField` do not — they are lightweight and painted by Java code onto their parent window's peer via `paintComponent(Graphics g)`. Hooking peers gives us Frame lifecycle and raw event injection, but not Swing widgets.
- **Swing widgets render through `Graphics`.** Routing them to Vaadin via peers would mean implementing a `Graphics` that emits DOM (a rasterizer-to-HTML, huge scope) or subverting `UIManager`/`LookAndFeel` paint delegates to maintain a shadow DOM keyed on each component. Fragile; paint is called at unpredictable times.
- **It would pull `java.desktop` back in.** Real Swing would run inside the JVM — real `EventQueue`, focus manager, `BasicButtonUI` — exactly the headless/toolkit baggage D_own_awt_package was built to avoid. We want to get *away* from Swing internals: Vaadin event handling replaces `EventQueue`, not wraps it.
- **The motivation evaporates.** The only thing peer hooking would buy over `vaadinx.*` is binary drop-in (no import rewrite). D_import_swap_target already rules that out — users recompile, so the import swap is free.

**Alternatives considered.**
- Custom `Toolkit` + full peer set — rejected for the reasons above.
- `LookAndFeel` delegate swap (`BasicLookAndFeel` → `VaadinLookAndFeel`) — same problems, different seam; still runs real Swing.

**Accepted limitation.** None — the rejected approach would have been strictly worse given our other decisions.

---

<a id="D_whitelist_porting"></a>
## D_whitelist_porting. Whitelist porting: Component hierarchy + Component-touching interfaces only

**Decision.** The generator maps only an explicit whitelist of JDK classes to `vaadinx.*`: the `java.awt.Component` hierarchy (`Component`, `Container`, `Window`, `Frame`, …), the `javax.swing.JComponent` hierarchy (`JComponent`, `AbstractButton`, `JButton`, `JFrame`, …), and the interfaces whose signatures reference Component (`Icon`, `Border`, `LayoutManager`, `LayoutManager2`). Every other JDK type reference — data types, events, listeners, models — is preserved as its original `java.*` / `javax.*` form.

**Rationale.** `java.desktop` is on every classpath; we don't need to re-ship `Color`, `Font`, `Dimension`, `Graphics`, `ActionEvent`, `ListModel`, etc. Porting only what actually needs porting keeps the library surface small, keeps user code linking against familiar JDK types, and keeps the generator simple.

**Alternatives.**
- Package-prefix mapping (map everything under `java.awt.*` and `javax.swing.*`) — rejected: massive transitive closure of stub generation, most of which duplicates JDK types we're happy to reuse.
- Per-call manual porting — rejected: no clear rule, easy to drift.

**Accepted limitation.** Types that transitively reference Component (e.g. `ComponentEvent`, `RootPaneContainer`, `MenuContainer`) can't be reused and must be ported separately when we need them. Flagged per-case (D_event_port_policy covers events).

---

<a id="D_event_port_policy"></a>
## D_event_port_policy. Event reuse policy: ActionEvent reused, Component-related events ported wholesale

**Decision.** Reuse `java.awt.event.ActionEvent` and `ActionListener` unchanged, plus any event whose source is `Object` (these reuse cleanly). Port the entire Component-related event surface under `vaadinx.awt.event.*` as one-off scaffolding: `ComponentEvent`, `ContainerEvent`, `InputEvent`, `FocusEvent`, `KeyEvent`, `MouseEvent`, `MouseWheelEvent`, `WindowEvent`, `PaintEvent`, `HierarchyEvent`, `InputMethodEvent`, and their matching listeners + adapters.

**Rationale.**
- `ActionEvent`'s source is typed as `Object`; we fire `new ActionEvent(ourJButton, …)` and user code casts `(JButton) e.getSource()`. Works without porting.
- `ComponentEvent`'s constructor requires a `java.awt.Component` source, and `getComponent()` returns `java.awt.Component`. Our `vaadinx.awt.Component` is not castable to either. Any reuse would either fail at the constructor or silently hand out wrong components at the `getComponent()` call.
- The set of "events that reference Component" is finite and knowable; an earlier lazy-port stance added a recurring judgment call for every new slice ("does this one need porting yet?") that bought nothing. One-off scaffolding removes the question.
- Ported events extend `java.awt.AWTEvent` unchanged (reused per D_whitelist_porting since AWTEvent's source is `Object`). We do not re-root AWTEvent; that would be scope creep with no benefit.
- Ported events keep AWT's constant values verbatim (`COMPONENT_ADDED = 300`, `VK_ENTER = '\n'`, …) so bitmask/ID arithmetic carries across.

**Alternatives.**
- Port lazily, class by class, as each slice demands — rejected after hitting the judgment-call tax: every new listener became a "port it? defer it?" decision with no durable answer.
- Make `vaadinx.awt.Component` extend `java.awt.Component` — rejected by D_own_awt_package (headless/toolkit baggage).
- Reuse AWT event classes by wrapping with a fake `java.awt.Component` proxy — rejected: `getComponent()` would return the proxy, not our emulator.

**Accepted limitation.**
- `instanceof java.awt.event.ComponentEvent` (or any other AWT event class) returns `false` on our events. User code walking the AWT hierarchy must rewrite those `instanceof` checks to use `vaadinx.awt.event.*` — consistent with the D_import_swap_target import-swap rule.
- Firing is not yet wired for most of these events — the types exist so peer-originating events can eventually land on user listeners, but today most `process*Event` / `add*Listener` methods are still `onUnimplemented` stubs. The port gives us the rails; wiring Vaadin peer events to them is later work.
- `InputMethodEvent`, `HierarchyEvent`, `PaintEvent` are ported for completeness even though they have no realistic near-term user. Skipping them would reopen the "is it worth porting?" judgment call this decision is meant to close.

---

<a id="D_generator_own_module"></a>
## D_generator_own_module. Generator is its own subproject, not embedded in `:emulators`

**Decision.** The stub generator lives in a separate `:generator` Maven module, run via the `exec-maven-plugin`. Invoked via `./mvnw -pl generator compile exec:java -Dexec.arguments="…"`. Not published.

**Rationale.** The generator is most useful exactly when `:emulators` doesn't compile — every scope expansion is "generate new stubs, then watch `:emulators` fail to build until we hand-finish". A generator that depends on `:emulators` compiling is useless at that moment. Splitting it out gives us a build artifact we can always run.

**Alternatives.**
- Generator in `vaadinx.internal` of `:emulators` — worked initially but broke the moment `:emulators` broke. Rejected after hitting the chicken-egg in practice.
- Separate source set within `:emulators` — possible but more build complexity than a sibling module; no real upside.
- `/tmp` throwaway outside the repo — rejected for reproducibility; we'll run this many times as scope expands.

**Accepted limitation.** One extra module to carry, with its own `pom.xml`. Minor.

---

<a id="D_ehelper_statics"></a>
## D_ehelper_statics. Static helpers in `vaadinx.EHelper`, not on `Component`

**Decision.** `onUnimplemented` (and any future shared plumbing) lives as `public static` methods on a standalone `vaadinx.EHelper` class, not as instance methods on `vaadinx.awt.Component`. The generator emits `vaadinx.EHelper.onUnimplemented("ClassName", "methodName", args)` uniformly — no instance/static split.

**Rationale.** `vaadinx.awt.Component` is now itself generated from `java.awt.Component` (after D_whitelist_porting gave us the whitelist and we needed its full JDK method surface). Any hand-written helper on Component would be clobbered on the next regeneration. Extracting helpers to a separate class keeps Component freely regenerable.

**Alternatives.**
- Hand-write Component forever, without the JDK method surface — rejected: user code calling `button.setEnabled(false)` wouldn't compile.
- Post-generation merge (splice helpers back in after regenerating) — rejected: brittle and tool-dependent.
- Protected instance method on a hand-written `ComponentBase` with generated `Component extends ComponentBase` — workable but adds a class with no other purpose. `EHelper` is simpler.

**Accepted limitation.** Loss of runtime-class-name in log messages (the emitted string is the declaring class at generation time, not `this.getClass()`). Subclasses inheriting an unimplemented method log the ancestor's name. Acceptable — the log is a dev aid, not user-facing.

---

<a id="D_peer_emulator_mapping"></a>
## D_peer_emulator_mapping. 1:1 peer ↔ emulator mapping via `ComponentUtil.setData`

**Decision.** Every `vaadinx.awt.Component` constructor registers itself as data on its peer: `ComponentUtil.setData(peer, vaadinx.awt.Component.class, this)`, wrapped as `EHelper.onCreated(peer, this)`. The reverse lookup `EHelper.getEmulator(peer)` throws when the mapping is missing — an intentional invariant signal, not a violation of D_never_fail_on_gaps (that rule scopes to emulation incompleteness; this is an internal-plumbing invariant).

**Rationale.** `getParent()` and similar navigation methods need to return the `vaadinx.awt.Container` emulator for a peer's Vaadin parent. Constructing a fresh emulator on demand would yield two emulators for one peer, each with independent state (name, listeners, size, locale, component orientation, …). We guarantee one canonical emulator per peer, always looked up.

**Alternatives.**
- Nullable `getEmulator` returning `null` on miss — swallows programming errors. If something asks for the emulator of an unregistered Vaadin component, we want to hear about it loudly.
- External `WeakHashMap<Peer, Emulator>` — extra moving part, GC-timing uncertainty. `ComponentUtil` already gives us a per-peer data slot tied to the peer's lifecycle.
- Identity map keyed on `System.identityHashCode` — collision-prone, no upside.
- Fresh emulator on each `getParent()` call — the bug we're preventing.

**Accepted limitation.** Raw Vaadin components constructed outside vaadinx (e.g. a user manually adding a plain `com.vaadin.flow.component.button.Button` to a vaadinx container's peer) have no registered emulator. Methods that call `getEmulator(...)` will throw when they encounter them. Revisit if this pattern turns out to be common — options include lazy emulator synthesis or an `orElse`-style lookup variant.

---

<a id="D_layout_css_on_content"></a>
## D_layout_css_on_content. Layouts apply CSS to the Container's peer content element

**Decision.** Built-in `LayoutManager` implementations (`BorderLayout`, `FlowLayout`, `GridLayout`, `BoxLayout`, …) drive browser layout by writing CSS directly to `Container.peerContentElement()` — no extra Vaadin wrapper peer. Container-wide CSS (`display: grid`, `grid-template-areas`, …) is applied from `layoutContainer(Container)`; per-child CSS (e.g. `grid-area: north`) is applied from `addLayoutComponent(comp, constraint)`. Both go through `EHelper.applyContainerCss(container, …)`, which refuses to write if the peer content element isn't a `<div>` — logs ERROR via `EHelper.onUnsupportedPeerShape(...)` and returns.

**Rationale.**
- No wrapper peer keeps the DOM flat and avoids reparenting children when `setLayout(...)` swaps managers. `peerContentElement()` is already the redirection seam `JFrame` uses for its inner content Div, so the mechanism composes with existing subclasses.
- Dispatching from `layoutContainer()` matches Swing's own ordering: a user LayoutManager that overrides `layoutContainer` without calling `super` loses CSS — the same "override-breaks-it" contract Swing has on the Java side. Gives custom LayoutManager breakage a predictable failure mode.
- Per-child CSS in `addLayoutComponent` matches the Swing hook for "new child with this constraint".
- Centralising the Div check in `EHelper.applyContainerCss` means each layout impl doesn't re-implement peer-tag inspection. One place to tighten if we ever want to whitelist other peer types.

**Alternatives.**
- Dedicated Vaadin wrapper peer per layout type — adds DOM nodes, forces child reparenting on `setLayout` swap, buys nothing CSS can't already express.
- Apply container CSS eagerly from `Container.setLayout(mgr)` — shorter call path, but hides the custom-LayoutManager breakage (override without super would still get CSS) and diverges from Swing's dispatch order.
- Each layout impl checks the peer tag itself — inlines the same guard N times.

**Accepted limitation.**
- Setting a `LayoutManager` on a `JComponent` whose peer isn't a Div (e.g. `JButton`) produces no CSS layout: `onUnsupportedPeerShape` logs ERROR, children still get added under the peer but render however the peer chooses. Doing this in real Swing is also a bad idea; we don't pretend to make it work.
- User LayoutManagers that don't extend a built-in, or that override `layoutContainer` without `super`, get no CSS dispatch.

---

<a id="D_callswing_funnel"></a>
## D_callswing_funnel. All peer → Swing callbacks funnel through `EHelper.callSwing`

**Decision.** Peer→Swing callbacks funnel through `EHelper.callSwing` rather than calling `fire*` directly. The operative contract — coverage, re-entrancy, the `UI.getCurrent()` throw and its shutdown carve-out — is [R_callswing_envelope](../CLAUDE.md#R_callswing_envelope); this entry holds only why the envelope exists and what was rejected to get it.

**Rationale.**
- Blocking modal dialogs are the central migration problem (D_blocking_dialogs_deferred). Their solution needs a thread-boundary envelope around every listener entry point. Establishing the envelope now, while there's one listener in the codebase, is trivial — doing it after a dozen have accumulated is a grep-and-retrofit across every `addClickListener`, `addValueChangeListener`, `addFocusListener`, …
- The seam is load-bearing even without virtual threads: it's where `UI.getCurrent()` capture + restore will go (so Swing code under `callSwing` can rely on a current UI even once it runs on a different thread).
- Exceptions intentionally propagate. Vaadin's `ErrorHandler` is the proper escalation path for listener failures — apps configure it for a reason. Swallowing inside `callSwing` would pre-empt user-configured error handling and hide real migration bugs from operational logging. D_never_fail_on_gaps's never-fail stance scopes to our unimplemented stubs, not to user listener code that runs under them.

**Alternatives.**
- Each listener calls `fire*` directly — rejected. Thirteen listeners = thirteen places to update when vaadin-loom lands.
- A base-class template method on `vaadinx.awt.Component` — rejected. Not every Vaadin peer type we bind to has a neat listener-registration shape (click, value-change, focus, key, window-close all differ). A static helper keeps the call site shape flexible.
- Defer until vaadin-loom arrives — rejected. That's exactly the retrofit we're trying to avoid.

---

<a id="D_notify_from_attach"></a>
## D_notify_from_attach. `addNotify` / `removeNotify` are driven by Vaadin attach/detach, not Container walks

**Decision.** Every `vaadinx.awt.Component` subscribes its peer's `AttachListener` / `DetachListener` in the base constructor and fires `addNotify()` / `removeNotify()` from them via `EHelper.callSwing` (R_callswing_envelope). `Container.addNotify` / `removeNotify` therefore do **not** walk children — the peer cascade already delivers the callback to every descendant. `Window.dispose()` likewise does not call `removeNotify()` explicitly; detaching the Dialog element fires the subtree detach and drives `removeNotify` for free.

**Rationale.** In real AWT, `addNotify` / `removeNotify` bracket the period when a Component has a live native peer. Our peers are eternal (D_peer_ctor_injection), so the literal AWT trigger doesn't exist — but Vaadin's attach/detach lifecycle brackets the period when a peer is part of the live UI tree, which is the semantic analogue that matters to user code (subscribe to singletons while live, unsubscribe when gone). Vaadin fires attach/detach for every descendant of a subtree change, so the cascade we'd otherwise hand-walk in Container is already happening at the peer layer. Hooking it once in `Component` covers every subclass uniformly, pairs `Window.dispose` + user-initiated Dialog close + `Container.remove` under one mechanism, and supports dispose-then-reshow cycles (each `setVisible(true)` re-attaches and refires `addNotify`).

**Alternatives.**
- Keep `Container.addNotify/removeNotify` walking children and do nothing at the peer level — rejected. Only fires when something else calls `Container.addNotify`; in practice nothing does, so user overrides on a real-world migration never run.
- Walk children **and** hook peer events — rejected. Double-fires on every subtree change, with ordering interleavings that depend on Vaadin internals and would be fragile to guard with a "did-we-already-fire-this-cycle" flag.
- Hook only `Window`'s peer and rely on Container walks for children — rejected. Works for the initial show but breaks for `container.remove(child)` on a displayed Window, where AWT requires `child.removeNotify` to fire and there's no Window-level event to hook.

**Accepted limitation.** Calling `container.addNotify()` directly in user code no longer cascades into children — the walk is gone. Real apps don't call `addNotify` directly (it's AWT-internal plumbing), but a hand-written test that does will see only the direct target's override fire. Migration doesn't rely on this path; Karibu-based tests attach peers to the UI instead.

---

<a id="D_no_silent_improvements"></a>
## D_no_silent_improvements. Emulation targets Swing's contract exactly — no silent improvements

**Decision.** Swing's contract is reproduced verbatim rather than silently improved on, even where an honest reading produces behaviour users might call "broken" — mutating a `LayoutManager` setter has no visible effect until `container.revalidate()` is called, and so it has none here. The rule is [R_no_silent_improvements](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_silent_improvements), the upward cap that pairs with [R_best_effort_behaviour](../CLAUDE.md#R_best_effort_behaviour)'s downward one. This entry holds why the stance is absolute rather than case-by-case.

**Rationale.**
- Migrated apps rely on Swing's contract to reason about their own code. An emulator that auto-revalidates where Swing doesn't will appear to work under vaadinx and then subtly diverge when the app is later rewritten against real Vaadin (or, worse, when the app is tested against real Swing for regression). The whole value proposition of the project is "runtime emulation of the Swing API"; silent kindnesses erode that.
- The "just works" paper cut (forgetting `revalidate()` after mutating a LayoutManager) is one the migrator *already learned* while writing the Swing app in the first place. Reproducing the paper cut keeps the mental model intact; fixing it per-component teaches migrators the wrong lesson about what our emulation guarantees.
- R_layouts_close_enough (layouts are close-enough) and R_infra_not_surface (no half-infrastructure) remain the explicit carve-outs where browser reality forces us to diverge. Those are about *capability*, not *UX polish*.
- Users can still "improve" behaviour in their own code — the difference is that they opt in visibly, rather than getting a surprise when porting to a different Swing target.

**Alternatives.**
- Auto-revalidate LayoutManager setters (track installed containers via a weak set, revalidate on mutation) — rejected. The convenience wasn't worth the divergence and it would have quietly set a pattern that grew every time some other Swing-quirk surfaced.
- Opt-in "strict mode" vs. "lenient mode" flag — rejected. Two modes means two codebases of test coverage, and users can't reason about *which* behaviour their app will see without knowing the flag state.
- Per-case judgment call at the API — rejected. Every new component would reopen the question; the predictable stance avoids the judgment-call tax.

**Accepted limitation.** Migrated apps that relied on Swing quirks they never understood (forgetting `revalidate()`, relying on an unspecified dispatch ordering, etc.) will look equally broken under vaadinx. That's the point — the user sees the same behaviour they'd see under Swing, so fixes transfer in both directions. Documentation and R_match_swing_errors's `onUnimplemented` logs cover the cases where Swing *does* work but we can't yet.

---

<a id="D_sync_reads_raw_model"></a>
## D_sync_reads_raw_model. Internal emulator↔peer sync reads the raw model, never `getText()`

**Decision.** When the R_swing_is_truth emulator→peer sync needs the component's "current value," it reads the backing model directly (e.g. `document.getText(0, document.getLength())` for text components) rather than calling the public `getText()` accessor. The public accessor is a potential override seam for subclasses that want to transform what user code sees; the peer must see the untransformed data.

**Rationale.**
- **The example originally given here was fiction, and the rule survives it.** This entry was introduced (2026-04-22) citing `JPasswordField.getText()` as an override that "returns a run of `echoChar` instead of the cleartext password (Swing's guard against accidental logging)" — the false premise [SD_sjpasswordfield](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_sjpasswordfield)'s correction note records. The JDK's `getText()` returns cleartext; SB-Emulators' masking override was SB-Emulators' own invention, and it is gone. Nothing about the *rule* rested on that example being real: the sync must read the model because the public accessor is an override seam, whoever overrides it.
- Real example, now that the fictional one is retired: `JFormattedTextField`'s formatter — the public accessor shows `"$1,234.56"` while the model holds `1234.56`. Pushing the display string into the peer as its value would round-trip a formatted string back through the formatter on the next edit.
- The pattern generalises to any subclass that legitimately overrides a public getter for user-facing purposes (think `JFormattedTextField`'s formatter, or a future currency-input subclass that displays `"$1,234.56"` while storing `1234.56`). The public getter is *for* user code; the sync is *internal plumbing*. Mixing them couples "what the user sees" to "what Vaadin sees" in a way that each subclass would otherwise have to un-break.
- The inverse direction (peer → emulator) already reads from the event payload (`e.getValue()`), which is the peer's raw value — so the asymmetry was only on the outbound side.

**Alternatives.**
- Make the sync call `getText()` and require subclasses with user-facing transformations to override the sync too — rejected. The sync is protected state in JTextComponent; exposing it for override invites the same coupling the base class is trying to prevent, and every future subclass reopens the "did I remember to override both?" judgment call.
- Split the public accessor into `getText()` (user-facing, transform-aware) and `getRawText()` (internal) and call the latter from the sync — rejected. `getText()` is the JDK accessor; adding a parallel internal method is surface bloat. Reading the Document directly is the already-available path and doesn't add new API.
- Cache the last-written peer value and skip the sync if the Document's raw text equals the cache — rejected as a workaround for the wrong problem. It papers over the `getText` mismatch for the identity case but fails the moment an override actually transforms the value.

**Accepted limitation.** Subclasses that legitimately need to intercept the outbound sync (to *transform* what reaches the peer, e.g. forcing uppercase in the rendered input) can't do so by overriding `getText()` — they'd need a future hook on the sync itself. Not needed now; revisit when a migration target actually asks for it.

---

<a id="D_rootpane_holder"></a>
## D_rootpane_holder. `JRootPane` is a server-side holder, not a peer-DOM wrapper

> **Superseded by [D_rootpane_containment](#D_rootpane_containment).** The holder stance and the DOM flattening this entry decided are both reversed: `JRootPane` now *is* the containment, and the chain under it is the JDK's. What survives is the `setDefaultButton` Enter-shortcut design (still owned by the button's peer) and `JComponent.getRootPane()`'s parent walk. The rest is kept for the cross-references it carries.

**Decision.** `vaadinx.swing.JRootPane` is a plain `JComponent` that holds references to the content pane, layered pane, glass pane, and default button. It does **not** sit between `JFrame`'s Dialog peer and the content pane in the DOM — the flattening (`Dialog → contentPane`, no intermediate wrapper) stays. `JFrame.getRootPane()` lazily constructs a holder seeded with the existing content pane; `setDefaultButton` attaches its Enter shortcut to the *button's* peer (not to a root-pane-owned DOM node); `JComponent.getRootPane()` walks up `getParent()` until it finds the enclosing `JFrame`.

**Rationale.**
- The useful pieces of `JRootPane` for migrated code — `setDefaultButton`, `getContentPane`, `getLayeredPane`, `getGlassPane` — all work as server-side field accessors. They don't need a DOM counterpart to be functionally correct. The holder shape closes the four `getRootPane` / layered / glass / default-button WARNs without touching rendering.
- Going structural (insert a wrapper element between the Dialog and the content pane) would force reparenting every existing content pane, updating `EHelper.applyContainerCss`'s peer-content-element lookup, and re-verifying every layout CSS write that lands through `peerContentElement()`. Substantial churn for near-zero rendering benefit right now: we don't yet model layered/glass-pane overlay behavior in the browser (that's a separate deferred slice).
- Default-button wiring attaches the Enter shortcut's *lifecycle owner* to the button's peer, which already has the right semantics: the shortcut is active whenever the button is in the UI tree, and goes away when the button detaches. That matches Swing's "default button lives as long as the root pane" contract without needing the root pane to be in the tree — the button's own lifecycle does the work.
- Keeping the holder minimal preserves an upgrade path: when a migration target forces real layered/glass-pane rendering (popup positioning, modal focus trapping), we'll know the constraints and can reshape then, with the holder's existing field references as a seed.

**Alternatives.**
- **Structural port** — insert a `JRootPane` wrapper element between Dialog and content pane. Rejected: big DOM churn, no rendering benefit today, and the overlay behavior a structural port would enable is itself deferred.
- **Skip `JRootPane` entirely** — `getRootPane` returns null + WARN. Rejected: migrated forms widely use `frame.getRootPane().setDefaultButton(...)` for Enter-to-submit, and returning null NPEs on the `.setDefaultButton` chain.
- **Make `JRootPane` extend `vaadinx.awt.Container` but skip DOM attachment** — strictly less useful than the current choice (loses `JComponent`-level conveniences like client properties, border storage, InputMap/ActionMap).

**Accepted limitation.** Code that expects `JRootPane` to sit in the component hierarchy (e.g. `frame.getRootPane().getParent()` returning the `JFrame`) sees null or an unrelated ancestor. **The glass-pane half is superseded by [D_glasspane_structural](#D_glasspane_structural)** — `getGlassPane().setVisible(true)` is now a real structural busy-curtain. The **layered pane stays a holder**: `JLayeredPane.moveToFront/moveToBack` are no-ops and z-order doesn't render (D_glasspane_structural keeps this deferred — no consumer forces the content-pane reparenting a structural port would need).

---

<a id="D_emulator_surrogate_split"></a>
## D_emulator_surrogate_split. `:emulators` stays bare-minimum for components `:surrogates` will cover; throw on inputs the peer can't represent

> **Superseded going forward by [D_surrogate_first](#D_surrogate_first).** D_emulator_surrogate_split describes the stance under which JSlider + JSpinner first landed as bare-minimum emulators ahead of their surrogates, with `UnsupportedOperationException` at peer-type-mismatch boundaries. That carve-out is now closed (SJSlider via SD_sjslider, SJSpinner via SD_sjspinner) and D_surrogate_first reverses the ordering: new emulator components wait for their surrogate to land in `:surrogates` first, so the bare-minimum / UOE pattern does not recur. D_emulator_surrogate_split remains the reference for (a) the subproject split itself and (b) the pre-D_surrogate_first bare-minimum components still awaiting backfill.

**Decision.** SB-Emulators splits into two subprojects with complementary stances: `:emulators` targets 100% Swing API compatibility (emulator has-a Vaadin peer, this project's original bet) and `:surrogates` targets 100% Swing *functionality* coverage (surrogate is-a Vaadin component, written once, full Swing semantics). `:emulators` depends on `:surrogates` and uses a surrogate as the peer for any component `:surrogates` has covered; for components `:surrogates` has not yet covered, `:emulators` carries only a **bare-minimum** implementation — enough to clear the current exit gate, not a full port of the Swing surface. When a bare-minimum emulator *cannot* function on a given input because its chosen peer type is fundamentally wrong for it (historical example: pre-SD_sjspinner `JSpinner` constructed with a `SpinnerDateModel` while the peer was `IntegerField`, or `setValue` called with a non-Integer), it throws `UnsupportedOperationException` at the point of input (constructor, `setModel`, `setValue`) rather than silently running on a wrong peer. Once `:surrogates` ships the corresponding surrogate, `:emulators` swaps the minimal peer for it and inherits full Swing coverage — the original `JSpinner` carve-out was closed this way by [SD_sjspinner](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_sjspinner).

**Rationale.**
- The two subprojects are complementary, not competitive: **`:emulators`** is 100% API compatibility (has-a Vaadin peer); **`:surrogates`** is 100% functionality coverage (is-a Vaadin component). Once `:surrogates` covers a component, its surrogate drops straight into `:emulators`' `peer` slot — `:emulators` keeps the Swing API surface, `:surrogates` delivers the behaviour underneath. Splitting them keeps each stance pure: an emulator author optimises for shape matching JDK Swing; a surrogate author optimises for reproducing Swing behaviour on a Vaadin component subclass.
- Porting the full Swing surface (Slider ticks + label dictionaries, all three `SpinnerModel` variants, editor composition) into `:emulators` *now* means tearing it out when the matching surrogate lands in `:surrogates`. Bare-minimum is honest about the transitional status and carries less to rip.
- Throwing at the input boundary is the right escalation when the emulator genuinely cannot function — this is what R_match_swing_errors's major-gap clause covers (formalized in D_gap_severity_triage). R_match_swing_errors's WARN-path survives degraded behaviour for minor gaps with no Vaadin counterpart; for peer-type mismatches that path isn't enough — a `JSpinner(SpinnerDateModel)` silently rendering as an `IntegerField` showing `0` is worse than crashing, because the migrator ships a wrong-but-running app and end users find the bug. A construction-time throw points the migrator at the exact line and offers two paths: switch to a supported model, or wait for the `:surrogates` coverage to land. Strictly more useful than silent corruption.
- The carve-out is narrow: only components `:surrogates` is expected to cover, and only at the construction / model-swap / value-type boundary where the peer type is fundamentally wrong for the input. Everything else (unimplemented paint flags, missing editor customisations, tick/label APIs) still follows R_match_swing_errors — `onUnimplemented` stubs, WARN, sensible defaults.

**Alternatives.**
- **Full Swing port for Slider / Spinner in `:emulators` now.** Rejected — volume of work for a surface we'll replace anyway once the surrogate lands. Migrators who need ticks or non-numeric spinners can wait for `:surrogates` coverage; in the meantime, the bare-minimum implementations exercise the JDK-model-reuse bet (the validation goal) without committing to the full surface.
- **Silent degradation via `onUnsupportedPeerShape` instead of throwing.** Rejected — `onUnsupportedPeerShape` is ERROR-logged but still returns, matching R_match_swing_errors's "never crash the host app" stance. For peer-type mismatches that stance is wrong: the emulator's public API (`getValue`, `setValue`, `ChangeListener`) will keep returning nonsense values from the wrong peer, and migrated code running on top of that produces running-but-broken apps where the bug surfaces far from the cause. Loud is better.
- **Seed `:surrogates` before touching `:emulators` for these components.** Rejected — `:emulators`' exit gate validates the JDK-model-reuse bet (that `SpinnerNumberModel` / `BoundedRangeModel` drive user code unchanged), which needs some implementation now. Bare-minimum Slider/Spinner in `:emulators` clear the gate without blocking on a surrogate being ready first. The surrogate work is scheduled as its own slice.
- **Pick a peer dynamically per model type** (IntegerField vs NumberField vs DatePicker vs …) so no input is unsupported. Rejected — `peer` is `final` by D_peer_ctor_injection (constructor injection, final field, no overridable methods at construction). Swapping the peer at `setModel` time would mean reparenting the DOM, rebuilding every listener subscription, and invalidating any caller that held a direct `peer` reference. The cost is large and the cases it would serve (migrated apps with non-numeric spinners) are exactly the ones a proper surrogate will solve cleanly.
- **Merge `:emulators` and `:surrogates` into one subproject.** Rejected — the two stances pull in different directions (API matching vs. behaviour matching), and the peer-swap handoff works precisely because the surrogate is a bare Vaadin component with no knowledge of the Swing API surface above it. Keeping them separate preserves that discipline and avoids accidental coupling.

**Accepted limitation.** Components whose bare-minimum implementation is still active (no matching surrogate yet) get loud `UnsupportedOperationException` at their respective input boundaries. Currently closed: JSlider (via SJSlider, SD_sjslider — non-tick/label surface now routes through the surrogate) and JSpinner (via SJSpinner + LongField, SD_sjspinner — all JDK `SpinnerModel` variants now work through the same API; the pre-SD_sjspinner UOE boundary is gone). Still deferred: Slider ticks/labels/paintTrack(false)/labelTable (blocked upstream on [vaadin/flow-components#9181](https://github.com/vaadin/flow-components/issues/9181) — field-round-trip + WARN, not UOE) and JSpinner custom editors (`JFormattedTextField` port outstanding — WARN, not UOE). Loud rather than silent wherever the rule still applies, so migrators see the gap immediately. Per-class javadoc flags the "bare minimum; full coverage pending `:surrogates`" stance for components the rule still governs.

---

<a id="D_surrogate_first"></a>
## D_surrogate_first. Surrogate-first policy for new emulator components (supersedes D_emulator_surrogate_split's bare-minimum stance going forward)

**Amended by [D_emulator_owned_state](#D_emulator_owned_state): the emulator is not a delegating shell.** It lands over its surrogate holding the JDK's state and running the JDK's bodies, with the surrogate as its renderer; the ordering and the completeness gate below stand.

**Decision.** Going forward, no new emulator component lands in `:emulators` until its matching surrogate exists in `:surrogates` and is **fully implemented within R_vaadin_first's capability cap**. The emulator then lands as a thin delegating shell over the surrogate — the SJSlider / SJSpinner post-SD_sjslider/SD_sjspinner shape generalised. `:surrogates` evolves in concert with `:emulators`, driving ordering within the current component scope on its own priorities (coverage value, reuse potential, design readiness) rather than running a parallel deferred-list. Surrogate gaps are either closed in-scope or properly classified per [D_gap_severity_triage](#D_gap_severity_triage) sub-bucket (a)/(b)/(c) — never carried as "we'll get to it." The long-running ambition is a surrogate for every existing emulator, so that every emulator eventually becomes a thin delegating shell over its surrogate.

**Rationale.**
- The fat-surrogate / thin-emulator split worked cleanly for JSlider and JSpinner post-SD_sjslider/SD_sjspinner — the emulators thinned down to ~170–330-LoC delegating shells with all substantial behaviour migrated into the surrogate. Generalising the pattern means every new component starts at that end-state on day one rather than going through a bare-minimum stage that gets ripped out when the surrogate lands.
- D_emulator_surrogate_split's original rationale — "bare-minimum in `:emulators` validates the JDK-model-reuse bet faster than waiting for a surrogate" — was specifically tied to an early exit gate. That gate is cleared; `BoundedRangeModel` / `SpinnerNumberModel` / `SpinnerDateModel` / `SpinnerListModel` all drive user code unchanged through SJSpinner. There is no remaining gating reason to keep landing bare-minimum emulators.
- Avoids concrete rework: SJSlider's landing tore out most of `:emulators.JSlider`'s body; SJSpinner's landing tore out `:emulators.JSpinner`'s D_emulator_surrogate_split boundary validation and peer plumbing. Surrogate-first lets the emulator land in its final shape.
- Keeps D_emulator_surrogate_split's UOE-at-input-boundary stance narrower: under D_surrogate_first, that pattern is a transient property of one already-landed batch of emulators rather than a recurring carve-out for every new component.
- Preserves the architectural discipline D_emulator_surrogate_split established: surrogates stay unaware of the Swing API surface above them; emulators still hold the Swing shape. D_surrogate_first is about *ordering* + *completeness gate*, not about the split itself.
- The "fully implemented within R_vaadin_first's cap" gate (added to D_surrogate_first's decision text) closes a velocity-driven escape hatch: under the original D_surrogate_first wording, surrogates could land partial and accrue a separate cross-cutting deferred-list (browser-side keyboard-action dispatch, SAncestorEvent, TitledBorder rendering, layout CSS in `:surrogates`) parallel to whatever `:emulators` was working on. The slow-and-methodical tempo retires that escape hatch — surrogate gaps are either capability-gap closure or properly R_match_swing_errors-classified, never just "deferred."

**Alternatives.**
- **Keep D_emulator_surrogate_split's bare-minimum-first stance for future components.** Rejected — its original rationale no longer applies, and the rework cost is concrete and measurable (SJSlider / SJSpinner both tore out substantial bare-minimum code).
- **Backfill surrogates for every existing emulator before any new `:emulators` work.** This is directional: capability-gap closure on existing emulators + surrogates clears before the new-component scope (JComboBox, JMenuBar, JTable, …) starts. The backfill surrogates all landed (SFrame / SJButton / SJRootPane / SJLabel / SJToggleButton / SJCheckBox / SJPanel / SJTextField + JTextComponentMixin / SJPasswordField / SJTextArea), each sequenced on `:surrogates`' own priorities.
- **Restrict the policy to components with non-trivial behaviour (exempt JLabel-shaped leaves).** Rejected — the cost of defining "trivial" and policing the boundary is higher than the cost of writing a thin surrogate for a simple component. Uniform policy is cheaper than a case-by-case exemption.

**Accepted limitation (resolved).** Existing bare-minimum emulators that predated D_surrogate_first (JButton, JPanel, JLabel, JTextField, JPasswordField, JTextArea, JCheckBox, JToggleButton, JFrame, JRootPane) all backfilled; each emulator now has a corresponding surrogate. SJButton shipped in its planned shape; capability gaps it left behind (plain `setIcon` etc.) closed as follow-up items, not as reopens.

---

<a id="D_gap_severity_triage"></a>
## D_gap_severity_triage. Incomplete emulation splits by severity: minor sub-buckets WARN, vaadin-loom rescue throws

**Decision.** [R_match_swing_errors](../CLAUDE.md) codifies the rule; D_gap_severity_triage records the reasoning. Two umbrellas:

**Minor / WARN.** Incomplete emulation calls `vaadinx.EHelper.onUnimplemented` — logs WARN, returns a sensible default, never throws. Minor gaps split into three sub-buckets that share the WARN behaviour but differ in actionability per migrator:

- **(a) Blocked-upstream-deferred.** We'd implement if upstream landed the API. Canonical case: SJSlider tick / label / track rendering blocked on [vaadin/flow-components#9181](https://github.com/vaadin/flow-components/issues/9181). The migrator's affordance: file the upstream too, or wait. Per-component log entries name the upstream issue.
- **(b) Permanently-deferred-by-policy.** Out of project scope; won't return to scope. Examples: user-authored paint via `Graphics` (`paintComponent`, custom-painted components), `JTable` cell editors as faithful in-cell swap (we'll ship click-opens-popover instead), `JApplet`, Look-and-Feel dispatch. The migrator's affordance: rewrite this part of the app for Vaadin idioms before migration completes; we won't fix this. CLAUDE.md §"Current scope" lists the canonical permanent-out-of-scope set.
- **(c) R_vaadin_first drop-and-WARN.** No upstream blocker, no policy bar, but [R_vaadin_first](../CLAUDE.md) says "no shadow cache for round-trip alone" — these are setters where Vaadin has no counterpart for the JDK contract and round-trip alone isn't a goal. Canonical case: `AbstractButton`'s six state-conditional icon setters, four alignment setters, four visual flags ([SD_sjbutton](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_sjbutton)). Migrator's affordance: rewrite to use a property Vaadin can render (e.g. plain `setIcon(Icon)` instead of `setSelectedIcon`). May graduate to a real implementation if a Vaadin counterpart materialises.

The three sub-buckets all flow through `EHelper.onUnimplemented` today and look the same in the WARN log; the split is for design-time triage and per-slice documentation, not for runtime dispatch.

**Major / throw — enumerated cases, not a general rule.** Throw fires for two specific cases today; the trigger is intentionally an enumeration (preserves judgment for future additions) rather than a unified principle:

1. **vaadin-loom rescue of a Swing-deadlock.** Canonical: `SwingWorker.get()` called from the EDT, `invokeAndWait` from the EDT. Real Swing deadlocks; vaadin-loom's VT-park can silently turn the deadlock into a successful continuation, steering user code into state branches the migrator never tested and never could have tested under Swing.
2. **`EXIT_ON_CLOSE` close-attempt on a JFrame.** Canonical: a user-driven close on a JFrame whose `defaultCloseOperation == EXIT_ON_CLOSE`. Real Swing terminates the JVM; log-and-noop leaves the migrator's intent (terminate) silently ignored — observable reality (app still running) diverges from Swing's behaviour at program-lifetime scope. **Resolution split by strategy ([D_jframe_as_route](#D_jframe_as_route)).** DialogStrategy (regular JFrames, Dialog peer) keeps the throw — that stance is permanent for that path. InlineStrategy (`@MainWindow` JFrames, Div peer) routes EXIT_ON_CLOSE through `dispose()` instead, and the session then ends the way any last-window dispose ends it ([D_auto_shutdown](#D_auto_shutdown)) — the typical Quit-menu shape (`frame.dispose()` relying on JVM-auto-exit) maps onto session-scope termination *because that is what the JVM-auto-exit it relies on does*, and the throw site (peer-originated Dialog close) doesn't exist in the InlineStrategy path. Log-and-noop remains rejected for either path. See [D_close_operation_dispatch](#D_close_operation_dispatch).

In both cases throw — preferably the same exception type Swing would throw under the equivalent observable failure (typically `IllegalStateException` with a pointer-at-cause message; not a new vaadinx-internal exception type). The throw trigger does NOT cover R_layouts_close_enough layout divergence (close-enough), dummy bounds from the layout-dispatch model, R_vaadin_first drop-and-WARN setters, or blocked-upstream visual flags — all of those are minor gaps under the WARN umbrella, even though their observable post-condition isn't one Swing would produce. The implicit pattern across the two enumerated cases: silent noop on a *large-scope directive* (program-lifetime: terminate-or-not, deadlock-or-not) where the migrator's mental model would diverge from observable reality at program-level. R_layouts_close_enough/R_vaadin_first small-scope per-component divergences continue under WARN. Future additions land case-by-case as they surface.

**Triage baseline.** When a gap surfaces, decide at design time which sub-bucket it falls in. Calibrate "is this gap acceptable?" against **a typical CRUD app** (list view on JTable + detail form with text/checkbox/combo/spinner + confirm/error dialogs + menubar) — not against [`:sampler`](../sampler/description.md)'s testbed scope (Sampler IN includes things like JColorChooser, JDesktopPane that aren't part of the typical-app baseline) and not against a specific JLawyer-shaped migration target (recalibration happens when such a target is taken on). Err inclusive when triaging marginal cases; the cost of false-omission (dropping something CRUD-typical needs) is higher than false-inclusion (building something CRUD-doesn't-need).

Extends [D_never_fail_on_gaps](#D_never_fail_on_gaps)'s "throw where Swing throws" along an additional axis: we also throw when a vaadinx-only mitigation would push the migrated program into a trajectory the original Swing program could never reach.

**Rationale.**
- The product's value proposition is *runtime emulation of the Swing API*, as articulated in [D_no_silent_improvements](#D_no_silent_improvements). A `worker.get()` that would deadlock in Swing and "magically works" under vaadinx is exactly the silent-improvement pattern D_no_silent_improvements rejects — worse here, because the rescued continuation can steer user code into state branches the migrator never tested and never could have tested under Swing.
- The pre-refinement wording of D_gap_severity_triage read "any state impossible under real Swing" as the throw trigger. That's too broad: R_layouts_close_enough layout divergence (a Vaadin-rendered panel doesn't pixel-match Swing), the dummy `getBounds() = (0,0,0,0)` carve-out, every R_vaadin_first drop-and-WARN setter, and every blocked-upstream visual flag all produce post-conditions Swing wouldn't produce. Throwing on all of them would force every migrated app to crash on startup. The narrow "vaadin-loom rescue" reading is what actually makes the rule operational; this entry tightens the wording to match.
- R_match_swing_errors's WARN-and-continue path is durable because it scopes to *gradual* incompleteness — the migrator watches WARN logs, reasons about what's missing, plans a fix. That reasoning model breaks down when the "incompleteness" is a deadlock silently re-routed into a live-but-Swing-impossible continuation. The migrator debugging such behaviour has no signal that their code has been re-routed.
- D_never_fail_on_gaps already carves out the case where *Swing* throws — we throw too. D_gap_severity_triage is the natural generalisation: we also throw where Swing would deadlock (a crash-equivalent for the migrated app, and also a latent bug the migrator can fix in the migrated code the same way they'd fix it under Swing).
- Fail-fast surfaces latent Swing bugs (EDT-calling-`worker.get()`, infinite `invokeAndWait`) *as if the app had been run under Swing* — preserving the mental model the migrator reasons in. The fail-fast message should name the cause so the fix is obvious ("`SwingWorker.get()` called from the EDT; this would deadlock under Swing — dispatch asynchronously or move the call off-EDT").
- The three minor sub-buckets share the WARN behaviour but encode different design intents. Per-slice docs (each `D*` / `SD*` entry that defers something) tag which sub-bucket the gap falls in; over time the union of those tags is the project's deferral list. Eventually that list could be consolidated into a single index, but the per-decision split is the source of truth — consolidation is documentation hygiene, not a separate rule.

**Alternatives.**
- **Use vaadin-loom to rescue the stuck call.** Rejected per D_no_silent_improvements. Silent improvement; steers migrated code into untested state branches; breaks "emulation targets Swing's contract exactly."
- **WARN-and-continue without throwing.** Right for tiny incompleteness; wrong for deadlock-equivalents. Either the continuation deadlocks for real (UI freezes forever — same as Swing, but we could have surfaced the cause) or some mitigation silently changes observable program behaviour. Both are worse than a loud throw with an explanatory message.
- **Throw on every "Swing-impossible observable state."** Pre-refinement reading of D_gap_severity_triage. Rejected — would force throws on R_layouts_close_enough layout divergence, R_vaadin_first drop-and-WARN, every blocked-upstream visual flag. The narrow "vaadin-loom rescue" trigger is what actually makes the rule operational without crashing every migrated app.
- **Introduce a new dedicated exception type** (`VaadinxBehaviourDivergence` or similar). Considered and rejected — the exception semantics should match what Swing would throw where possible, and invent a new type only where none fits. The migrator debugging the throw wants the stack trace to read like a Swing bug, not like a vaadinx-internal novelty.
- **Single-bucket minor gaps (no a/b/c split).** Rejected — the three sub-buckets give migrators different actionable affordances (file upstream vs rewrite app vs wait for slice). Lumping loses the signal even though all three flow through the same `EHelper.onUnimplemented` runtime path.

**Accepted limitation.** Apps that happened to run fine under Swing *because* their latent deadlock path never fired at runtime (but the code is reachable under different input) may throw earlier under vaadinx when the path fires for the first time. That's arguably a feature — a latent bug becomes observable — but it's a behavioural divergence from "runs on Swing; let's get it running on vaadinx." Fail-fast messages name the cause so the fix is obvious and transfers cleanly back to the Swing codebase too.

The triage baseline calibrates against an *imagined* CRUD-shape app today (the CRUD baseline is conceptual until a real CRUD-shaped target ships). False-omission — dropping something CRUD-typical depends on — is bounded but real; discovered late, the fix is to re-implement the dropped surface and pull it off the deferral list. The asymmetric cost (false-omission worse than false-inclusion) is why the rule says err inclusive on marginal calls.

---

<a id="D_icon_rendering"></a>
## D_icon_rendering. Icon rendering Path 1 — `ImageIcon` → Vaadin `Image` via the surrogates SHelper, both layers funnel through it

**Decision.** Closes the SD_sjbutton R_vaadin_first-trim around `AbstractButton.setIcon(Icon)`. Three pieces:

1. **Port `vaadinx.swing.ImageIcon`.** Implements `vaadinx.swing.Icon`; holds a `javax.swing.ImageIcon` delegate so all the JDK construction shapes (filename, byte[], URL, java.awt.Image, …) plus the `getImage` / `getDescription` / `getImageLoadStatus` / `getImageObserver` accessors come for free. `paintIcon` itself is a `EHelper.onUnimplemented` stub — Path 3 (offscreen-paint) is permanently deferred per [R_match_swing_errors sub-bucket (b)](#D_gap_severity_triage). A public `asJdk()` accessor exposes the delegate for the bridge + for migrators who need the JDK form.

2. **Bridge body lives in `com.vaadin.swingbridge.surrogates.SHelper`.** `imageIconToVaadinImage(javax.swing.ImageIcon)` allocates a `BufferedImage` sized by `getIconWidth/Height`, draws the icon's `Image` onto it, encodes as PNG via `ImageIO.write`, and wraps the byte array in `new com.vaadin.flow.component.html.Image(bytes, "icon.png")` (the non-deprecated ctor — auto-derives mime from the suffix and installs an inline-disposition `DownloadHandler` under the hood). `toVaadinIconComponent(self, javax.swing.Icon)` is the single public entry point that dispatches: `null` → `null`, `ImageIcon` → bridge, anything else → `onUnimplemented` + `null`.

3. **Both layers funnel through it.** `com.vaadin.swingbridge.surrogates.swing.AbstractButtonMixin.setIcon(Icon)` calls `EHelper.toVaadinIconComponent` and pushes the result to `Button.setIcon(Component)` when the peer is a `Button` (no-op WARN otherwise). `vaadinx.swing.AbstractButton.setIcon(vaadinx.swing.Icon)` calls `vaadinx.EHelper.toVaadinIconComponent`, which type-tests for `vaadinx.swing.ImageIcon`, calls `asJdk()`, and forwards to the surrogate-layer bridge — `:emulators → :surrogates` reuse direction matches SD_shelper_statics.

**PCE shape.** Differs by layer per the stage-2 / stage-3 API split (CLAUDE.md §"Migration arc"):

- *Emulator (`vaadinx.swing.AbstractButton`):* fires `"icon"` PCE with `vaadinx.swing.Icon`-typed values — the field shadow round-trips, so old/new are both honest JDK Icon refs.
- *Surrogate (`AbstractButtonMixin`):* fires `"icon"` PCE with `com.vaadin.flow.component.Component`-typed values per [R_vaadin_first](../CLAUDE.md). The surrogate doesn't shadow-store the user's `Icon` ref (R_vaadin_first forbids round-trip-only state), so the PCE values come from the Vaadin Button's own slot: `oldValue = btn.getIcon()` before write, `newValue` = the post-conversion Image. PropertyChangeListeners that need JDK-Icon-typed values must register on the emulator layer.

**Rationale.**
- **Port `vaadinx.swing.ImageIcon`** despite [D_whitelist_porting](#D_whitelist_porting)'s "interfaces only, classes preserved as JDK." `javax.swing.ImageIcon` implements `javax.swing.Icon` (paintIcon takes `java.awt.Component`); `vaadinx.swing.Icon`'s paintIcon takes `vaadinx.awt.Component`. Without porting ImageIcon, post-import-swap user code calling `new ImageIcon(...)` (which under D_import_swap_target's import-swap rule binds to `vaadinx.swing.ImageIcon`) wouldn't compile. The port is mechanical (delegate to JDK ImageIcon for state + loading + observer wiring; only paintIcon's signature differs). Treat D_whitelist_porting as listing the *minimum* port surface, not a prohibition — if a JDK class must be ported because the import-swap rule would point user code at it, the port lands. ImageIcon is the first such case; future ones (e.g. specific `*Border` impls if they grow Component-touching members) follow the same logic.
- **Bridge in `:surrogates.SHelper`, not `:emulators.EHelper`.** The surrogate side needs the bridge (it pushes Vaadin Image directly to its peer); the emulator side delegates. Putting the body in `:surrogates` keeps the cross-module direction `:emulators → :surrogates` ([SD_shelper_statics](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_shelper_statics)) — the alternative ("body in emulators, surrogate calls up") would invert the dependency arrow, which we've ruled out. The emulator-side wrapper is just dispatch glue (`vaadinx.swing.ImageIcon` instanceof check + `asJdk()` unwrap).
- **`new Image(byte[], "icon.png")` ctor, not the deprecated `Image(StreamResource, alt)`.** Vaadin 24.8 deprecated `StreamResource` in favour of `DownloadHandler`; the byte-array ctor wraps `DownloadHandler.fromInputStream(...)` and sets `Content-Disposition: inline` automatically. Encoding happens once at call time; the `DownloadHandler` replays the same byte buffer on every fetch.
- **Path 1 vs Path 2 vs Path 3 — only Path 1 lands here.** Path 2 (UIManager keys → VaadinIcon) is small and high-value but coupled to JOptionPane / FileChooser surfaces that aren't in this slice; it lands alongside JOptionPane. Path 3 (`paintIcon` to a server-side Graphics2D) overlaps the user-authored-paint stance and is permanently deferred per [R_match_swing_errors sub-bucket (b)](#D_gap_severity_triage). The non-`ImageIcon` branch in `toVaadinIconComponent` WARNs and clears the slot — drop-and-document for now, replaceable with the Path 2 lookup table when it lands.
- **JLabel wiring deferred to SJLabel backfill.** JLabel's peer is a Vaadin `Span`; `Span.setText` calls `Element.setText` which removes all child nodes, so a naive prepend-Image strategy is fragile. Wiring the icon onto a Span-shaped DOM is part of the SJLabel surrogate's design, not an in-place patch on the existing emulator. JLabel's `setIcon` keeps its field round-trip + PCE; only the browser-side rendering is missing.
- **Six state-conditional icon setters stay R_vaadin_first drops.** Per [SD_sjbutton](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_sjbutton): Vaadin Button has no per-state icon slot (no `pressedIcon` / `selectedIcon` / `disabledIcon` / etc. concept), and Path 1 doesn't change that. Migrated code wanting per-state icons either rewrites to use plain `setIcon` + reactivity, or rebuilds the per-state behaviour in user code (Path 2's UIManager lookups don't help here either).

**Alternatives.**
- **Don't port `vaadinx.swing.ImageIcon`; require migrators to use `vaadinx.swing.Icon` directly.** Rejected — breaks the import-swap contract. Migrated code that says `new ImageIcon("logo.png")` is the canonical case for icon assets; forcing migrators to either find a different class or write their own Icon impl is not the bargain D_import_swap_target promises.
- **Port `vaadinx.swing.ImageIcon` as a fresh implementation (no JDK delegate).** Rejected — ImageIcon's loading semantics (URL fetch, MediaTracker observer, async paint completion via `imageUpdate`) are tedious to reimplement and add no value over delegating to the JDK class. The delegate ctor lets the surrogate-layer encoder hand back the raw `javax.swing.ImageIcon` for the byte extraction without needing to re-bridge our own state.
- **Push bytes directly without the `BufferedImage` round-trip.** Considered for `ImageIcon(byte[])` ctors specifically (the user already gave us bytes). Rejected — `javax.swing.ImageIcon`'s `getImage()` always returns a `java.awt.Image` after the ctor processes the input; we'd need a side channel to retain the original bytes for that one path while still BufferedImage-encoding for the URL/filename/Image variants. The unified BufferedImage path is one code path for all variants and re-encodes one time when `setIcon` is called, not on every render.
- **Cache the encoded PNG bytes per ImageIcon instance.** Considered, deferred. The current implementation re-encodes on every `setIcon` call. For a button rendered once and never re-iconed, that's one encode. For a button whose icon is swapped on hover via state-conditional setters, the state-conditional setters drop-and-WARN today (no real swap), so caching has no payoff. If Path 2 / Path 3 land and a hot setIcon-loop emerges, attach a `WeakHashMap<javax.swing.ImageIcon, byte[]>` to the surrogate SHelper at that point, not now.
- **Surrogate-side store for the JDK Icon ref so PCE fires JDK-Icon-typed.** Rejected per [R_vaadin_first](../CLAUDE.md) — adding a `Store` field for round-trip alone is what R_vaadin_first explicitly forbids. The Vaadin-typed PCE on the surrogate side is the documented R_vaadin_first lossy direction; users wanting JDK-typed PCE register on the emulator layer.

**Accepted limitations.**
- **Non-`ImageIcon` `Icon` impls drop with a WARN today.** A custom `paintIcon`-implementing class, a `vaadinx.swing.Icon` user subclass with its own raster, or a `UIManager.getIcon(...)` return value (`OptionPane.errorIcon` etc.) all reach `setIcon`'s WARN path today. Path 2 will close the UIManager-keyed subset; the truly-arbitrary case stays under R_match_swing_errors sub-bucket (b)'s permanent deferral.
- **JLabel icons are invisible in the browser.** Field round-trip + PCE work; the rendering doesn't. Migrators relying on `JLabel(icon)` constructors see the text but no image until the SJLabel backfill lands. WARN-free path though — no migration log noise.
- **PCE values diverge across layers.** Emulator fires JDK-Icon-typed; surrogate fires Component-typed. Migration convention: pick one layer and register listeners there. Code that bridges (registers on the emulator and casts the value to JDK Icon) keeps working unchanged after Path 1; code that registers on the surrogate sees Vaadin-typed values per R_vaadin_first.
- **`Image` + `BufferedImage` + `ImageIO.write` require a working `java.desktop` runtime.** All available headless on standard Java 21 deployments; flagged here so an exotic runtime environment that strips `java.desktop` (rare) knows the bridge needs it.

**Validation.** Surrogate test suite extended: `setIcon ImageIcon installs Vaadin Image on peer with no WARN per Path 1` + `setIcon null clears the peer icon and is silent` + `setIcon ImageIcon then null round-trips the slot` + `setIcon non-ImageIcon WARNs and clears the slot pending Path 2-3` + `setIcon fires icon PCE with Vaadin Component-typed values per R_vaadin_first`. Emulator test suite extended: `setIcon ImageIcon installs Vaadin Image on peer per Path 1` (end-to-end through Karibu — frame visible, peer's Vaadin `Image` reachable) + `setIcon null clears the peer icon slot`. Replaces the SD_sjbutton-era `setIcon null is silent no-op, non-null WARNs per R_vaadin_first` test (R_vaadin_first-trim assumption invalidated by Path 1).
