<a id="D_focus_property_registry"></a>
## D_focus_property_registry. `KeyboardFocusManager`'s bound properties — a per-UI registry fed by `FocusTracker`, and the three fires that stay refused

The last open item of the property-fan-out audit, and the one [D_reverse_fanout_rows](#D_reverse_fanout_rows) deferred rather than fixed: it found seven `(class, method, property)` rows on `KeyboardFocusManager` and concluded they were **one design question, not seven missing lines** — `addPropertyChangeListener` registered nothing, so every fire would have reached nobody and satisfying the diff would have changed nothing observable. This closes that question.

**Decision — the registry is per UI, in the UI's own data.** `PropertyChangeSupport` lives in `ComponentUtil` UI data (a private `Bound` holder), created on the first registration and torn down with the tab. A `PropertyChangeSupport` *field* on the class was the shape to avoid: both facades are process-wide singletons ([D_focus_managers](#D_focus_managers) — deliberately, so a migrator's `static final FocusManager FM = FocusManager.getCurrentManager();` is safe), so a field there would pool every session's listeners on one list and deliver every tab's focus change to all of them. That is the same cross-tab hazard the stateless-facade decision exists for, arriving through the listener list instead of through state. Per UI matches where the fact itself lives ([SD_focus_tracker](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_focus_tracker)).

**The fires come from the pointer's move, not from a setter.** The JDK fires these from `setGlobalFocusOwner` and friends, which SB-Emulators cannot: the browser owns focus, and SB-Emulators' `setGlobal*` mutators WARN. The transition that actually happens is `FocusTracker`'s pointer move, so `:surrogates` gained a listener seam ([SD_focus_owner_listener](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_focus_owner_listener)) and the emulator layer subscribes to it — the CLAUDE.md dependency rule's listener inversion, since the module direction forbids `FocusTracker` knowing what an emulator is. The subscription is installed lazily with the first listener, so a UI nobody listens on pays nothing, and the callback is wrapped in `EHelper.callSwing` ([R_callswing_envelope](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules)) because its far end is migrated app code that may open a modal dialog.

**Four properties fire, in the JDK's own order.** `focusOwner`, `permanentFocusOwner`, `focusedWindow`, `activeWindow` — window activation first, then the owner pair, which is the sequence `DefaultKeyboardFocusManager` produces (`WINDOW_ACTIVATED` → `WINDOW_GAINED_FOCUS` → `FOCUS_GAINED`). A move within one window fires only the owner pair, because `firePropertyChange`'s guard drops the unchanged window values. `defaultFocusTraversalPolicy` fires from its own setter, and its delivery is narrower than the value it announces: the field is process-wide, so another tab's listeners miss a change they can read back. Per-UI is the widest delivery a tab-scoped registry can honestly offer.

**No `null` intermediate, and this is the sharp call.** The desktop delivers a focus move as two halves — `FOCUS_LOST` fires `focusOwner (old, null)`, then `FOCUS_GAINED` fires `(null, new)` — so reproducing the JDK's *event count* means synthesizing the null step. **Rejected**, on the reasoning [D_owed_events](#D_owed_events) applied to `JPopupMenu.setVisible`: SB-Emulators' pointer moves atomically, so a listener reading `getFocusOwner()` back inside its own callback would see the new owner while holding an event that says `null`. Firing a transition the getter denies is the failure mode that decision refused, and it is worse here than a missing intermediate, because a listener's own read is the natural thing to do in a focus callback. The pair still arrives whenever the pointer genuinely passes through `null` — a blur into empty space followed by a click elsewhere — which is the desktop shape in the case where the desktop's shape is real.

**Three of the JDK's seven stay silent, each because its getter would deny the event.**

| property | why refused |
|---|---|
| `currentFocusCycleRoot` | no state behind it — `getCurrentFocusCycleRoot()` WARNs and answers `null` (D_focus_managers tier 3) |
| `managingFocus` | `setCurrentKeyboardFocusManager` does not swap the manager, so the event would report a handover that did not happen |
| the four `*DefaultFocusTraversalKeys` names | `getDefaultFocusTraversalKeys` answers the honest empty set; there is nothing to announce a change to |

**Vetoable properties stay declined** — `addVetoableChangeListener` still WARNs and registers nothing. The JDK vetoes *before* the change; here the browser has already moved focus by the time the server hears about it, so honouring a veto could only mean re-requesting focus on the loser, which is an **effect**, not the notification [R_decline_effect_only](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) owes. A registry that collected vetoable listeners and then ignored their vetoes would be strictly worse than the WARN.

**One R_match_swing_errors fix found in the same JDK body:** `setDefaultFocusTraversalPolicy(null)` now throws `IllegalArgumentException("default focus traversal policy cannot be null")`, as the JDK's does. SB-Emulators had stored the null.

**Validation.** `emulators/src/test/java/vaadinx/awt/KeyboardFocusManagerPropertyTest.java` (14 — the four-property fan-out and its order, the same-window subset, the cross-window pair through a `JDialog`, `clearFocusOwner`'s loss, the no-op re-focus, the read-back-inside-the-callback contract above, named-property registration, unregistration, both facades sharing one registry, per-UI isolation, the no-current-UI WARN, the policy fire plus its identity guard and null throw, the three silent properties, and the still-declined vetoable registry) plus `surrogates/src/test/java/com/vaadin/swingbridge/surrogates/FocusOwnerListenerTest.java` (6) for the seam. `FocusManagerTest.kt`'s two inverted claims are edited in place: the tier-3 WARN count now counts `addVetoableChangeListener` where it counted `addPropertyChangeListener`, and "no bound property is fired here" is gone — replaced by the Java suite above.

**Not browser-verified.** The fires ride `FocusTracker`'s pointer, whose browser-driven half is verified in SD_focus_tracker; what a real browser adds here is the `focusin`-driven path rather than the optimistic one, and both call the same `moveOwner`.

---

<a id="D_frameinit_shape"></a>
## D_frameinit_shape. The `*Init` constructors' remaining three lines — and why two of them land on deliberate nothings

**Decision.** `frameInit` / `dialogInit` / `windowInit` carry the JDK's bodies line for line, including the per-class asymmetry:

| line | `JFrame.frameInit` (:255) | `JDialog.dialogInit` (:640) | `JWindow.windowInit` (:260) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enableEvents(KEY \| WINDOW)` | ✓ | ✓ | — |
| `setLocale(JComponent.getDefaultLocale())` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `setRootPane(createRootPane())` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `setBackground(UIManager.getColor("control"))` | ✓ | ✓ | — |
| `setRootPaneCheckingEnabled(true)` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

The asymmetry is reproduced rather than regularised: a migrator's `setBackground` override must fire from a `JFrame` or `JDialog` constructor and **not** from a `JWindow`'s. This closes the last front of the [R_no_vaadin_in_api](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) limb-2 call-graph audit — the root-pane pair landed with [D_rootpane_containment](#D_rootpane_containment); these three lines are what that front deferred.

Skipped, each with a javadoc line saying so: the `isDefaultLookAndFeelDecorated()` branch (the guard already answers `false`, and L&F dispatch is permanently out per R_match_swing_errors sub-bucket (b)) and `sun.awt.SunToolkit.checkAndSetPolicy` (no peer lifecycle to set a policy on).

### `getDefaultLocale` answers the browser, and that is replication rather than improvement

`setLocale(JComponent.getDefaultLocale())` on every window would, read naively, pin every window to `Locale.getDefault()` — the **server's** locale — and make `Window.getLocale`'s browser preference (`UI.getLocale`, from Accept-Language) dead code, since the field is never null again. Every user of a multi-user app would then localise to whatever the host happens to run under.

So the browser preference **moves up**, from `Window.getLocale`'s orphan-catch into `JComponent.getDefaultLocale` itself: a current UI's locale, else the JVM default. This is faithful, not a carve-out from [R_no_silent_improvements](#D_no_silent_improvements) — real Swing scopes `getDefaultLocale` to an `AppContext`, i.e. **per app, not per JVM**, so answering per-UI is that scoping reproduced. Same argument, and the same analogue, that [D_window_registry](#D_window_registry) used to put the window registry in tab scope rather than reasoning from "a static is a static".

Two consequences worth knowing:

- **Every window's peer element now carries a `lang` attribute** — the DOM equivalent `Component.setLocale` already wrote, now reached during construction. It names the browser's language, which is the a11y-correct answer.
- **`Window.getLocale`'s orphan-catch stays live, for the AWT windows.** `vaadinx.awt.Window` / `Frame` have no `*Init` hook, so they never take an explicit locale and still bottom out in the catch. Deleting it as dead code would break them.

`JComponent.setDefaultLocale` keeps its WARN. It is not the write side of this getter: the value has nowhere to go that `getDefaultLocale` would read back, and a migrator overriding the per-user locale wants a real per-UI store rather than a mutation of the JVM default that leaks across unrelated code.

This also **converges with the surrogate layer**, which had already reached the same conclusion independently: `JComponentMixin.getDefaultLocale()` reads `VaadinSession.getCurrent().getLocale()` ([SD_vaadin_first_binding](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_vaadin_first_binding)'s default-locale row). Two differences remain, neither a disagreement:

- **Scope is finer here** — the emulator reads the **UI**'s locale, the surrogate the **session**'s, so a `ui.setLocale()` moves the emulator and not the surrogate. Left as is: the emulator side inherits `Window.getLocale`'s existing `UI.getLocale` read, and per-view code never sees both layers ([D_emulator_surrogate_split](#D_emulator_surrogate_split)).
- **The setter works there and WARNs here.** `JComponentMixin.setDefaultLocale` writes the session locale; the emulator's does not write the UI's. Deliberately not resolved on this front: `UI.setLocale` also drives Vaadin's own i18n (date pickers, component captions), where `JComponent.setDefaultLocale` in Swing does nothing but change what *later* components are born with. Making it a real write is a decision about that side effect, not a line this front is entitled to add (R_infra_not_surface).

### `Q_enableevents_meaningful` — DECIDED: `onNoop`, and `disableEvents` keeps its WARN

`Component.enableEvents` becomes a documented `EHelper.onNoop`; `disableEvents` stays `onUnimplemented`. The asymmetry is the whole answer, and it falls out of what unconditional dispatch actually grants:

- AWT's `eventMask` exists so `processEvent` can **skip** a category nobody asked for. SB-Emulators has no mask and `Window.processEvent` dispatches unconditionally, which **satisfies** any request `enableEvents` could carry — there is no gap, so there is nothing to report.
- `disableEvents` asks for the opposite and SB-Emulators cannot honour it: a migrator muting a category keeps receiving it. That is a real unmet expectation and stays a WARN.

**One honest caveat about what the edge buys.** `enableEvents` is `protected final` in the JDK and in SB-Emulators, so nobody can override it — limb 2's "a migrator's override silently never runs" argument does **not** apply here, and the call is reproduced for shape rather than for reachability. Stated rather than borrowed, because every other edge on this front does earn the limb-2 justification.

**And a tripwire, because the no-op rests on a property that a planned front would break.** "Unconditional dispatch grants every request" is true of SB-Emulators *today*. [ideas/awt-textfield.md](../ideas/awt-textfield.md) plans to reproduce the JDK's `eventEnabled` gate on `processTextEvent` / `processActionEvent` — and the moment any component gates dispatch on a listener being registered, `enableEvents(TEXT_EVENT_MASK)` becomes a request SB-Emulators silently drops and this `onNoop` becomes a lie of exactly the shape R_decline_effect_only exists to catch. A gate landing there must therefore either model the mask or revert `enableEvents` to `onUnimplemented`, and the second costs a WARN per `JFrame` / `JDialog` constructed — which is the whole reason the no-op was needed. Recorded in both places rather than left to be rediscovered.

### The WARN gate is what forced the design, on both lines

Both missing lines route through methods that were WARN stubs, so the verbatim JDK body emits **two self-inflicted WARNs per window constructed** and takes every Sampler `WarnInventoryTest` red. `onNoop` logs at DEBUG and does not feed `EHelper.warnHook`, which is the lever for `enableEvents`.

`setBackground` needed a different one, because `UIManager.getColor` must keep WARNing: a *migrator* reading an L&F key has a real unmet expectation, where SB-Emulators reading its own is noise. So a package-private `UIManager.controlColor()` returns what `getColor("control")` answers with no L&F installed — `null`, clearing the CSS so the theme shows through — and the public getter is untouched. Note what the null makes observable: `PropertyChangeSupport` dedupes `null → null`, so the call fires no event and stores nothing. Its **entire** observable effect is reaching a migrator's `setBackground` override, which is exactly the property this front exists to restore, and exactly why the line is worth having despite doing nothing on its own.

Rejected: downgrading `UIManager.getColor` to `onNoop` (most faithful call graph, but silences a real migrator signal), and giving `UIManager` a real `"control"` default (that is L&F, permanently out of scope).

> **Superseded on both counts by [D_theme_is_lookandfeel](#D_theme_is_lookandfeel).** That entry installs exactly the per-class table of Metal defaults this paragraph rejected, so `controlColor()` returns `ColorUIResource(238,238,238)` and `UIManager.getColor` answers from the table for the keys it covers. Two consequences land here: `frameInit`'s `setBackground` now stores a real colour and **fires** a `PropertyChangeEvent` (which real Swing does, so the "fires no event and stores nothing" note above no longer holds, and `WindowFrameInitTest` inverts deliberately); and the out-of-scope line *moves* rather than vanishing — a constant colour table is emulation of observable app state, while L&F **dispatch** stays permanently out. The rest of this entry — the `*Init` call order, the locale reasoning, `Q_enableevents_meaningful` — is unaffected.

### Validation

Full reactor `clean install` green; `:emulators` 1928, Sampler's `WarnInventoryTest`s at zero. **No existing assertion inverted** — the first front in this audit where none did, because the three lines add call-graph edges without moving any value a test had pinned.

`WindowFrameInitTest` (Java, 9 tests) pins what no value assertion can: a spy subclass sees `setLocale` → `createRootPane` → `setBackground` in the JDK's order from a `JFrame` constructor, `setLocale` alone from a `JWindow`'s, the browser locale landing on all three plus the `lang` attribute, and the AWT window still falling back through the orphan-catch. Two carry the WARN gate as a pair, deliberately: constructing all three windows captures **zero** WARNs, and `disableEvents` captures **one** — so the zero is a real zero rather than a harness that stopped listening.

<a id="D_instance_field_surface"></a>
## D_instance_field_surface. Instance fields were never swept, 88 protected JDK fields had been narrowed to private, and widening one rebinds Kotlin property syntax

[D_missing_constants](#D_missing_constants) swept `static final` fields and left `PublicConstantsTest` as the durable gate. It said so explicitly — "the rule is **all** public/protected `static final` fields, any type" — and `PublicConstantsTest` gates exactly `isStatic && isFinal`. **JDK *instance* fields were therefore ungated, and nobody had looked.** Found 2026-08-28 while re-checking `Q_gbl_fields` from the inventory probe: the question "we added constants, is `GridBagLayout` now inconsistent?" has the answer "not via constants — via a front the constants sweep defined itself out of".

The failure mode is D_missing_constants' own, and its sentence transfers verbatim: SB-Emulators' bodies reach for SB-Emulators' **own private copy**, so the build stays green, the behavioural suites are silent, and the break lands as a compile error in a migrator's subclass — the subclass [R_leaf_peer_lockdown](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) promises "works fine".

### The measurement: 216 fields, and the split is not random

`javap` every JDK class that has an emulator, take its public/protected non-static fields, compare against what the emulator declares:

| | n | who |
|---|---|---|
| carried faithfully (`protected`→`protected`) | 47 | `TableColumn` 11, `JTableHeader` 8, `DefaultTableColumnModel` 7, `TitledBorder` 6, `BevelBorder` 5, `EtchedBorder` 3, `DefaultCellEditor` 3, `TableColumnModelEvent` 2, `JSlider`/`JProgressBar.changeListener` |
| **narrowed to `private`** (fixed here) | **88** | `JTable` 17, `JOptionPane` 11, `JTree` 10, `JScrollPane` 7, `JInternalFrame` 7, `JSplitPane` 6, `JRootPane` 5, borders 7, `JComboBox`/`JScrollBar` 3 ea., `rootPane` pairs on `JFrame`/`JDialog`/`JWindow` 6, `DefaultTreeCellRenderer` 3, `Timer.listenerList`, `JLabel.labelFor`, `ButtonGroup.buttons` |
| absent | 83 | deferred; see the open half below |
| **widened `protected`→`public`** (fixed here) | 1 | `GridBagLayout.defaultConstraints` |

The fault line for the 88 correlates with *how the emulator was written*, and was never stated as policy: classes ported close to JDK source shape keep `protected` (the JDK's field **is** their storage), while hand-written peered emulators narrowed to `private` because the real state moved to the surrogate and the leftover field reads as an implementation detail. That is not sloppiness — it is what happens when state migrates to the peer and nobody asks whether the JDK's *access level* was part of the contract.

### `GridBagLayout` diverged in both directions at once, and each was the only one of its kind

- **Its four `public` hint fields** — `columnWidths` / `rowHeights` / `columnWeights` / `rowWeights` — are the **only** JDK public instance fields in the entire ported surface, and SB-Emulators carried none of them. That is exactly why the gap survived: there was no second class to look inconsistent against. They cost a GUI-builder app four compile errors per form (Matisse/WindowBuilder emit all four unconditionally), which is how the inventory probe hit them. Declared here as [R_decline_effect_only](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) in its plainest form: keep the state, decline the effect — and the declined effect is pixel track-sizing, which [R_layouts_close_enough](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) defers anyway. Nothing reads them; `layoutContainer` derives its CSS Grid tracks from the children's constraints as before.
- **`defaultConstraints` was `public` here and is `protected` in the JDK** — the surface's only widening, now matched. The comment that justified omitting the arrays asserted "JDK GridBagLayout exposes a few public fields (defaultConstraints, columnWidths, …)"; only the four arrays are public. **The omission rested on a misreading of the JDK it cited**, which is the more useful half of this finding: a comment stating what the JDK does is worth checking against `javap`, not against memory.

### The cost nobody would predict: widening rebinds same-package Kotlin property syntax

`protected` in Java also grants **package** access. The Kotlin test corpus lives in `package vaadinx.swing`, so the moment a field became `protected`, Kotlin stopped resolving `pane.contentPane = null` to the synthetic property (→ `setContentPane`) and started resolving it to the **now-visible field** — silently skipping the setter, its validation and its `PropertyChangeEvent`. 19 tests failed for this reason alone, in three flavours that name the risk precisely: a `setContentPane(null)` that no longer threw, a `defaultButton` PCE that no longer fired, and slot setters that no longer reached `Container.addImpl`.

Fixed by rewriting those assignments to explicit setter calls (`rp.setContentPane(null)`), which is a no-op wherever the receiver was a surrogate and already meant the setter. **The generic lesson: a visibility widening is not a no-op in a mixed Java/Kotlin module** — Kotlin prefers a visible field over a synthetic property, so `protected` silently converts property-syntax *writes* into field writes for every same-package Kotlin caller. Java callers are unaffected (they have no property syntax), and library code is pure Java per [R_pure_java_library](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules), so the blast radius is exactly the Kotlin test corpus. This is [R_java_karibu_tests](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules)' rationale arriving from a new direction: Kotlin's resolution rules are not javac's, and here the difference is silent rather than a compile error.

Residual risk, stated rather than chased: the same rebinding applies to property *reads*, where it is invisible because a field read and a trivial getter return the same value. It only matters for a getter that computes, and no such read failed.

**Moot since [D_kotlin_retired](#D_kotlin_retired).** The Kotlin test corpus was the entire blast radius, and it is gone — a future widening pass (the absent 83) pays none of this cost. Kept because it is the measured record of *why* R_java_karibu_tests' "Kotlin's resolution rules are not javac's" is not hypothetical.

### `InstanceFieldSurfaceTest` is the gate, and only its narrowing half is armed

Modelled on `PublicConstantsTest` / `R12ProvenanceTest`, same package-prefix mapping, so a new emulator joins by existing. Two departures:

1. **Visibility, never value.** An instance field has no value until something is constructed, and constructing an emulator needs a Vaadin UI. Hence a separate class rather than a third assertion on the constants gate.
2. **The narrowing half is allow-list-free, and that is why it is the half that ships.** It speaks only about fields the emulator already declares, so the state is demonstrably there and a narrower modifier has nothing to excuse.

Type fidelity is **not** checked: emulator types legitimately diverge under [R_no_vaadin_in_api](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) limb 1, so a type comparison needs the prefix mapping applied through every type argument. Worth doing, not done. One known deviation it would catch: `ButtonGroup.buttons` is kept `final` where the JDK's is not — the audit is about reachability, and letting a subclass null out the group's own storage buys a migrator nothing.

### The absent 83 (closed since — [D_field_write_reconcile](#D_field_write_reconcile)) needed a decision this entry did not make

Landing the presence half would need an 83-entry allow-list, roughly a third of whose entries would read "we'll get to it" — which [D_gap_severity_triage](#D_gap_severity_triage) forbids. The blocker is a design question, not effort. Three groups:

- **Genuinely unportable** (~33) and sanctionable on sight: `JComponent.ui` (L&F dispatch, sub-bucket (b)), six `accessibleContext`s, `JViewport`'s five paint internals, `Toolkit`'s two, `GridBagLayout.comptable` (typed `Hashtable<java.awt.Component, …>`, so R_no_vaadin_in_api limb 1 forbids the JDK type and the emulator's own map is differently keyed) and `layoutInfo` (`GridBagLayoutInfo` is package-private in `java.awt` — unnameable), `JTree.selectionRedirector` and `JMenu.popupListener` (JDK protected inner classes), `JTable.editorComp`.
- **Mechanical renames** (~10): `JInternalFrame` holds all six under different names — `closed` for `isClosed`, `icon` for `isIcon`, `maximum` for `isMaximum`, `selected` for `isSelected`, and `iconifiable` where the **JDK spells it `iconable`**. That last one is a silent tidy-up of a JDK spelling quirk on a protected field name, which [R_no_silent_improvements](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) would rather we reproduced.
- **State that lives only in the surrogate** (~30) — the undecided ones: `AbstractButton.model` and its four listener fields, `JSlider`'s six, `JProgressBar`'s six, `JComboBox`'s six, `JTabbedPane`'s four, `JTree`/`JTable`'s models, `JScrollBar.model`. Declaring a `protected` field here would create a **second source of truth**, which is the shadow-cache shape [R_vaadin_first](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) prohibits on the other side of the split. The honest options are "declare and delegate the accessors to the surrogate" or "sanction permanently and accept that this subclass does not compile"; picking between them is a decision, and it wants its own entry.

All three groups are since resolved: the mechanical renames and permanent sanctions landed with the absence gate's allow-list, and the surrogate-owned group is [D_field_write_reconcile](#D_field_write_reconcile). The one still-open thread is type fidelity (above): the gate checks visibility, not type, and a type comparison needs the package mapping applied through every type argument.

### Validation

Full reactor `clean install` green; `:emulators` 1945 (one new test), Sampler's `WarnInventoryTest`s unaffected. 88 fields widened, 5 `GridBagLayout` changes, 59 Kotlin assignments rewritten to explicit setters across 8 test files; `InstanceFieldSurfaceTest` reports **147** instance fields carried at or above the JDK's visibility (143 pre-existing plus `GridBagLayout`'s four new arrays).

**19 existing assertions inverted, and every one was the Kotlin rebinding above** — no emulator behaviour changed, which is the point: a widening cannot change what Java callers do, and the Kotlin corpus was asserting through property syntax that silently stopped meaning the setter. Two of the 19 needed a second pass because they sat inline in `assertFailsWith { … }` rather than on their own line, and one rewrite swallowed a trailing comment into the call parens — both worth knowing if this is repeated for the absent 83.

<a id="D_field_write_reconcile"></a>
## D_field_write_reconcile. Surrogate-owned JDK fields are declared as Swing-side truth; direct field writes are repaired at SB-Emulators' "repaint" and logged as a loud ERROR

Closes [D_instance_field_surface](#D_instance_field_surface)'s open half. The ~30 absent fields whose state lived in the surrogate on purpose (`JSlider.sliderModel`, `JTable.dataModel`, `orientation`/`tabPlacement`-style knobs) are now declared, and the absence gate's allow-list is down to 26 permanent sanctions. The old "second source of truth" objection dissolved on inspection — a model field is a second **pointer** to the one object the surrogate runs on, not a second copy — but its serious kernel survived as the **direct-field-write problem** this entry solves.

### The fidelity baseline: the JDK is broken here too, and convergence is repaint-shaped

`this.sliderModel = m` in a migrated subclass is legal (the JDK made the field `protected`) and partially broken **on the desktop**: it skips the setter's validation, `PropertyChangeEvent`s and listener rewiring. What still works there works because JDK bodies read the field at use time — so the write takes effect at the next repaint/interaction. SB-Emulators' peer has no repaint that re-reads fields, so an undetected write would do *nothing*, which is worse than the JDK. The mapping: **the client-response flush is the emulator's repaint.**

### The mechanism: `FieldReconciler`, two triggers, no self-rearm

- **Declared fields are Swing-side truth** per R_swing_is_truth's standard shape: getter reads the field (JDK-faithful body), setter validates JDK-first (so the field never holds a value the peer rejected), writes the field, pushes the surrogate, records the push. The surrogate keeps its own live copies (rendering, server-side snapping) fed by the write-through — R_vaadin_first untouched, zero surrogate API changes required (one exception below).
- **Detection baseline:** models compare the field against the peer's own reference (`field != surrogate.getModel()`); values compare against a private *last-pushed shadow* (`pushed*`), because a value has no shared reference and comparing against the surrogate's read-back would false-positive on lossy mappings. The shadow is emulator-side write-detection, not the surrogate-side getter round-trip cache R_vaadin_first bans.
- **Steady-state trigger: the `EHelper.callSwing` epilogue** (outermost envelope only, after the drain, under the session lock). R_callswing_envelope guarantees every mutation path — peer events, Timer fires, SwingWorker callbacks, post-park continuations — runs inside one, so the write is repaired within the roundtrip that made it, before the browser renders a stale frame.
- **Bootstrap trigger: a one-shot `beforeClientResponse`** armed at emulator-ctor registration, consumed at the first flush, covering app code that field-writes while building the UI during navigation attach. **Never re-armed from inside the callback** — measured 2026-08-31: Flow's `StateTree.runExecutionsBeforeClientResponse` executes registrations made *during* the flush in the same pass (it loops to a fixpoint), so a self-rearming callback livelocks; `MockVaadin.clientRoundtrip()` hung and the stack dump caught the spin inside the stream loop.
- **A detected write logs a loud ERROR** (`FieldReconciler.reportDirectWrite`) naming class, field and the setter to call — deliberately not the `onUnimplemented` WARN lane, because this is an app antipattern that causes stale data on the desktop too, not an SB-Emulators coverage gap. Registry: session-scoped (survives the F5 teleport, like D_session_scoped_pools), `WeakHashMap`-backed.

**Accepted R_no_silent_improvements wobble:** the repair re-runs the setter-equivalent push, which *rewires* listener plumbing the JDK leaves permanently stale. The ERROR names it; the alternative (reproduce the stale wiring) would mean deliberately shipping a browser-side stale frame the desktop's incidental repaints don't have.

### Per-class notes that don't generalise

- **`JScrollBar` needed no reconcile at all**: a shadow component (inert `Div`, no surrogate), so the JDK's `protected BoundedRangeModel model` became the *actual storage* (a real `DefaultBoundedRangeModel` replacing four flattened ints) — every accessor reads it at use time, giving JDK-identical direct-write semantics for free. When nothing renders, honest JDK machinery beats detection.
- **`SJTabbedPane.setModel` graduated from drop-and-WARN to a real swap** (the one surrogate change): the standard write-through would have ERROR-spammed every roundtrip after a legitimate `setModel` call the surrogate declined. The drop's stated ground ("wiring assumes the original instance") was three lines of rewiring. See [SD_sjtabbedpane](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_sjtabbedpane).
- **`JTabbedPane`'s bucket-3 bridge fixed a latent source-identity bug**: `addChangeListener` forwarded raw to the surrogate, whose `ChangeEvent.getSource()` is the SJTabbedPane — a migrated `(JTabbedPane) e.getSource()` cast would have thrown. Now the JSlider-shape bridge (`createChangeListener` → emulator `listenerList` → cached `changeEvent`) re-sources the fire.
- **`JTree.selectionModel`'s repair routes through the emulator's own `setSelectionModel`** (after pointing the field back at the installed model so the unhook targets the right instance) — a raw surrogate push would leave `selectionHandler` + `rowMapper` on the old model.
- **`JComboBox.selectedItemReminder`** is maintained by the ported `selectedItemChanged`, as in the JDK, rather than reconciled — the next selection overwrites it, so a direct write has exactly the JDK's local consequences. Same for the inert `editor`.

### Sanctioned rather than declared (the surviving allow-list)

The D_instance_field_surface permanent sanctions, plus **`AbstractButton`'s five** (`model` + four listener fields) — the emulator deliberately flattens `ButtonModel` (D_buttongroup), and handing subclasses an inert model whose `setArmed(true)` does nothing is the silently-wrong shape a compile error beats; un-flattening is its own scope decision.

**Alternatives rejected:** supplier indirection (surrogate reads its model through an injected `Supplier` — most faithful read semantics, but rewrites ~10 surrogates' internals and still needs the refresh push, i.e. it degenerates into this same reconcile); method-entry-seam reconcile (a write-then-never-touch leaves the browser stale forever, where this design repairs within the writing roundtrip); sanctioning the whole bucket (punishes the common, harmless field-*read* case — `this.dataModel` in an old JTable subclass — to guard the rare write).

**Validation:** `FieldReconcilerTest` (value write + model write repaired at the callSwing epilogue; bootstrap write caught by the one-shot flush hook; setter writes produce no false positives), both `InstanceFieldSurfaceTest` halves green with the allow-list at 24 (the test prints the count), full reactor green.

<a id="D_theme_is_lookandfeel"></a>
## D_theme_is_lookandfeel. The Vaadin theme is the Look & Feel — app-set colours are intent, everything else is the theme's

**Status: core implemented; Tier-1 components still to land** (see "Still to land"). The doctrine, the colour table, the marker, the two-directional gate, the exemption predicate and the class/stylesheet seam are all in. What remains is per-component work, each slice citing this entry.

L&F dispatch is permanently out of scope (R_match_swing_errors sub-bucket (b)) — but a migrated app still has to get its colours from *somewhere*, and today that somewhere is "nowhere, unless the Swing app said so explicitly", which is why an opaque `JPanel` used as a glass pane renders transparent and fails to curtain what it covers.

**Decision. The Vaadin theme plays the role the L&F played.** Colour is the app's CSS responsibility; SB-Emulators stays out of the way *except* where the Swing app expressed a real colour intent. Traffic lights drawn as three `JPanel`s must be red, amber and green, and no theme overrules that. The goal this serves, and that today's behaviour fails: **a migrated app is fully themable through standard Vaadin mechanisms.** Rendering Metal's `#EEEEEE` would nuke that.

| condition | CSS emitted | how |
|---|---|---|
| `isOpaque()` && background is **not** a `UIResource` | the literal colour — app intent beats the theme, always | **inline** |
| `isOpaque()` && background **is** a `UIResource`, peer not exempt | `var(--vaadin-background-color)` | **class + shipped stylesheet** |
| otherwise | nothing — the widget's theme paints it, or it is genuinely transparent | — |

Surrogate side: [SD_surrogate_theme_css](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_surrogate_theme_css) — the CSS rules apply there, the table does not.

### What real Swing does, measured (JDK 25, Metal, headless)

Ground truth for the whole entry; almost none of it matched what memory suggested, and it should not have to be re-measured.

| | `isOpaque()` | default `getBackground()` |
|---|---|---|
| JPanel, JButton, JCheckBox, JRadioButton, JToggleButton, JViewport, JScrollPane, JComboBox, JSlider, JProgressBar, JSpinner, JSplitPane, JToolBar, JMenuBar, JMenuItem, JPopupMenu, JScrollBar, JInternalFrame, JOptionPane | **true** | `#EEEEEE` |
| JTextField, JTextArea, JEditorPane, JTable, JList, JTree, JDesktopPane | **true** | `#FFFFFF` |
| JLabel, JMenu, JTabbedPane, JSeparator | **false** | `#EEEEEE` (installed, never painted) |
| JLayeredPane, JRootPane, Box | **false** | `null` — no UI delegate, so no colours installed |

Foreground is `#333333` on nearly everything, and the exceptions matter: **`JSlider` and `JProgressBar` are `#A3B8CC`** — not text colour at all, but the *filled track* and *filled bar* — `JSeparator` `#6382BF`, `JSpinner` `#EEEEEE`, and `JTree` / `JSplitPane` / `JInternalFrame` / `JDesktopPane` / `JLayeredPane` / `JRootPane` / `Box` are `null`. Also: `label.setBackground(GREEN)` leaves `isOpaque()==false` and so **paints nothing** — the classic paper cut, which SB-Emulators currently "fixes"; and `getBackground()`'s parent walk is dead code for JComponents (the L&F filled every one) but live for the AWT lane.

### Install Metal's colours as `ColorUIResource`; discriminate by the marker

SB-Emulators installs a per-class table of Metal's defaults as real `javax.swing.plaf.ColorUIResource` instances, exactly as a L&F would, and the render discriminator is the JDK's own — `!(bg instanceof UIResource)` means "the app set this". Everything falls out, all verified headless:

- `getBackground()` **never returns `null`** → the NPE class is gone. This is the load-bearing requirement: `getBackground().darker()` is an ordinary Swing idiom, safe under a real L&F, and an NPE stops the migrated app working. The emulator layer exists to let the app *run*.
- `isBackgroundSet()` stays faithful — `true` from construction, as in real Swing.
- `setBackground(new Color(238,238,238))` yields a plain `Color`, **not** a `UIResource`, so a deliberately default-coloured panel still renders literal. Zero false positives.
- `setBackground(UIManager.getColor("control"))` yields a `ColorUIResource` and renders as the theme token — exactly the "reset me to the default" semantics the app intended.
- **The parent walk self-corrects.** Every JComponent carries its own installed colour, so the walk never fires — matching Swing, and fixing a live divergence: SB-Emulators today propagates a red parent's background to its children, where real Swing does not (measured: a child of a RED parent answers `#EEEEEE`). The AWT lane stays unfilled and keeps walking to `null`, also matching the JDK.
- **One table, two fronts.** It is `installColorsAndFont(c, "Panel.background", …)` as a constant, so it also supplies the `isOpaque()` defaults — ten of which SB-Emulators answers wrongly today (`JViewport`, `JTextComponent`, `JMenuBar`, `JToolBar`, `JTable`, `JList`, `JTree`, `JInternalFrame`, `JProgressBar`, `JScrollBar`).

**Why Metal:** the JDK's own cross-platform default on every platform including Linux — GTK engages only on an explicit `setLookAndFeel(getSystemLookAndFeelClassName())`, and its values come from the user's desktop theme, so they are neither deterministic nor testable.

**Two mechanical notes.** `ColorUIResource` instantiates fine headless, so it costs nothing in tests. Metal's foregrounds are `sun.swing.PrintColorUIResource`, which SB-Emulators cannot instantiate — it extends `ColorUIResource`, so the marker test still holds and SB-Emulators uses a plain `ColorUIResource(51,51,51)`.

**`SystemColor` must join the discriminator.** `java.awt.SystemColor` is `final` and extends `Color`; javac *statically rejects* `instanceof UIResource` on it. So `setBackground(SystemColor.control)` would classify as app intent and render literal grey — yet it means "the platform's control colour", the AWT-era spelling of `UIManager.getColor("control")`. One clause fixes it: `bg instanceof UIResource || bg instanceof SystemColor` → default. Value-equality could not have caught this either (`SystemColor.control.equals(new Color(sameRGB))` is `true`). SB-Emulators need not port the class — it is a `Color`, outside the Component hierarchy, reused per [D_whitelist_porting](#D_whitelist_porting). Today `SystemColor` has **zero** references in SB-Emulators, so migrated code binds the JDK's own and it is invisible to the WARN inventory.

**Accepted limitation: derived colours do not survive dark mode.** `getBackground().darker()` on `#EEEEEE` yields `#A6A6A6`, pinned as a literal, so against a dark theme the "darker" relationship inverts. The migrator's fix is to write a CSS class and delete the Java line. The alternative — a token-carrying `Color` deferring arithmetic to CSS `color-mix()` — is a large surface for a rare idiom, and is the escape hatch if a real migration makes it hurt.

### The cascade is the priority mechanism — inline vs class is not a detail

An **inline style outranks every stylesheet rule short of `!important`**; a class binding is ordinary cascade a migrator can override from their own stylesheet. So the two mechanisms mean exactly the two things the doctrine needs to say: **app-set colour → inline** (intent, must beat the theme); **SB-Emulators-supplied default → class** (a default, must *lose* to the migrator's CSS). Writing a theme token inline would be nearly as unthemable as writing `#EEEEEE` inline.

SB-Emulators therefore needs no priority machinery of its own: choose the CSS mechanism that matches the intent and the cascade enforces the doctrine for free. The corollary is a lint-able rule — **SB-Emulators library code never writes a colour inline unless the app set that colour** — violated today in at least `JOptionPane.colorForMessageType`, `SJToolBar.java:165` and `SJSeparator.java:101`.

The *lever* differs by peer kind, because a raw `background-color` on a themed host races the widget's shadow DOM:

| peer kind | app-set colour written as |
|---|---|
| `HtmlContainer` / `Scroller` | `background-color: rgb(…)` |
| themed Vaadin widget | the component's own style property, e.g. `--vaadin-button-background: rgb(…)` |
| native UA widget | `background-color: rgb(…)`, best-effort — UA styling may ignore it |

`--vaadin-button-background` and its siblings are documented as supported by **both** Aura and Lumo, so this stays theme-neutral.

### Which token, and why the theme choice never has to be made

Vaadin 25's **base style properties (`--vaadin-*`) are defined in every theme** — Aura (the 25+ default), Lumo, and bare base styles alike. So SB-Emulators emits `var(--vaadin-background-color)` and whatever theme the migrator installed binds it.

**Measured in a live browser (Sampler, Vaadin 25.2.6 + Lumo, 2026-08-28), not merely argued:** `--vaadin-background-color` resolves to `rgb(236,234,227)` — *exactly* Sampler's own `--lumo-base-color: #ECEAE3` override. The base tokens really are wired through Lumo, and a migrator's re-skin flows into SB-Emulators' fill without SB-Emulators knowing. With the re-skin disabled the same token reads `rgb(255,255,255)`, tracking stock `--lumo-base-color: light-dark(#fff,#233348)` — so **both tokens are `light-dark()`-based and adapt to dark mode for free.** This is the answer to "what colour is Metal grey in a themed, dark-mode-capable browser": not SB-Emulators' to answer.

**The base-vs-container split is mechanical, not aesthetic.** `--vaadin-background-container` is **translucent** — `rgba(0,0,0,0.05)` under Sampler's theme, a nested `light-dark()` alpha expression under stock Lumo. It composites over what is behind it and so **can never curtain**: a glass pane filled with it would be 5% black over the content it must hide. The opaque fill therefore takes `--vaadin-background-color`, and the container token is reserved for the two chrome strips below, which only tint.

### Honour `opaque` by default; the exemption is one predicate

The fill triggers on `isOpaque()`, and the rule is a **denylist, not an allowlist**. An allowlist makes silence the default, so a component nobody thought about renders wrong and no one finds out — the exposed-but-unreachable failure shape [R_no_vaadin_in_api](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) limb 2 exists to catch, one layer down. A denylist makes faithfulness the default and forces every divergence to be argued.

**Exemption applies to the theme-default row only — never to app intent.** "Exempt" does not mean "ignores `setBackground`"; it means "needs no *default* fill, because its peer already paints one".

**The exemption is a property of the peer, not a list of class names:**

> `peer instanceof com.vaadin.flow.component.HtmlContainer` → fill; otherwise exempt.

`HtmlContainer` is Flow's base for plain HTML elements that paint nothing. Verified against Flow 25.2.6: `Div`, `Span` and `NativeLabel` extend it; `Input` and `RangeInput` do **not** (they are `AbstractSinglePropertyField`), and neither does any `vaadin-*` web component. Across the whole emulator surface this is right everywhere but twice:

- **`Scroller`** — not an `HtmlContainer`, but a transparent overflow container, and both `JScrollPane` and `vaadinx.awt.ScrollPane` are Metal-opaque, so it must fill.
- **`MenuBar`** — the predicate exempts it, but `vaadin-menu-bar`'s host computes to `rgba(0,0,0,0)` and so does its whole ancestry, so exempting it leaves a Swing menubar with no chrome at all (measured). It fills, with the **container** token — the base token is invisible there, being identical to the page.

`JToolBar` also takes the container token: measured transparent, and the tint reads as a proper strip on all three Sampler demos, horizontal and vertical.

`JFrame`'s two peer strategies fall out correctly and for free: an `@MainWindow` frame is an `SJPanel` `Div` and fills, giving the app its page surface; every other `JFrame` is a `Dialog` overlay and is exempt, so it looks like a Vaadin dialog. Same class, opposite answers, no special case.

**Three groups need no entry at all.** (1) *Metal-non-opaque classes* — the opaque gate stops the default row before the predicate is consulted. (2) *The whole AWT lane* — no `UIResource` is ever installed there, so the default row's condition is never met. (3) *Inert peers* — `JViewport`, `JScrollBar`, `JTableHeader`, the `JMenuItem` family's `Span`s, `JDesktopIcon`, `JSpinner`'s editors: the predicate says "fill", and filling an element that is never rendered is a **no-op**.

Counted as class names the exemptions (~25) outnumber the honoured (~9), which would make "denylist" look like the wrong call. But the rule is one property read off the peer, so **as a rule it has two entries**, and it keeps the virtue it was chosen for: a new emulator inherits correct behaviour from its peer type with nobody having to remember to add it.

**`JOptionPane` / `JFileChooser` need no exemption**, though their `Div` peers sit inside a `Dialog` overlay that already paints: before/after screenshots of filling them are pixel-identical, because Lumo derives the overlay's surface from `--lumo-base-color`, the same value the base token maps to. *Verified under Lumo only* — Aura paints overlays from the elevated, semi-transparent `--aura-surface-color`, so recheck when Aura lands.

### Opacity is half of the intent, not a competing rule

A Swing app says "paint me this colour" with the *pair* `setOpaque(true)` + `setBackground(red)` — the traffic-light panels have to be opaque in order to turn red, and `JPanel` is opaque by default precisely so they can. So the non-opaque gate is what gives `setOpaque` its meaning rather than an exception carved out of "if the app wants red, it gets red": a non-opaque component never expressed the intent. This also settles a standing [R_no_silent_improvements](#D_no_silent_improvements) violation — SB-Emulators paints a non-opaque `JLabel`'s background today where real Swing paints nothing. **The gate applies in both directions:** `setBackground` must consult `isOpaque()`, not only `setOpaque` consult the background. Today's gate is one-shot (applied only at `setOpaque` time) and `setBackground` writes unconditionally, undoing it — the accepted limitation recorded at `JComponent.java:152-155`.

### How far this reaches: values in, machinery out

The doctrine governs **colour values on components**; it does not govern **L&F machinery**. The line is principled rather than convenient: a colour value on a component is observable app state ([R_decline_effect_only](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) says it is never droppable) with a defined CSS lever; the machinery is pluggable-delegate dispatch, which has no browser counterpart and is already sub-bucket (b).

The reach is wide because the same API shape currently has **six different stances**, which is itself the bug: `setCaretColor` works with real CSS; `JTable`/`JList` selection and grid colours keep state and fire a PCE with no effect and **no WARN**; `JTextComponent`'s three other colour setters store, fire *and* WARN; `DefaultTreeCellRenderer`'s five WARN and keep **no state at all**; `JTabbedPane`'s per-tab pair keeps no state so even the getter returns `null`; and `JProgressBar`/`JSlider` foreground is silently absorbed by the generic `color` write. Two of those violate `R_decline_effect_only` outright, independent of this doctrine — only the *effect* is droppable.

- **Tier 1 — in scope, same rule, only the CSS lever differs.** `JTable`/`JList` selection + grid colours; `DefaultTreeCellRenderer`'s five; `JTabbedPane`'s per-tab pair; `JTextComponent`'s four; `JProgressBar`/`JSlider` foreground-as-fill. **Each lands as its own slice citing this entry** — the doctrine decides *what* to write, the slice researches *where* (which Vaadin part tints a Grid's selected row, a TabSheet's tab, a ProgressBar's indicator). Two carry findings: `setSelectionColor`'s recorded blocker (`JTextComponent.java:747-754`, "`::selection` cannot be inline CSS") **dissolves** once defaults go to a class + stylesheet, where `::selection` is expressible; and `setForeground` is not always text colour, per the measured `#A3B8CC` above.
- **Tier 2 — in scope, one extra decision each.** The `SystemColor` clause (above); `UIManager.getColor`'s key coverage; and the border null-colour derivation, where the JDK computes `EtchedBorder`/`BevelBorder` highlight and shadow from `getBackground().brighter()/.darker()` and SB-Emulators substitutes a flat literal (`#808080` in the emulator, `Color.GRAY` in `BorderCss`) — which should become a token, and where **the two layers additionally pick opposite ends of the pair**, which is simply a bug.
- **Tier 3 — out, but one verdict improves.** `updateUI` / `setUI` / `getUIClassID` / `updateComponentTreeUI`, `UIDefaults`, `LookAndFeel`, `UIManager.put` stay out as machinery. **But `updateComponentTreeUI` becomes a correct `onNoop`**: with one fixed table, re-running `installColorsAndFont` changes nothing, and the JDK's own "overwrite only a `null` or a `UIResource`" rule means app-set colours survive — which the marker gives us for free. So there is no unmet expectation to report, the same argument shape [D_frameinit_shape](#D_frameinit_shape) used for `enableEvents`. The honest WARN belongs on `setLookAndFeel`, where it already is.

**One edge explicitly out:** `RteHtmlCodec`'s `color:` / `background-color:` emission for `StyledDocument` runs is *document content*, not component chrome — always app intent, no defaults to substitute, so no theme substitution applies.

### This overturns `D_frameinit_shape`'s `controlColor()`

[D_frameinit_shape](#D_frameinit_shape) chose `UIManager.controlColor() → null` on the grounds that "giving `UIManager` a real `control` default is L&F, permanently out of scope". **Superseded.** The table above *is* such a default, and unlike the `opaque` case its values are observable through the public API as `Color`s, so this is a change of stance rather than a coexistence. `controlColor()` returns what Metal returns — `ColorUIResource(238,238,238)` — and `UIManager.getColor(key)` answers from the table for the keys it covers, keeping its WARN for the rest (which is also what makes the "reset to default" idiom above work).

Two consequences for the implementation: `frameInit`'s `setBackground(UIManager.getColor("control"))` now stores a real colour and **fires a `PropertyChangeEvent`** from the `JFrame` constructor where today's `null → null` dedupe fires nothing — which is what real Swing does, so it is a fidelity gain, but it inverts `WindowFrameInitTest` deliberately. And the out-of-scope line *moves* rather than vanishing: a constant colour table is emulation of what the app observes; **L&F *dispatch*** — pluggable `ComponentUI` delegates, `updateUI` swapping renderers, `setLookAndFeel` — stays permanently out.

### Where the Java/CSS boundary now sits

The table means `getBackground()` does return an L&F value, so the earlier "a theme token is not a `java.awt.Color`, therefore nothing can leak" argument no longer applies. The boundary that remains is narrower and still real: **a `UIResource` is a promise about rendering, not a claim about it.** `getBackground()` answers Metal's `#EEEEEE` while the browser paints `var(--vaadin-background-color)`, and those differ on purpose — the marker is precisely the flag saying "this value is a default, so the renderer may substitute the theme's". An app-set `Color` carries no such licence and is reproduced exactly. `CssConvert.colorFromCss` returning `null` for `var(--…)` stays correct: nothing should read a token back as a `Color`.

### Rejected alternatives

- **Metal's literals as CSS** (`#EEEEEE` / `#FFFFFF`). Maximally faithful, and it nukes themability and dark mode — the one hard no.
- **Leave `getBackground()` null**, faithful to the JDK's written contract. Rejected: an NPE stops the app working, and the idioms that hit it are ordinary Swing.
- **A `getFont`-style non-null walk-bottom** (`Component.java:770-786`'s `DEFAULT_FONT` precedent). Fixes the NPE but makes `isBackgroundSet()` answer `false` where Swing answers `true` — one divergence traded for another.
- **Value-equality against the default** instead of the marker. Strictly weaker, and measurably so: `new ColorUIResource(238,238,238).equals(new Color(238,238,238))` is `true`, so it cannot tell a deliberate `setBackground(new Color(238,238,238))` from the installed default.
- **A hand-maintained exemption list** instead of the peer predicate. Rots silently; a new emulator is wrong until someone remembers it.
- **`--lumo-*` tokens.** Undefined under Aura, the Vaadin 25 default.
- **Aura's `.aura-surface` / `.aura-surface-solid`** class names. Aura-specific, and elevation is a concept Swing does not have.
- **`--vaadin-background-container` for opaque fills.** Translucent; cannot curtain.
- **A `--SB-Emulators-*` status-token namespace** for the JOptionPane glyph colours. A namespace to invent, document and teach, where a CSS class the migrator already knows how to override does the job.

### Still to land

Landed: the core (table, marker, both-direction gate, predicate, tokens, the class/stylesheet seam in `emul/emulator-theme.css`); the `--lumo-*` lock-in sweep; and the JOptionPane status-colour gap, where **base styles define no semantic error/warning/info colour by design** — Vaadin's own answer is a component *theme variant* (`error`/`warning`/`success`, supported by both Aura and Lumo), which `vaadin-icon` does not offer — so the glyph takes a class bound in the shipped stylesheet with an Aura → Lumo → literal fallback chain.

**Still open — the five Tier-1 components**, one slice each, because each needs its own CSS-lever research rather than doctrine work: which Vaadin part or style property tints a Grid's selected row (`JTable`/`JList` selection + grid colours), a TabSheet's individual tab (`JTabbedPane`'s per-tab pair, whose *state* is now correct but whose effect is still declined), a ProgressBar's indicator and a Slider's filled track (`JProgressBar`/`JSlider` foreground-as-fill), and `JTextComponent`'s four — where `setSelectionColor`'s recorded blocker dissolves, since `::selection` is expressible in the shipped stylesheet the class mechanism now has.

Also open: the border null-colour derivation (Tier 2 above — flat literal to a token, and the two layers picking opposite ends of the highlight/shadow pair), and `updateComponentTreeUI`'s downgrade to `onNoop`.

~~Two of the silently-wrong items found by the reach survey are `R_decline_effect_only` violations independent of this doctrine~~ — **both fixed.** `JTabbedPane`'s per-tab colours now live in an emulator-side lockstep list (the state is the emulator's, the effect stays the surrogate's declined WARN — the first time [SD_surrogate_theme_css](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_surrogate_theme_css)'s split answered a design question on its own), and `DefaultTreeCellRenderer`'s five are `protected` fields defaulted to Metal's values. Two JDK details there were not guessable and are worth recording: a fresh tab's `getBackgroundAt` returns the **tabbed pane's own background**, not null — so null means "no colour of its own" and the getter falls back — and `setBackgroundAt` fires **no** `PropertyChangeEvent`, so neither do we.

Sampler's own theming is backwards for this and should change with it ([`sampler/description.md`](../sampler/description.md)): it pulls `Lumo.STYLESHEET` and then redefines ~60 Lumo tokens, where it should demo the **untouched default theme** so a theming regression is visible, with the Swing-look override as a separable opt-in stylesheet — which is incidentally the artefact a migrator most wants shipped.

### Validation

Full reactor `clean install` green: `:emulators` 1966, `:surrogates` 1341, Sampler 92 with its `WarnInventoryTest`s at zero. Landed in four commits — the table + marker, the default-fill classes, the `--lumo-*` sweep, and the two R_decline_effect_only state restorations.

**Six assertions inverted, each deliberately.** `JComponentTest.kt` (a background on a non-opaque component now paints nothing — the paper cut reproduced), `UIManagerTest.kt` (`getColor` answers a covered key silently, and a *new* test keeps the WARN pinned for an uncovered one), `WindowFrameInitTest` ×3 (the now-firing `frameInit` PCE, plus the recorded colour), and Sampler's `TreesWarnInventoryTest` (which pinned that `setTextSelectionColor` WARNs — it no longer does, so the gate asserts the round-trip instead).

**Three things stayed green that were expected to invert, each informative rather than lucky:**

- `ContainerTest.kt:210-238`'s walk-to-null cases are **AWT-lane**, where no `UIResource` is ever installed — the "the AWT lane needs no entry" claim above, confirmed by a test predicted to break.
- `SJPanelTest.java:129` and `JComponentMixinTest.kt:166` pin behaviour [SD_surrogate_theme_css](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_surrogate_theme_css) preserves, so their staying green **is** the check that the colour table did not leak across the module boundary.

**One inversion was not predicted, and is the find worth keeping.** `JTableRendererHookTest` went red because `DefaultTableCellRenderer` extends `JLabel` and therefore now carries Metal's `#333333`, which `JComboBox.withRendererColors` copied straight into every grid cell — bypassing the gate entirely and pinning the L&F palette into the Grid. The snapshot path now skips L&F defaults too. The lesson generalises: **a colour that reaches the DOM by a path other than `setBackground` needs the marker test at that path**, and `withRendererColors` was the only such path in the emulator layer.

**Two build gates caught real mistakes while implementing, both correctly.** [D_instance_field_surface](#D_instance_field_surface)'s field-visibility check rejected `DefaultTreeCellRenderer`'s five new colour fields as `private` where the JDK declares them `protected` — that gate doing exactly its job on the first new fields added since it landed. And Sampler's exit gate caught the WARN that stopped firing.

**Browser-verified** on Sampler (Vaadin 25.2.6 + Lumo): the stylesheet loads via `SwingBridgeEmulatorsBootstrap`, the fill class resolves to `rgb(236,234,227)` — Sampler's own `--lumo-base-color` override flowing through untouched, which is the themability claim working end to end — and toolbars render the chrome strip.

<a id="D_modality_blocking"></a>
## D_modality_blocking. AWT modality blocking re-declined on measured grounds — Vaadin's active-modal curtain + modality stack already play `updateChildrenBlocking`'s role

Closes `Q_non_goals_recheck` from the Window/Frame/JFrame audit residue (2026-08-31). The audit's non-goals list declined modality blocking as "there is no z-order to block" — wrong-ish grounds, and [D_window_registry](#D_window_registry)'s owner links later made `updateChildrenBlocking` mechanically buildable, so the entry was re-examined rather than carried by inertia. The re-examination **re-declines it, on new grounds: the effect is already delivered.** An AWT modal dialog does three separable things, and each is accounted for:

1. **Caller parks, events keep pumping** (`EventDispatchThread.pumpEvents` secondary loop) — that is [D_callswing_loom](#D_callswing_loom), closed long ago; the released Vaadin request thread plays the secondary pump.
2. **Other windows are input-blocked** (`Dialog.blockWindows` / `updateChildrenBlocking`, per-window `modalBlocked` consulted at dispatch) — this entry: delivered by Vaadin server-side modality, measured below.
3. **Modality-type state round-trip** — plain field storage, already in place ([SD_sjdialog](../surrogates/decisions.md#SD_sjdialog) maps modal→`ModalityMode.STRICT`).

**Measurement (Karibu, `ModalBlockingProbeTest`, 2026-08-31)** — desktop truth is `APPLICATION_MODAL` (`JDialog`'s default when `modal=true`); the production-semantics signals are the UI's active-modal pointer and the element attachment point, because `StateNode.isInert()` never resolves under Karibu (InertData computes during UIDL change collection, which MockVaadin doesn't run):

| case | desktop | SB-Emulators | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| pre-existing frame while modal parked | blocked | body-sibling of active modal → inert in production | match |
| new modeless dialog owned by the frame | blocked | inert | match |
| new `JFrame` | blocked | inert | match |
| modeless dialog owned by the modal itself | **interactive** — AWT never blocks the modal's own owned hierarchy | interactive — attaches *under* the active modal (`D_owned_window_attach`, 2026-09-10) | match |
| nested modal (cascading `JOptionPane` shape) | interactive, becomes front modal | becomes active modal; outer demoted; **restored on dispose** | match, incl. stack pop |
| modeless dialog owned by a modal a nested modal has demoted | blocked — an application-modal dialog blocks its owner's chain too | outside the curtain | match |

**Decision.** Porting `updateChildrenBlocking` / per-window `modalBlocked` bookkeeping stays declined: every case (including the modality *stack*) is delivered by machinery SB-Emulators does not own or maintain, and the JDK's blocking state has no public API surface to be faithful *to* — `Window.isModalBlocked` is internal, so R_decline_effect_only's state+notification halves have nothing to keep. What a port would have bought is precisely the fifth row, and that turned out cheaper fixed at the attach seam than by importing the whole desktop algorithm — which is the sub-decision below.

<a id="D_owned_window_attach"></a>**D_owned_window_attach — a window whose owner chain reaches the active modal attaches *under* it, and the split that makes that safe lives in the surrogate's `add`.** The gap this closes was the table's fifth row: a wizard-style modal opening a floating detail/tool window gave the user a dead window where the desktop gives a live one — structural, not cosmetic, so R_layouts_close_enough did not cover it. Three points, all in `:surrogates`:

- <a id="D_window_split"></a>**`D_window_split` — a window is never content.** A host's `add` treats an `SWindow` child as *not* content: it nests under the host element instead of routing to the content pane, and `remove` mirrors it. One place, at the head of `RootPaneScaffold`'s routing bodies, which all four Dialog-backed hosts already delegate to. This is faithful rather than a workaround — `vaadinx.awt.Container.add` throws AWT's own `"adding a window to a container"`, so "a window is not content" is a rule the emulator layer states by exception and the surrogate layer states by containment. It also fixes a latent stage-3 bug: `sjDialog.add(otherSWindow)` used to land silently in the content pane, where the next `getContentPane().removeAll()` would detach it.
- <a id="D_surrogate_attach"></a>**`D_surrogate_attach` — the attach decision is `SWindow.setVisible`'s, not the emulator's.** Walk `owner` upward; if some owner *is* the UI's active modal component, `ui.addToModalComponent(this)`, else `ui.add(this)`. Surrogate-side because `SWindow.owner` is a parallel owner chain populated at construction, so the surrogate knows Swing ownership too — which also means a stage-3 pure-surrogate app gets the fix. The test is the **active** modal specifically, never `addToModalComponent` unconditionally: a window owned by a modal that a nested modal has demoted must stay curtained, which is the sixth row.
- <a id="D_reparent_each_show"></a>**`D_reparent_each_show` — recompute the attach point on every show.** Hiding an owner cascades the hide to its owned windows, so a later show can find the modal it was nested under demoted, disposed, or detached — and under a closed `Dialog` the child's content is not rendered at all. Attach is therefore "compute the desired parent, move if it differs", not "attach once if unattached".

The mechanism is element parentage and nothing else: `UIInternals.setChildModal` sets `inert` on the **UI** element and `ignoreParentInert` on the **modal's**, and `InertData` inherits down the StateNode parent chain, so anything parented under the active modal is live by inheritance. Nesting a *nested modal* under its owner falls out of the same rule and is correct for the same reason — the inner's own `ignoreParentInert` exempts it while its parent chain stays inert.

**Browser-verified** on Sampler's Dialogs route (Vaadin 25.2.6, Firefox, 2026-09-10), which carries the scenario as a durable demo. Baseline, with the fix reverted: the owned window attaches at `parent=BODY`, its text field refuses focus (it bounces back to the modal) and its button's `ActionListener` never runs. With the fix: the owned window attaches under the modal's content root, takes focus and keystrokes, and its listener fires while the modal is still parked; hiding the modal cascades the child closed and the reshow cycle re-renders both; disposing the modal takes the whole owned tree with it. The nested-modal consequence measured the same way — the nested modal is live, the demoted outer modal *and* its owned window both stop responding, and closing the nested one restores them.

Server-side, `ModalBlockingProbeTest` (`:emulators`) and `SWindowModalAttachTest` (`:surrogates`) pin the parentage; neither can see the client-side focus trap, which is why the browser run above is part of the record and not a nicety.

**Accepted limitation — modality *scope* stays coarser than AWT's.** `DOCUMENT_MODAL` / `TOOLKIT_MODAL` / `ModalExclusionType` all collapse into the all-or-nothing curtain: a desktop document-modal blocks only its owner document chain, while Vaadin's curtain blocks every other window. Effect-only divergence in edge-case scopes, R_match_swing_errors sub-bucket (c) territory; revisit only if a migration target actually mixes modality scopes.

**Also settled here: the "native peer lifecycle" non-goal is confirmed, not open.** It was declined on the prediction that `addNotify()` is "a flag write plus a registry promotion", and the audit then *measured* exactly that ([D_window_displayable](#D_window_displayable), [D_component_displayable](#D_component_displayable), the registry's pin/unpin edges). Recorded so nobody re-litigates it.

**Validation.** `ModalBlockingProbeTest` pins the Vaadin facts the decline rests on (parked modal is the active modal; unrelated windows sit outside it; a window owned by the modal sits inside it; nested modal takes over, and a window owned by the demoted outer one falls back outside; dispose pops back). If a Vaadin upgrade breaks one, this entry's ground moved. `SWindowModalAttachTest` covers the same seam from the surrogate side, plus both re-parenting directions; `SJDialogTest`'s three window-child cases cover `D_window_split`.

---

<a id="D_graphics_environment"></a>
## D_graphics_environment. `vaadinx.awt.GraphicsEnvironment` + `GraphicsDevice` + `GraphicsConfiguration` — the browser viewport as a one-screen display, and `isHeadless()` is false

**Status: landed.** Trigger: the `testapps/inventory` stage-2 probe (`Q_graphics_env`, stumble 8). The app's `AppFrame` constructor runs the standard maximize-to-screen idiom —

```java
GraphicsEnvironment e = GraphicsEnvironment.getLocalGraphicsEnvironment();
setMaximizedBounds(e.getMaximumWindowBounds());
setExtendedState(getExtendedState() | JFrame.MAXIMIZED_BOTH);
```

— which, with `java.awt.GraphicsEnvironment` unported, compiled fine and threw `HeadlessException` from inside the frame's constructor. The probe's migrating agent rewrote it by hand onto `Toolkit.getScreenSize()`; that rewrite is now unnecessary and the idiom ports by import swap.

**Decision.** Port all three classes as full-surface emulators, on [D_toolkit_full_surface](#D_toolkit_full_surface)'s model: standalone (they do *not* extend the abstract JDK classes — they are the import-swap surface, not a platform environment), `final`, one instance each, and per-method behaviour selected by the same empirical tiers. This closes the deferral D_toolkit_screen_size's non-goals recorded verbatim ("`java.awt.GraphicsEnvironment` / `getMaximumWindowBounds()` emulation … lands when a migration target needs it") — a target needed it.

<a id="D_ge_not_headless"></a>**D_ge_not_headless — `isHeadless()` returns false, and this is the half of the entry that matters most.** The loud failure the probe found is not the dangerous one. `java.awt.GraphicsEnvironment.isHeadless()` answers `true` on a server, so a migrated app's `if (!GraphicsEnvironment.isHeadless()) { … }` guard — the standard "am I on a display?" test — **silently skips the UI it was about to build**, with no exception, no WARN and nothing in a log to triage. A browser is a display, so the emulator reports one: `isHeadless()` and `isHeadlessInstance()` are both false, and every screen query answers instead of throwing. This is not an improvement on the JDK contract ([R_no_silent_improvements](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_silent_improvements)) — it is the same contract evaluated against the environment SB-Emulators actually runs in, where the answer genuinely differs.

<a id="D_ge_tiers"></a>**D_ge_tiers — two tiers, from a headless probe, and nothing WARNs.** Running every method under `-Djava.awt.headless=true` split the surface exactly as it did for `Toolkit`:
- **Browser-backed** (the JDK throws `HeadlessException`): `getMaximumWindowBounds`, `getCenterPoint`, `getScreenDevices`, `getDefaultScreenDevice` — all resolving through `BrowserToolkitInfo`'s viewport, so they track a browser resize like `Toolkit.getScreenSize` does (D_toolkit_screen_size).
- **Delegate to the headless JDK environment** (verified to return real values): `createGraphics(BufferedImage)` (a genuinely working `Graphics2D` — the one thing a headless JVM does perfectly), `getAllFonts`, `getAvailableFontFamilyNames(…)`, `registerFont`, `preferLocaleFonts`, `preferProportionalFonts`. Delegation is what keeps the font list consistent with what `Toolkit.getFontMetrics` will actually measure with, which is the only sense in which a font query can be right when the glyphs are ultimately rendered by the browser. `registerFont`'s false-on-conflict and NPE-on-null come free.

`GraphicsEnvironment` has **no WARN path at all**: every method has a real answer. The only WARN in the trio is `GraphicsConfiguration`'s `createCompatibleVolatileImage` family, which needs an accelerated surface a server JVM has not got.

<a id="D_ge_call_graph"></a>**D_ge_call_graph — `getMaximumWindowBounds` is derived, not computed.** The JDK's body is `SunGraphicsEnvironment.getUsableBounds(getDefaultScreenDevice())` — config bounds minus `Toolkit.getScreenInsets(gc)` — and the port reproduces that call graph rather than reaching for the viewport directly ([R_no_vaadin_in_api](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_vaadin_in_api) limb 2). The chain GE → device → configuration → `Toolkit.getScreenInsets` is therefore load-bearing: the day insets stop being `(0,0,0,0)` — a browser chrome inset, say — `getMaximumWindowBounds`, `getCenterPoint` and `getDisplayMode` all follow with no further edit. Computing the rectangle inline would have been one line shorter and would have had to be found and fixed three times.

<a id="D_ge_fullscreen_works"></a>**D_ge_fullscreen_works — `setFullScreenWindow` is ported verbatim from the JDK and actually works; it is not a stub.** `java.awt.GraphicsDevice`'s *base-class* bodies are all concrete, and they are the behaviour of a device with no exclusive-mode capability: `isFullScreenSupported()` false, and `setFullScreenWindow` then takes the windowed-mode path — resize the window to the screen bounds, show it, raise it, and restore the saved `windowedModeBounds` when full-screen is released. That ports unchanged onto `vaadinx.awt.Window` and delivers a real effect, so **no WARN is logged**. Its decoration-reset preamble (`setShape(null)`, `setOpacity(1f)`, opaque background) is kept even though every branch is dead against our `Window` — `getShape()` is null, `getOpacity()` 1.0f, `isOpaque()` true — because R_decline_effect_only asks for the whole method and the branches cost nothing. The one substitution: the JDK scopes the full-screen window per `AppContext`; SB-Emulators scopes it **per UI**, this runtime's analogue, since two browser tabs are two screens and neither may see the other's full-screen window.

<a id="D_ge_config_sweep"></a>**D_ge_config_sweep — porting `GraphicsConfiguration` forced a signature sweep, which is R_no_vaadin_in_api limb 1 working as designed.** Ten shipped signatures took `java.awt.GraphicsConfiguration` and were legitimate while SB-Emulators did not port the type ("a JDK type SB-Emulators does not port stays as it is — nothing to swap for"); the moment the port exists they become uncallable after an import swap, so all ten moved: `JFrame(String, GC)` / `JFrame(GC)`, `JWindow(GC)` / `JWindow(Window, GC)`, three `JDialog` ctors, `Frame(String, GC)` / `Frame(GC)`, `Window(Window, GC)`, plus `Toolkit.getScreenInsets(GC)`. Their bodies still ignore the argument, but the *reason* changed and the comments were corrected with it: not "GraphicsConfiguration doesn't map onto a browser — no screen devices" (now false) but "there is exactly one configuration, so choosing one cannot change where the window lands".

`Component.getGraphicsConfiguration()` moved further — from `onUnsupported` + null to returning the real configuration. Its old comment reasoned that the method "needs a real screen device — not available in a headless server", which is the [D_r12_jdk_typed_half](#D_r12_jdk_typed_half) pathology in miniature: a body that gave up because its return type had nothing satisfiable in it, and then read as a documented limitation. One WARN fewer, and a non-null answer where AWT's own is non-null.

<a id="D_ge_maximized_bounds"></a>**D_ge_maximized_bounds — the slice's test found `Frame.setMaximizedBounds` throwing its state away.** `java.awt.Frame.setMaximizedBounds` assigns `this.maximizedBounds = bounds` **unconditionally** and only then pushes to the peer, so the field is ours to keep even though the pixel-exact maximize is not (R_layouts_close_enough). SB-Emulators stored nothing and `getMaximizedBounds()` returned a hard-coded null — so the probe's own idiom, `setMaximizedBounds(e.getMaximumWindowBounds())`, was unobservable to the app that set it. Fixed to store the field; the WARN now reports the declined peer push alone. Textbook [R_decline_effect_only](../CLAUDE.md#R_decline_effect_only), and a reminder that the rule's "read the JDK body, don't reason about it" clause is what catches these.

**Alternatives considered.**
- **Port `GraphicsEnvironment` alone; WARN from `getScreenDevices` / `getDefaultScreenDevice`.** Rejected. Cheaper, and the evidence supported it — zero `GraphicsDevice` references across all three testapps and Sampler — but it leaves two of the four abstract methods as give-up bodies in a brand-new class, which is exactly the shape D_r12_jdk_typed_half was written about. The measured cost of the full graph turned out to be low: the JDK's base bodies are concrete and portable, so most of `GraphicsDevice` and `GraphicsConfiguration` is the JDK's own code.
- **Reproduce the JDK faithfully: `isHeadless()` true, screen queries throw `HeadlessException`.** Rejected — it is faithful to the JDK's *answer* while being wrong about SB-Emulators' *environment*, and it preserves the silent-branch trap (D_ge_not_headless) that is the worst failure in the area.
- **Have `getMaximumWindowBounds()` read `BrowserToolkitInfo` directly.** Rejected — one line shorter, and it breaks the GE → device → configuration → insets chain the JDK actually uses (D_ge_call_graph).
- **Add a `GraphicsEnvironment` grep to `hazard-scan.sh`.** Rejected as a consequence of this entry, and the reasoning generalises: what retires a hazard from that script is the type gaining a **swap-table row**, not the import-swap tool deleting `java.awt.*` (deletion re-emits stay-JDK types verbatim, so an unported type sails through, compiles, and fails at runtime). With the row present the reference rewrites and the hazard cannot occur. This closes `Q_hazard_scan_headless`'s remaining half — the `Toolkit` half was already closed the same way — leaving that follow-up with nothing to scan for.

**Accepted limitations.**
- **One screen, always.** `getScreenDevices()` has length 1; multi-monitor code sees a single display. A browser gives no per-monitor geometry, and window placement is viewport-relative regardless (D_toolkit_screen_size).
- **`getIDstring()` is `"browser-viewport"`** — platform-specific by contract, so any string is faithful; code that parses it (X11's `":0.0"`) will not match.
- **Full-screen is windowed-mode emulation, never exclusive mode.** The Fullscreen API needs a user gesture and is not wired; `isFullScreenSupported()` reports false, which is what the JDK reports on such a device, so the fallback path is the correct one to be on.
- **`createCompatibleVolatileImage` (all four overloads) → WARN + null**, and `isTranslucencyCapable()` / every `WindowTranslucency` kind → false, since `Window.setShape` / `setOpacity` have no browser counterpart.
- **`getNormalizingTransform()` scales by `Toolkit.getScreenResolution()`** (96 × devicePixelRatio) and so inherits that value's best-effort accuracy.
- **Bounds go stale across a browser resize** exactly as `Toolkit.getScreenSize()` does — re-read rather than caching.

**Source:** D_toolkit_full_surface / D_toolkit_screen_size / D_toolkit_from_client_details (the model, the viewport semantics and the client-details channel), D_whitelist_porting, R_no_vaadin_in_api, R_decline_effect_only, R_no_silent_improvements; triggered by the inventory stage-2 probe, whose `getMaximumWindowBounds()` maximize idiom is the one this entry had to make port.

**Validation.** `emulators/src/test/java/vaadinx/awt/GraphicsEnvironmentTest.java` (25): the singleton; `isHeadless()` false *asserted alongside the JDK's true*, so the divergence is pinned rather than assumed; viewport bounds and centre point, and that both track a viewport change; one device, and it is the default; font queries asserted **equal to the headless JDK's own**; `createGraphics` draws a red pixel that reads back red; `registerFont(null)` NPEs; the whole environment emits zero WARNs.
