Device: raster type, one configuration, `getDisplayMode` at viewport size and 32-bit depth, `setDisplayMode` throwing, no translucency, `getAvailableAcceleratedMemory()` = -1 (the JDK's "unknown", not 0), and the full-screen round trip restoring the pre-full-screen bounds with no WARN. Configuration: bounds, `getDevice` round-trip, both `createCompatibleImage` arities, `IllegalArgumentException` on an unknown transparency, the DPR-scaled normalizing transform, and the one WARNing family. Wiring: `Component.getGraphicsConfiguration()` reaching the same instance WARN-free, `Toolkit.getScreenInsets` accepting the ported type, and the probe's maximize idiom compiling and round-tripping verbatim. `ComponentGraphicsTest.getGraphicsConfigurationIsTheViewports` replaces the old returns-null assertion; `PortedTypesTableTest` regenerated (three new rows, derived — no exclusion list touched).

<a id="D_hierarchy_parity"></a>
## D_hierarchy_parity. The constants gate sees dropped interfaces only when they carry constants — the type hierarchy itself is now gated, and `RootPaneContainer` was a port all along

[D_missing_constants](#D_missing_constants)'s inherited-constants sweep found 532 gaps that were **all three dropped interfaces**. That is the shape worth naming: the constants were the symptom, the dropped `implements` was the defect — and an interface that carries *no* constants leaves no symptom at all while still breaking `instanceof`, still refusing to compile a migrator's `implements` or parameter declaration, and still leaving whatever hooks it declares unreachable. `PublicConstantsTest` cannot see those. That entry left the question open; measured 2026-09-02, the answer is that the residue is real and worth a gate of its own.

**Method.** Every `vaadinx.**` class in `:emulators` with a JDK counterpart by package prefix (`PublicConstantsTest`'s mapping), skipping anonymous/synthetic classes and non-public/protected counterparts — those are name collisions (`JTable$1` against `javax.swing.JTable$1`), not counterparts. For each pair: the JDK type's interface closure, each interface mapped to its `vaadinx` port when one exists and to itself otherwise, the emulator asserted assignable to the mapped type; same for the direct superclass.

| measure | count |
|---|---|
| emulator ↔ JDK pairs | 178 |
| interface checks (full closure) | 518 |
| **missing** — JDK type declares it, emulator not assignable | **20 rows, 9 interfaces** |
| wrong one — emulator implements the JDK interface where a port exists | 0 |
| missing but only inherited from a superclass (the superclass's own row covers it) | 12 |
| extra — emulator implements, JDK does not | 16 rows, 3 interfaces, none actionable |
| superclass mismatch | 2 — 1 sanctioned, 1 filter artefact |

### The 18 real ones

| JDK interface | emulator(s) | the fix |
|---|---|---|
| `javax.swing.RootPaneContainer` | `JFrame`, `JDialog`, `JWindow`, `JInternalFrame` | Ported as `vaadinx.swing.RootPaneContainer`. All four already carried all seven members with exactly the ported types, so the port is one interface file plus four `implements` words. See below |
| `javax.swing.MenuElement` (port existed) | `JMenuBar` | Five members. The JDK's `getSubElements()` collects the `MenuElement` children and `getComponent()` returns `this`; **the other three are empty in the JDK, so they are empty here** rather than `onUnimplemented` — WARNing where real Swing does nothing is [R_no_silent_improvements](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_silent_improvements) in the reporting direction. `JMenu` (via `JMenuItem`) and `JPopupMenu` already implemented the port; the bar was the one left out |
| `javax.swing.event.CellEditorListener` | `JTable` | The anonymous listener the edit path installed is hoisted into public `editingStopped` / `editingCanceled` and the table registers **itself** on the editor, as the JDK's `editCellAt` does. Bodies unchanged |
| `javax.swing.event.RowSorterListener` | `JTable` | `sorterChanged(RowSorterEvent)`, with `setRowSorter` unregistering from the old sorter and registering on the new — the JDK does this inside `SortManager`'s ctor. The *effect* is the surrogate's (SD_sjtable already drives the Grid off the same sorter) so the body is a documented no-op; what it may not be is unregistered, per [R_no_vaadin_in_api](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_vaadin_in_api) limb 2 |
| `javax.accessibility.Accessible` | `JFileChooser`, `JRootPane`, `JLayeredPane`, `JViewport`, `ImageIcon` | `implements` + `getAccessibleContext()` in the shape the other 33 `J*` classes already use. These five were hand-trimmed |
| `java.io.Serializable` | `AbstractBorder` (+7 borders inherit), `EmptyBorder`, `TransferHandler`, `UIManager`, `ImageIcon` | The marker. `AbstractBorder` is `implements Border, Serializable` in the JDK and its subclasses inherit that — assignability is what the gate checks, so no re-declaration |
| `java.awt.LayoutManager` (port existed) | `JSpinner.DefaultEditor` (+`NumberEditor` / `DateEditor` / `ListEditor` inherit) | The five JDK bodies are plain `Dimension` / `Insets` arithmetic and compile unchanged against `vaadinx.awt.Container`. **The JDK ctor's `setLayout(this)` is deliberately not added:** this editor never `add()`s the formatted field (it is never attached to the DOM), so `layoutContainer` would have nothing to lay out and installing the manager would only route through [M1D_custom_layoutmanager](../migration/1-swing-to-emulators/decisions.md#M1D_custom_layoutmanager)'s WARN fallback. Layout is R_layouts_close_enough-exempt; the members exist for hierarchy parity |

### `RootPaneContainer` is a port, not a skip

D_missing_constants called it "the one interface a `vaadinx.*` class genuinely cannot implement", `Generator.SKIP_INTERFACES` held it as its sole member, and `architecture.md` wrote it up as a documented limitation. All three were the wrong frame. It is exactly the `MenuElement` case of [D_r12_jdk_typed_half](#D_r12_jdk_typed_half): a JDK interface whose members traffic in ported types cannot be *reused*, so it is *ported* — which [D_whitelist_porting](#D_whitelist_porting) already names it as an example of. Nothing about the interface is unsatisfiable; only reusing the JDK's copy is.

**And SB-Emulators was already paying for its absence.** `vaadinx.swing.SwingUtilities.getRootPane(Component)` had degenerated into an `instanceof` chain: it tested `c` against `JRootPane`, then walked from `c.getParent()` testing `JFrame` / `JDialog`. So `getRootPane(frame)` returned **null** where the JDK returns the frame's root pane, and `JWindow` / `JInternalFrame` were not in the chain at all (their descendants still resolved, because [D_rootpane_containment](#D_rootpane_containment) puts the real `JRootPane` on the parent path). With the port the body is the JDK's verbatim, container test first. **The stand-in is the tell:** an `instanceof` chain over concrete classes where the JDK tests one interface is a dropped interface wearing a disguise, and it degrades silently as new implementors appear.

`SKIP_INTERFACES` is empty now and keeps only its javadoc, rewritten to say what the set is for and that every member it ever held was a mistake — `MenuContainer` and `ImageObserver` named no mapped type at all, `RootPaneContainer` named several and was still portable. `javax.swing.RootPaneContainer → vaadinx.swing.RootPaneContainer` is a `MAPPING` row, so the generator emits the port in an `implements` clause rather than dropping it.

### The two sanctioned omissions, and the two superclass rows

`vaadinx.awt.KeyboardFocusManager` does not implement `java.awt.KeyEventDispatcher` or `KeyEventPostProcessor`, per [D_focus_managers](#D_focus_managers): key-event dispatch is R_match_swing_errors sub-bucket (b), and both interfaces reference `java.awt.Component`, so honouring them means porting two interfaces for methods that could only WARN. Their absence is the point — a migrated `implements KeyEventDispatcher` fails at compile time naming the class, rather than compiling into a dispatcher that never dispatches.

Superclass: `vaadinx.swing.FocusManager extends KeyboardFocusManager` where the JDK's extends `DefaultKeyboardFocusManager` — D_focus_managers' four→two flattening, sanctioned by the same entry. The other mismatch, `GroupLayout.Group` against the JDK's `GroupLayout.Spring`, is a filter artefact: `Spring` is private, so nothing outside its package could sit under it. The superclass check skips non-public JDK superclasses the same way the pair scan skips non-public counterparts.

### Extras stay informational

Three interfaces emulators implement that their JDK types do not: `vaadinx.FieldReconciler.Reconcilable` (8) and `vaadinx.awt.CssEmittingLayoutManager` (6) are SB-Emulators-invented types, free by provenance per R_no_vaadin_in_api; `java.io.Serializable` on `KeyboardFocusManager` / `FocusManager` (2) is Vaadin session state that has to serialize. None is a migrator-visible divergence, so the reverse direction is printed by the gate and never fails it.

**Alternatives considered.**
- **Leave it to `PublicConstantsTest`.** Rejected on the measurement: of the nine interfaces in the residue, only `MenuElement` and `LayoutManager` would ever have shown up there, and only if an emulator's own constants sweep happened to notice. `RootPaneContainer` — the largest row, and the one with a live bug behind it — carries no constants at all.
- **Gate the full interface closure rather than each type's own declarations.** Rejected: an interface a JDK type inherits from its superclass is that superclass's row, so closure-gating reports every gap once per descendant (12 duplicate rows here) and points the maintainer at the wrong class.
- **Keep `RootPaneContainer` skipped and document the limitation harder.** Rejected — it was documented in three places and still produced a wrong `getRootPane`. A limitation nobody can implement around is a defect with better PR.

**Accepted limitations.**
- **`JTable.sorterChanged` is reachable only for a sorter installed through `setRowSorter`.** A sorter `SJTable` auto-creates for `autoCreateRowSorter` never passes through that setter. Invisible while the body is empty; the first thing to fix if it stops being empty.
- **The gate checks assignability, not members.** An emulator that satisfies an interface by inheriting members from an unrelated ancestor passes. Member-level faithfulness is `R12ProvenanceTest` / `R12DeadHookTest`'s job.
- **Pairs are found by package prefix**, so an emulator whose JDK counterpart lives in a package the mapping does not carry is not gated at all.

**Source:** D_missing_constants (the open question this closes), D_whitelist_porting, D_r12_jdk_typed_half, D_r12_provenance (the allow-list-free gate shape), D_focus_managers, D_rootpane_containment; R_no_vaadin_in_api, R_no_silent_improvements.

**Validation.** `emulators/src/test/java/vaadinx/TypeHierarchyParityTest.java`, three `@Test`s — interfaces forward, the wrong-one direction (zero today, and this test is the only reason it stays zero: it is the `JTable implements javax.swing.event.TableColumnModelListener` shape D_r12_jdk_typed_half fixed by hand), and superclass. Allow-list-free like `PublicConstantsTest`; both sanction maps fail on a stale entry, and a pair-count floor (> 150, currently 178) guards against a silent zero-scan pass. Run against the pre-fix tree it reports exactly the 18 rows above and nothing else; after them it is green at 198 interfaces matched plus the 2 sanctioned. Full reactor `clean install` green; `ported-types.tsv` regenerated for the new `vaadinx.swing.RootPaneContainer`.

---

<a id="D_auto_shutdown"></a>
## D_auto_shutdown. The app ends when its last displayable Window is disposed — AWT's auto-shutdown, not a close-operation consult

**Decision.** A migrated app's session closes when the app disposes its last displayable `vaadinx.awt.Window`, **under every `defaultCloseOperation`**, with a running `javax.swing.Timer` as the one veto. This *replaces* [D_close_operation_dispatch](#D_close_operation_dispatch)'s `EXIT_ON_CLOSE`-only bend on the programmatic `dispose()` path (`InlineStrategy.afterDispose`, and with it the whole `FrameStrategy.afterDispose` hook, are gone). The tab-close path ([D_shutdown_lifecycle](#D_shutdown_lifecycle): always close the session) and DialogStrategy's [D_gap_severity_triage](#D_gap_severity_triage) case-2 throw on a peer-originated `EXIT_ON_CLOSE` close are untouched.

Closes `Q_dispose_axis`, raised by the 2026-08-27 `testapps/inventory` stage-2 probe: the guide told a migrator that a bare `frame.dispose()` on the `@MainWindow` frame is enough, while the code only closed the session for `EXIT_ON_CLOSE`, so the guide was right in one row of four. The probe's agent hedged with `dispose()` + an explicit `session.close()` — correctly, as it turned out.

**What the JDK actually does — measured, not recalled** (2026-09-02, `xvfb-run` on JetBrains Runtime 25, one JVM per scenario: show a 200×200 `JFrame`, act at +500 ms, a daemon watchdog exits 2 if the JVM is still alive 4 s later; exit 0 therefore means AWT ended the JVM on its own). This table is the oracle `AutoShutdownTest` is written against:

| Scenario | What runs at +500 ms | JVM ended on its own | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DO_NOTHING_ON_CLOSE` | `dispose()` | yes, ~1.3 s later | |
| `HIDE_ON_CLOSE` | `dispose()` | yes | |
| `DISPOSE_ON_CLOSE` | `dispose()` | yes | |
| `EXIT_ON_CLOSE` | `dispose()` | yes | **`defaultCloseOperation` plays no part** |
| `hide` | `setVisible(false)` | no | hidden-but-displayable keeps the JVM alive |
| `timer` | `dispose()`, then a repeating 100 ms `Timer` | no | a running `Timer` keeps the JVM alive |
| `worker` | `dispose()`, then a `SwingWorker` sleeping 2.5 s | yes | the JVM ended **before** `done()` — worker threads are daemons, `done()` is lost |
| `dialog` | `dispose()`, then an ownerless non-modal `JDialog` shown | no | any displayable `Window` counts, not only frames |
| `handoff` | `dispose()`, then `new JFrame().setVisible(true)` in the same event | no | the login→main handoff survives |
| `laterhandoff` | `dispose()`, then the new frame via `invokeLater` | no | a pending event survives too |
| `thread` | `dispose()`, then a non-daemon `Thread` sleeping 2.5 s | yes, after the thread | the JVM waited for it, then ended |

The ~1.3 s lag is `AWTAutoShutdown`'s idle window: it fires once there are **no displayable peers, no pending events, and the EDT has been idle for a second.** That condition — not the close operation — is the desktop's "the app is over" signal, and `session.close()` is its analogue at the one scope SB-Emulators has (one session is one running app instance, [D_active_ui_pointer](#D_active_ui_pointer)).

**Mechanism** — `vaadinx.AutoShutdown`, over seams that already existed:

- **Enabled by the app, not by the library.** `enableForApp(session)` runs where the `@MainWindow` JFrame already registers itself as the session's main window (D_shutdown_lifecycle's pointer, the same fact read twice). Nothing arms before that. "The app is over" needs an app: Sampler's per-component routes, a Karibu test popping a bare `JDialog`, a Vaadin page borrowing an emulator window — none has a program lifetime to end, and closing such a session because its one dialog was disposed would invent a lifecycle it never had. A migrated app always has an `@MainWindow` frame ([D_jframe_as_route](#D_jframe_as_route)), so the supported shape is covered in full.
- **Armed** from `EHelper.onWindowUndisplayable` — `Window.dispose() → removeNotify()` is the only path that undisplayables a Window ([D_window_displayable](#D_window_displayable)), and it is guarded on the bit, so arming is a real edge and never a repeat. Skipped while `isShuttingDown()`: the teardown detach cascade undisplayables everything in a session that is already closing.
- **Decided in the `EHelper.callSwing` epilogue**, after the access-queue drain — the EDT-idle analogue, and what makes both handoff rows work: the drain runs the deferred constructor *before* the check looks, so `dispose(); new MainFrame()` and its `invokeLater` form both find a displayable window. Deciding inside `dispose()` itself would kill both.
- **Checked** as `WindowRegistry.anyDisplayable()` over the app instance's own registry ([D_window_registry](#D_window_registry)) — which is why the `dialog` row needs no special case: a `JOptionPane` / `JFileChooser` / `JColorChooser` overlay is a real `vaadinx.swing.JDialog`, so a parked modal dialog is a displayable window and vetoes on its own.
- **Vetoed** by `holdOpen` tokens, whose only holder today is a started `Timer` (released on `stop()`, and on a non-repeating timer's fire before its listener runs — a one-shot that disposes the last window must not veto its own shutdown). Holds are **strong** references, faithfully: the JDK's `TimerQueue` holds a started Timer too, which is *why* it keeps the JVM alive; the bound is the session where AWT's is the process.
- **A veto never disarms.** The holder's own callbacks are the re-check ticks — a repeating Timer fires through `callSwing`, and the fire that stops it closes the session on that same epilogue. Finding a displayable window *does* disarm (the app is back); the next dispose re-arms.

**What the user sees: "The application has ended".** The response that closes the session carries the frame's detach *and* Flow's `sessionExpired` meta, and Flow's client then acts on the `SystemMessages` bootstrapped into the page. Flow's default is a silent reload, and for a migrated app a reload is a relaunch: measured in Chromium (2026-09-25, `testapps/crud`), `File → Exit` came back as a new app instance in ~0.4 s, under the same `JSESSIONID`. The crud round read that as a frozen frame. So `SwingBridgeEmulatorsBootstrap` installs messages whose session-expired notice reads *"The application has ended / Click here, or press Esc, to start it again."* The client has already marked the UI terminated, which stops heartbeat and push, so **nothing reaches the server, and no session is created, until the user acts** (measured: no request for 15 s). The relaunch becomes the user's choice. Details:
- **Every expired session, not only this one.** A session timeout ends the app instance too, and silently restarting it was the same bug. The Timer case gets the notice when the Timer stops and the session actually closes; until then the tab is empty, like an invisible process still running on the desktop.
- **Only over Flow's default provider.** An app's own `SystemMessagesProvider` wins whichever init listener runs first: set earlier, ours sees a non-default provider and steps back; set later, it replaces ours.
- **Vaadin's stock look**, English only; an app wanting other wording or styling installs its own provider.
- **Not a closed tab.** `window.close()` is refused for a tab the script did not open: Chromium keeps even a fresh tab, whose history already holds `about:blank`, and logs *"Scripts may close only the windows that were opened by them."*

**Rationale.** This is the [R_swing_is_truth](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules) answer, and it *removes* an un-faithful bend instead of documenting it — D_close_operation_dispatch already conceded that real Swing's `dispose()` skips the default-op consult. It also makes the migration guide's "bare `dispose()` suffices" true in all four rows rather than one. And in the one case the old bend differs it was actively wrong: main frame disposed while a tool `JFrame` stays open — the JDK keeps running, the bend killed the session.

The two paper cuts are reproduced rather than smoothed ([R_no_silent_improvements](../CLAUDE.md#hard-rules)): a running Timer that keeps the app alive is the classic "my app won't exit because of the status-bar clock", where the desktop user kills the process and the web user sees a blank tab — the same bug, and now one the guide can name; and an in-flight `SwingWorker`'s `done()` is abandoned with the app, exactly as its daemon threads are on the desktop.

**Alternatives.**
- **Fix the docs, keep the code (state the four-row table in the guide).** Rejected: it documents a divergence SB-Emulators can simply not have, and leaves the wrong-in-one-case bend in place.
- **Any `dispose()` of the `@MainWindow` frame closes the session.** Rejected — it fails the `dialog`, `handoff` and `laterhandoff` rows, i.e. the login→main handoff every migrated app of that shape performs.
- **Keep `EXIT_ON_CLOSE` special on the programmatic path.** Rejected: the measurement says the close operation plays no part in `dispose()`, and the special case is what made the guide wrong.
- **Model a non-daemon `Thread` as a hold.** Rejected as unmodellable — server threads are not per-app, and there is no seam that could tell a migrated app's thread from the container's. R_best_effort_behaviour: we fall short, the session closes anyway (the inventory app's `main()` port-probe thread is the live example).
- **Decide inside `dispose()` rather than in the envelope epilogue.** Rejected on the two handoff rows.

**Accepted limitations.**
- **A non-daemon thread does not hold the app open** (above), where the JDK would wait for it.
- **No 1.3 s grace period.** The decision lands at the end of the disposing envelope, so a dispose-then-reopen that crosses *two* user events (not one envelope and its drain) closes the session where the desktop would have held on. Nothing in a migrated app can span two events without a pending one in between, so this has no known reachable shape.
- **A dispose from outside any envelope arms the check and waits for the next one** — a `dispose()` in `mainUI()`/`bootstrap()`, or in a test's own call. That *is* the EDT-idle shape (the desktop also waits for idle), but it means the session closes at the next user interaction rather than immediately.
- **An emulator window in a session with no `@MainWindow` frame never auto-shuts-down** (the anchor above). Deliberate for Sampler and for tests; a shape outside the migration arc.
- **Session-scoped state, not tab-scoped.** `AutoShutdown`'s flags live on the session where [D_window_registry](#D_window_registry)'s registry lives in tab scope. Identical while one session is one app instance, which is enforced elsewhere; a second app instance per session would need this moved.

**Source:** the inventory stage-2 probe's stumble 10, which asked what `dispose()` does on the `@MainWindow` frame under each close operation and found the docs conditioned the answer on the frame's role instead, D_close_operation_dispatch (the bend this retires), D_shutdown_lifecycle, D_window_displayable, D_window_registry, D_jframe_as_route, D_timer_swingworker; R_swing_is_truth, R_no_silent_improvements, R_best_effort_behaviour.

**Validation.** `emulators/src/test/java/vaadinx/swing/AutoShutdownTest.java` — one test per row of the oracle table above (the four dispose rows separately, since each needs its own session to close, as the probe needed its own JVM), plus `hide`, `dialog`, `handoff`, `laterhandoff`, `timer` (stays open while running, ends on `stop()`) and `worker` (ends; `done()` never runs). `JFrameMainWindowTest`'s three bend tests are gone, replaced by a pointer. One collateral fix in `EHelper.callSwing`: it now holds `ui.getSession()` in a local for the whole envelope, because the app can end mid-envelope — a nested envelope inside the drain closes the session, and Vaadin unlinks a closed session from its UI, so the epilogue's re-read handed `FieldReconciler` a null. Full reactor `clean install` green. The ended notice: `AppEndedMessagesTest` (installed by the bootstrap, replaces Flow's default, leaves an app's own provider alone); the browser half is Flow's client, verified in Chromium.

<a id="D_mouse_listener_bridge"></a>
## D_mouse_listener_bridge. `Component.addMouseListener` gets a DOM bridge — all five callbacks, emulator-side, with the two motion interfaces WARNing at registration

**Status: landed.** Trigger: booting `testapps/inventory/1-emulators` past login (2026-09-02). The app's entire left navigation is `ActionButton extends JLabel` with `addMouseListener(new MouseAdapter(){ mousePressed → setWindow(panel); mouseEntered/mouseExited → highlight })` — seven items. Clicking them produced **no server traffic at all**.

`vaadinx.awt.Component.addMouseListener` was dead storage: the listener went into `listenerList` and nothing ever fed it. The fan-out *below* it was complete and correct all along (`dispatchEvent` → `processEvent` → `processMouseEvent` → per-id callback); the only callers were three per-component wires (`JList`, `JTable`, `JTree`) fed by their surrogate's Grid item-click. Every other component's mouse listeners were inert, and — unlike `addFocusListener`, which WARNs when its peer cannot report focus — **silently so**: the migrator's listener compiles, looks wired, and never runs. [R_no_vaadin_in_api](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_vaadin_in_api) limb 2 and [R_decline_effect_only](../CLAUDE.md#R_decline_effect_only) exist to forbid exactly that shape.

**Decision.** One lazily-installed set of DOM subscriptions on `peer.getElement()`, fanned out over `listenerList` via `processMouseEvent` inside an [R_callswing_envelope](../CLAUDE.md#R_callswing_envelope) envelope — `installMouseBridge`, modelled on `installFocusBridge` down to the install-once guard field. **Emulator-only**: no surrogate seam, because `MouseListener` is a Swing/AWT type and per [R_vaadin_first](../CLAUDE.md#R_vaadin_first) a stage-3 migrator has Vaadin's own `addClickListener` and needs no Swing-shaped duplicate. Accepted consequence: the three grid surrogates keep an `SMouseListener` surface nothing else has.

<a id="D_mouse_five_not_three"></a>**D_mouse_five_not_three — all five methods, because the capability boundary *is* the interface boundary.** `MouseListener` has exactly five methods and every one has a clean DOM counterpart, `mouseEntered`/`mouseExited` included: `mouseenter`/`mouseleave` are bounded by real pointer transitions, not per-pixel, so hover costs nothing like motion tracking does. Shipping a click-only trio would have fixed inventory's navigation and left the same adapter's hover borders dead — the identical silent failure, one level down. The two interfaces we decline are separate *registration methods*, so they WARN at the point of registration:

| registration method | verdict |
|---|---|
| `addMouseListener` (5 methods) | **fully live**, WARN-free |
| `addMouseMotionListener` (`mouseMoved` / `mouseDragged`) | declined — a `mousemove` subscription is a server round trip per pixel of travel. WARNs at registration |
| `addMouseWheelListener` | declined — a round trip per notch, and the browser owns scrolling |

Both declines still *store* the listener, so `getMouseMotionListeners()` / `getMouseWheelListeners()` answer truthfully: R_decline_effect_only drops the effect, not the state. Nothing is half-implemented behind a single registration call.

<a id="D_mouse_browser_is_the_state_machine"></a>**D_mouse_browser_is_the_state_machine — forward the DOM's events; do not synthesise AWT's.** Raw element listeners, not `ClickNotifier`. Deriving a press and a release *from* a click invents two events out of one with a fabricated `when`; and it is unnecessary, because the browser already **is** the state machine AWT describes. Measured on both sides, they agree:

| behaviour | real JDK (Xvfb + `Robot`, JBR 25) | the DOM (Playwright on real peers) |
|---|---|---|
| order | `mouseEntered → mousePressed → actionPerformed → mouseReleased → mouseClicked` | `mouseenter → mousedown → mouseup → click` |
| `mouseClicked` / `click` | **last**, after the release | last |
| double click | escalates **1-then-2**, a full trio each | `detail` 1-then-2, a full trio each |
| release landing elsewhere | **no** `MOUSE_CLICKED`; the release carries `cc=0` | no `click` is sent at all |
| right button | `isPopupTrigger()` **true on the press only** (X11 convention) | `mousedown`+`mouseup` with `button==2` and **no `click`** |
| coordinates | component-relative | see D_mouse_offsetx_is_a_trap |

Two consequences look like omissions and are not: a right button produces no `MOUSE_CLICKED` (the DOM sends no `click`), and `isPopupTrigger()` rides the press — which is what a migrated app's `mousePressed` + `isPopupTrigger()` → `popup.show(...)` idiom already expects. A click-only bridge would have dropped right-button handling entirely.

`ActionEvent` interleaving between pressed and released is the JDK's listener ordering (`BasicButtonListener` is installed at UI-install time, so it precedes the app's listener and its own `mouseReleased` fires the action). Nothing to reproduce deliberately — our `ActionListener` fan-out is independent — but it is the order migrated code was written against.

<a id="D_mouse_offsetx_is_a_trap"></a>**D_mouse_offsetx_is_a_trap — `getX()`/`getY()` come from `clientX/Y` minus the host's own box, never from `offsetX/Y`.** `offsetX` is relative to the event **target**, and whether the target is the peer host depends on which kind of boundary the event crossed: a **shadow root retargets** to the host, while a **slot or a plain light-DOM child does not**. Vaadin mixes both inside one component set, so the property reads correct on one peer and silently wrong on the next — measured:

| peer | boundary | `e.target` at the host listener | `offsetX` vs host-relative |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vaadin-button` | shadow root (innermost target a `SLOT`) | retargeted to the host | `76,16` vs `77,17` — matches |
| `vaadin-text-field` | `<input>` is **slotted light DOM** | stays `INPUT` | `145,10` vs `155,18` — **off by the input's inset** |
| `Span` (JLabel) | none | whatever child was hit | same hazard |

So the bridge collects `event.clientX - element.getBoundingClientRect().left` as an `addEventData` expression and keeps `clientX/clientY` for the `xAbs`/`yAbs` slots. A ~10px error would never have failed a test; it would have quietly mis-hit-tested a migrated app's coordinate-reading listener.

**No `preventPeerEvents` guard, deliberately.** The R_swing_is_truth feedback-loop guard exists for a Swing→peer write echoing back; nothing pushes a synthetic click *down* to a peer, so this direction has no echo to suppress.

<a id="D_mouse_grid_suppression"></a>**D_mouse_grid_suppression — the three that source their own events opt out explicitly, via `suppressMouseBridge()`.** `JList` / `JTable` / `JTree` re-source their surrogate's Grid item-click wire, and those wires are **not** redundant with this bridge: each reports the clicked row/index, which the emulator holds so `rowAtPoint` / `columnAtPoint` / `locationToIndex` can answer *during* the dispatch ([D_jlist](#D_jlist), [D_jtable](#D_jtable), [D_jtree](#D_jtree)), which a pixel-level DOM click cannot do. So they keep their wires and call `protected final suppressMouseBridge()` from their constructor. A `protected` opt-out rather than a comment, because a second click delivered to every migrated `JTable` listener is precisely the kind of regression a comment does not prevent.

**Accepted limitation: a disabled component is mouse-silent, where the desktop keeps talking.** Measured — AWT never gates mouse *delivery* on `isEnabled`: a disabled `JButton` and a disabled `JTextField` both fire all five callbacks, and only `actionPerformed` is suppressed (the `ButtonModel` declines, not the dispatcher). Flow's `disabled` blocks element RPC outright, so DOM listeners on a disabled peer receive nothing. Not worth fixing: the alternative is to stop using Flow's `enabled` on leaves, losing the visual grey-out and the RPC block, to serve a `MouseListener` on a *disabled* widget. Same root cause as [D_container_enabled_no_cascade](#D_container_enabled_no_cascade), which fixes the container half; the leaf half stays as described here.

**Rejected: routing through `dispatchEvent`.** Real AWT's peer-sourced path is `dispatchEvent` → `processEvent` → `processMouseEvent`, so a user subclass overriding `processEvent` is reached; this bridge calls `processMouseEvent` directly. That follows the house convention set by [D_own_awt_package](#D_own_awt_package) — no Toolkit/EventQueue, each `fire*Event` calls its matching `process*Event`, and `processEvent` exists so *user* code calling `dispatchEvent()` still sees AWT's routing — which `addFocusListener` and all three grid wires already follow. The cost is that a `processEvent` override does not see bridged mouse events; consistency across the emulator's whole dispatch surface is worth more than that one hook, and changing it is a decision about every listener type, not this one.

**Source:** R_no_vaadin_in_api limb 2 (the exposed-but-unreachable hook this was), R_decline_effect_only, R_callswing_envelope, R_vaadin_first, R_swing_is_truth, D_own_awt_package (direct `process*Event` dispatch), D_focus_managers / SD_focus_tracker (`installFocusBridge`, the shape copied here), D_jlist / D_jtable / D_jtree (the three item-click wires kept); triggered by the inventory stage-2 boot, whose dead sidebar is the worked example.

**Validation.** `emulators/src/test/java/vaadinx/awt/ComponentMouseListenerTest.java` (16): the `JLabel`-plus-`MouseAdapter` idiom that was dead, as the regression guard; the entered/pressed/released/clicked order; each DOM event's id mapping with `getSource()` rebound to the emulator; host-relative `getX/getY` alongside `clientX/clientY` in `getXOnScreen/getYOnScreen`; DOM button 0/1/2 → `BUTTON1/2/3`; `isPopupTrigger` true only on the button-3 press; click count from `detail`; modifier masks; a release off-target yielding no click; remove-stops-delivery plus getter round-trip; two listeners in registration order; WARN-free registration; the D_mouse_grid_suppression opt-out proven for all three grid components; and a registration-time WARN plus truthful getter for each of the two declined interfaces. `SJList.addMouseListener`'s javadoc claim that the browser does *not* match AWT's 1-then-2 escalation is corrected — measured, it does. Full reactor `clean install` green, then the inventory app re-booted and its sidebar driven in a browser.

<a id="D_container_enabled_no_cascade"></a>
## D_container_enabled_no_cascade. A populated container never writes Flow's `enabled` — Flow's disable cascades to the subtree and Swing's does not

**Status: landed.** Trigger: booting `testapps/inventory/1-emulators` and walking to the first panel (2026-09-02) — the same boot that found [D_mouse_listener_bridge](#D_mouse_listener_bridge). Every button on every one of the app's 12 `AbstractFunctionPanel` panels was dead, `New` among them, so nothing past a panel's read-only state could be reached. No WARN, no exception: it rendered perfectly and did nothing.

`vaadinx.awt.Component.setEnabled` wrote straight through to the peer. For a leaf that is right. For a container it is not: **Flow's disabled state is subtree-scoped and cannot be narrowed from below.** `StateNode.isEnabled()` (flow-server 25.1.3) is a derived walk up the ancestors —

```java
boolean isEnabledSelf = isEnabledSelf();
if (getParent() != null && isEnabledSelf) return getParent().isEnabled();
return isEnabledSelf;
```

— so `setEnabled` writes only `enabledSelf` and the walk ignores it for any node with a disabled ascendant. There is no per-child opt-out and no element-level `DisabledUpdateMode`. A container's disable therefore killed its whole subtree with no way back, which is exactly what the stock Swing form idiom relies on: inventory's `UIUtils.toggleAllChildren(buttonPanel, false)` followed by `btnReadAll.setEnabled(true)`. The app's own helper recursing over `getComponents()` is itself the evidence that Swing does not cascade — nobody writes that if disabling the parent were enough.

**Measured on JDK 25 under Xvfb with a real peer and `Robot`.** A disabled `JPanel` does not cascade at any level: its child keeps `isEnabled() == true`, can be disabled and re-enabled independently, and still receives `ENTERED, MOVED, PRESSED, ACTION, RELEASED, CLICKED`. The **container itself** clicked on its own bare area fires the identical five callbacks disabled or not. AWT never gates mouse *delivery* on `isEnabled` — a disabled `JButton` also fires all five and loses only `actionPerformed`, which is the `ButtonModel` declining, not the dispatcher. **So a disabled Swing container is observably identical to an enabled one except that `isEnabled()` returns `false`.**

**Decision.** A component pushes Flow's `enabled` to its peer only while no emulator children live inside its element — `Component.pushesEnabledToPeer()`, package-private in `vaadinx.awt`, `!(this instanceof Container c && c.getComponentCount() > 0)`. The field write and `JComponent.setEnabled`'s bound `PropertyChangeEvent` are unconditional, so [D_property_fanout_audit](#D_property_fanout_audit) is untouched and `isEnabled()` stays the honest Swing answer. Three edits total: the conditional push, `Container.releasePeerDisableForNewChild()` called from both insertion paths (`addImpl` and `addSlotChild`), and `Window`'s override back to always-push.

**The child count, because the discriminator has to be dynamic.** `instanceof Container` is the natural-looking test and is useless — `JComponent extends Container` exactly as the JDK's does, so a `JButton` answers true and the test would never fire. `peer instanceof HasComponents` is true for many leaf peers besides (Flow's `HasComponents extends HasEnabled`) and answers a Swing question in Vaadin terms. The count is the one signal already present, and the only one that survives *a panel disabled while empty and populated afterwards* — which is why `addImpl` lifts the flag on the way in rather than the predicate merely being consulted once.

**Flow's RPC block is not lost.** A leaf has no emulator children by construction, so leaves keep Flow's `enabled` untouched — grey-out, `[disabled]` theming and the server-side block against a client-side re-enable all survive where they do work. A container has no affordance of its own to protect.

**Nothing is gated emulator-side, deliberately.** Suppressing a disabled container's own event fan-out would invent a suppression Swing does not have ([R_no_silent_improvements](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_silent_improvements)). The correct behaviour falls out of doing less: a container that does not push keeps receiving browser events, so its `MouseListener`s keep firing. The no-push branch is also deliberately **not** routed through `onUnsupported` — a container declining on purpose is not a peer that cannot comply, and conflating the two WARNs about no gap.

**`Window` is the carve-out, and it is measured, not assumed.** `java.awt.Window.setEnabled(false)` blocks input to the entire window: with the frame disabled, a `Robot` click on an untouched child produced *nothing* — not even a `MouseListener` callback — and `b.setEnabled(false); b.setEnabled(true)` underneath did not rescue it, while every child still reported `isEnabled() == true`. The block is at the native window, not in `LightweightDispatcher`: the frame stayed `isActive()`/`isFocused()` and kept naming its focus owner. This is AWT's own mechanism for blocking a modal dialog's owner, and an app calling `frame.setEnabled(false)` as a poor-man's modal depends on it. Here Flow's cascade is the faithful answer, and a closer match than the leaf case is.

**Accepted costs.**
- `button.add(child)` — legal in Swing, rare — stops greying that button.
- `JTabbedPane` and `JMenu`, whose Swing disable *does* have a real effect, lose it once populated. [R_decline_effect_only](../CLAUDE.md#R_decline_effect_only): the flag and the fan-out stay, only the effect goes, and it is recoverable per-component by disabling the tab-strip element specifically.
- A container disabled while *empty* does push, and if emptied again the flag stays cleared. Invisible either way — a `Div` has no disabled rendering.

**Rejected.**
- **Re-assert descendants after a container disable.** Structurally impossible, not merely expensive: the ancestor walk ignores what a descendant writes.
- **Aggregate subtree state — disable Flow-side once the component and every descendant is disabled.** Strictly negative value. Every disabled leaf already carries its own Flow `disabled`, hence its own grey-out and RPC block, so the ancestor adds one redundant attribute and zero behaviour; nothing in Swing computes or observes "whole subtree disabled", making it invented derived state; it costs two independent observers (every `setEnabled` in the subtree *and* every tree mutation including reparenting); and any moment the aggregate is stale-true, a re-enabled child is dead again — real complexity bought to reintroduce this very bug on a rarer path.
- **A hand-maintained opt-out** overridden on `JPanel` / `Box` / `JToolBar` / `JScrollPane` / … Explicit, and its default points the wrong way: a future container emulator that forgets the override reproduces this bug, silently.
- **Bypassing Flow and writing `element.setProperty("disabled", true)`.** The most faithful option — zero cascade at every level, no discriminator at all, and Vaadin components style and block on their own `disabled` property — but it discards Flow's server-side RPC block. Swing offers no such guarantee either; the difference is that a browser has an adversary a desktop app never had, and migrated apps do use a disabled button as an authorization affordance.
- **Accept and document.** The failure is silent and total, the shape [R_no_vaadin_in_api](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_vaadin_in_api) limb 2 exists to forbid.

**`:surrogates` keeps Flow's semantics, period** (maintainer's call, 2026-09-02). Flow's cascade *is* Vaadin's behaviour and a stage-3 migrator expects a Vaadin component ([R_vaadin_first](../CLAUDE.md#R_vaadin_first)). This lands entirely in `vaadinx.awt`, so honouring that costs nothing.

**Left open, deliberately non-blocking:** what a disabled container looks like on the desktop. Expect nothing — `TitledBorder.paintBorder` does not consult `isEnabled()`. If a screenshot comparison later says otherwise, the answer is a functionally-inert CSS class, addable without revisiting any of the above.

**Source:** R_swing_is_truth (Swing's behaviour is the specification), R_no_silent_improvements (we were diverging in the *stricter* direction, which is its named trap even when the divergence looks like tidiness), R_decline_effect_only, R_no_vaadin_in_api limb 2, D_property_fanout_audit (the fan-out this does not move), D_mouse_listener_bridge (same boot, same root cause for its disabled-leaf limitation).

**Validation.** `emulators/src/test/java/vaadinx/awt/ContainerEnabledCascadeTest.java` (8): the inventory idiom, with the re-enabled child live in the DOM and its sibling still dead; a child **added after** the disable via `addImpl`, and another via `addSlotChild` (`JSplitPane.setLeftComponent`), each the sole guard on its insertion path; nested containers, two levels deep; a populated container's own peer never reaching `disabled`, so re-enabling has nothing to undo; a disabled container recording `isEnabled()` and firing its bound property while its child stays untouched; and the `Window` carve-out through both peer shapes — `JFrame` (which may peer on `SJPanel`) and `JDialog` (always a Vaadin `Dialog`) — asserting the opposite — a child of a disabled frame *is* dead in the DOM. Each guard was confirmed by mutation: reverting `pushesEnabledToPeer` to the pre-fix always-push reddens 6 of the 8, dropping the `addSlotChild` lift reddens exactly the slot test, and removing `Window`'s override reddens both carve-out tests. Full reactor `clean install` green, then the inventory app re-booted and driven in a browser: `ItemEntry` in status `NONE` now reports `Read All` and `New` enabled with the other four disabled and **no `ancestorDisabled`** (it was all six disabled, each under `DIV.emul-bg-default`), and clicking `New` reaches the form — Save/Cancel enabled, the other four off, all nine fields live.

<a id="D_layout_owns_child_sizing"></a>
## D_layout_owns_child_sizing. A preferred size reaches CSS through `var(--emul-layout-w, Npx)` — the child owns the value, the parent layout owns the axis

**Decision.** `Component.setPreferredSize` no longer writes `width: 850px`. It writes
`width: var(--emul-layout-w, 850px)` (and the `-h` counterpart), and every
`CssEmittingLayoutManager` writes those two custom properties for every child it visits, one per
axis: `auto` — "this layout sizes the axis, the pref is ignored" — or `initial`, the
guaranteed-invalid value, which makes the child's `var()` fall back to its own pref. Built with
`com.vaadin.swingbridge.surrogates.util.LayoutCss.sizingCss(layoutSizesWidth, layoutSizesHeight)`; the two axis
constants and `prefWidth` / `prefHeight` live beside it.

**A preferred size means nothing on its own, which is why this cannot live on the child.** In AWT
the child never sizes itself — `layoutContainer` calls `setBounds` on it, and each manager decides
per axis whether the pref is consulted, clamped or ignored outright. Read off the JDK's own bodies:

| layout | pref width | pref height | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| `BorderLayout` N/S | **ignored** (container width) | honoured | `BorderLayout.java:826-831` |
| `BorderLayout` W/E | honoured | **ignored** (container height) | `:838-849` |
| `BorderLayout` CENTER | **ignored** | **ignored** | `:850-851` — the leftover rect |
| `FlowLayout` | honoured | honoured | `c.setSize(c.getPreferredSize())` |
| `GridLayout` | **ignored** | **ignored** | every cell is `w/ncols × h/nrows` |
| `GridBagLayout` | honoured unless `fill` covers the axis | same | `fill` + `weightx`/`weighty` |
| `BoxLayout` major axis | honoured (tiled) | — | `calculateTiledPositions` |
| `BoxLayout` cross axis | **stretched** to `min(alloc, getMaximumSize())` | — | `calculateAlignedPositions`; an unset max is `Short.MAX_VALUE` (`Component.java:2856-2861`), so the common child fills |
| `GroupLayout` | honoured unless the component resizes in that band | same | per-band `resizable` |
| `null` (absolute) | irrelevant — `setBounds` owns everything | | |

It is not only a different *value* per layout but a different *property*: the faithful expression of
`BoxLayout`'s major axis is `flex-basis`, of a grid track a track size. A child-side write hardcodes
one layout's answer — FlowLayout's — for all of them.

**The measured bug.** `testapps/inventory`'s toolbar is a `BorderLayout.NORTH` panel that does
`setPreferredSize(new Dimension(getWidth(), 80))`. Stage 1 fills the frame; stage 2 rendered it
**854px wide inside a 1400px region**, half the window empty. The north grid track was 1400px with
`place-items: stretch`, but an explicit inline `width` beats `stretch`. Clearing that one
declaration in devtools snapped the bar to 1400. Not an [R_layouts_close_enough](../CLAUDE.md#R_layouts_close_enough)
cosmetic gap — that rule names "a resizable component rendering at preferred width instead of
filling its region" as *structural*, hence in scope. `getWidth()` was 850 at construction, a number
the desktop never used and which the app's own maximize would have made meaningless anyway.

<a id="D_layout_sizing_var_channel"></a>**D_layout_sizing_var_channel — the variable, not the property, is what makes this work.** Three properties fall out of the indirection, and each replaces something that had to be managed by hand before:
- **Order-immunity.** `var()` resolves at use time, so `setPreferredSize` and the layout pass may run in either order, any number of times. This is the actual bug class: the toolbar happens to work at add time and would break if the app set its pref *after* `add`, with nothing in the old design to catch it.
- **No co-ownership of `width`.** Field surrogates write their own inline `width` from `setColumns`, which is why `GridBagLayout.removeLayoutComponent` deliberately did *not* clear `width` and why `applyChildCss` grew its "a fill-stretched cell can drop a field surrogate's inline width" caveat. Layouts writing only the variables dissolves the conflict instead of managing it — and `removeLayoutComponent` can now clear its own policy safely, which it could never do for `width`.
- **`auto`, not `100%`.** `auto` restores the container's own `stretch`, which sizes the *border box*; `width: 100%` on a content-box element overflows by its border — exactly the +4px groove the 854 included. It also reads as the JDK's meaning: the layout decides this axis.

`GridBagLayout` already wrote `width: auto` for `fill` axes for precisely this reason, so the change
generalizes a fix that was already load-bearing in one layout and moves it into a channel that
cannot clobber a sibling.

<a id="D_layout_sizing_inheritance"></a>**D_layout_sizing_inheritance — custom properties inherit, and that is the one sharp edge.** A `BorderLayout` CENTER panel carries `--emul-layout-w: auto`; if that panel's own layout is `null` (absolute) and its children carry pref widths, they would read the ancestor's `auto` through inheritance and lose every width. Two defences, both shipped: `@property --emul-layout-w { syntax: "*"; inherits: false; }` in `emul/emulator-theme.css` (which `SwingBridgeEmulatorsBootstrap` installs per UI), and — because that stylesheet is one wiring mistake away from absent — every layout writing **both** variables for **every** child, `initial` included, so a laid-out child never reads past itself. `Container.doLayout` does the same for its two manager-less paths (no manager; a non-`CssEmittingLayoutManager` custom manager on the vertical fallback), where the policy is "child owns both axes".

<a id="D_layout_sizing_immediate"></a>**D_layout_sizing_immediate — the pref takes effect without `revalidate()`, and that is a stated carve-out** (maintainer's call, 2026-09-02). Real Swing shows nothing until `revalidate()`, so an immediate effect diverges from [R_no_silent_improvements](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_silent_improvements) / [D_no_silent_improvements](#D_no_silent_improvements). It is also what SB-Emulators has always done — the old inline `width` write was immediate too — and freezing declarative CSS until `validate()` would need a shadow-state machine holding every child's would-be geometry. Accepted as an R_layouts_close_enough *capability* carve-out (the browser lays out continuously; there is no "don't lay out yet"), and written down here rather than left as an implementation accident.

<a id="D_layout_west_keeps_pref"></a>**D_layout_west_keeps_pref — the sibling half-empty region on the same screen is faithful, and was measured rather than argued.** Stock Query's search form stops 431px short of the right edge, which looks like the same bug one level down and is not: the app adds it to `BorderLayout.WEST` (`StockQueryPanel:358`), and WEST takes the child's *preferred* width by contract. A probe on a real JDK 25 with the app's own shape — a WEST panel of pref 969×293 plus a SOUTH row — reports the child at **969px in a 1400px pane, 431px of space to its right**, and still 969px in an 850px frame, i.e. clipped. SB-Emulators reproduces both numbers (west track `968.8px`, gap `431px`, SOUTH row full width at 1400), and the desktop hides the gap only because the app's window is narrower than its own form — which is why the baseline screenshot cuts the `Reset` button off. Stretching WEST to close it would be exactly the kindness [R_no_silent_improvements](../CLAUDE.md#R_no_silent_improvements) forbids: the app would look right under SB-Emulators and wrong under Swing. **The general lesson for the next report of this shape: `WEST`/`EAST` honouring a preferred width and `NORTH`/`SOUTH` ignoring it are the same contract read on two axes — the fix is to check which region the child is in before believing the screenshot.**

<a id="D_layout_pref_intrinsic"></a>**D_layout_pref_intrinsic — the pref width is also the child's intrinsic width, because a layout that stretches the child still reports its pref upward.** The variable settles how *this* child is sized; it said nothing about what the child tells a *parent* that sizes itself from content. In AWT that is `preferredLayoutSize`, and it consults every child's pref, CENTER included. So a CENTER child stretched to fill its panel still sets that panel's preferred width, and with it an `EAST` region's width. In CSS the stretched child's `width: auto` hands the parent its *content* width instead. Measured on `testapps/crud`, 2026-09-25: the preview panel (`setPreferredSize(280, 0)`, in the CENTER of a panel in the frame's `EAST`) rendered 144px with nothing selected and 390–584px with a row selected, following the bio text, and the table beside it shrank from 1136px to 696px. So `setPreferredSize` also writes `contain: inline-size` and `contain-intrinsic-inline-size: Npx`: the element's intrinsic inline size becomes the pref whatever its content, while `width: auto` still stretches it. Applied in Chromium, the panel measured 282px (280 plus its border) for every selection, with the bio wrapping inside it. **Width only**: CSS has no block-axis-only size containment (`contain: size` covers both axes and would discard content height), so a pref *height* still does not reach a content-sized parent. A `display: inline` peer ignores containment and keeps the old behaviour. The intrinsic size is the content box, so a border-box peer's contribution can be off by its border, which R_layouts_close_enough allows.

**Also routed through the variable: the columns→width writers** (`SJTextField`, `SJTextArea`,
`SJPasswordField`, emulator `JTextField`). `setColumns` is a preferred width in Swing — pref size via
`FontMetrics` — so a `GridBagLayout` cell with `fill=HORIZONTAL` stretches past it on the desktop,
and now here, by the same one-variable mechanism rather than by a layout reaching into the
surrogate's own property.

**Deliberately out of scope.** `setMinimumSize` / `setMaximumSize`, which have the same disease
(`GridLayout` ignores min too) but far less load-bearing CSS — and `BoxLayout`'s cross-axis clamp
wants max size first, so it is one change, not two. `setBounds` / `setSize` transience under a
manager (faithful, since `layoutContainer` overwrites bounds, but no measured bug drives it).
`Box.Filler` and struts, whose width is min=pref=max and so genuinely non-negotiable — a hard
`width` there is correct.

**Accepted behaviour change.** A `GridLayout` child that carried a pref size stops honouring it, and
a `BoxLayout` cross-axis child starts filling. Both move *toward* the desktop, and the second
retires an R_layouts_close_enough divergence `boxLayoutCss` had documented as accepted.

**Source:** R_swing_is_truth (the JDK's `layoutContainer` is the specification), R_layouts_close_enough
(structural vs. cosmetic, and the `revalidate` carve-out), [R_decline_effect_only](../CLAUDE.md#R_decline_effect_only)
(the pref *state* was never in question — only which axis it reaches),
[D_layout_css_on_content](#D_layout_css_on_content) (the emission seam this extends),
[M1D_custom_layoutmanager](../migration/1-swing-to-emulators/decisions.md#M1D_custom_layoutmanager)
(a migrator's own layout gets the same per-axis contract, documented on `CssEmittingLayoutManager`).

---

<a id="D_distribution_zip"></a>
## D_distribution_zip. The distribution kit — one download that runs a migration, carrying no library jar, mirroring the repo's geometry, with the testapps out of the reactor

**Decision.** `:zip-distro` assembles `swingbridge-emulators-<version>-dist.zip`: the migrator-facing guides, the two migration tools as `tools/bin` + `tools/lib` (unpacked from the zip `:migration-tool` builds of itself, per D_kit_tool_zip), three example apps (D_kit_what_ships), an agent prompt, four Claude Code skills — the three migrate commands and the `/lsp-preflight` they run first, which is also why they migrate in their own session rather than a subagent (D_kit_lsp_preflight, D_kit_no_subagent) — and a `your-app/swing/` slot for the customer's own app (D_kit_your_app_slot). A person downloads it, unzips it, and runs a Swing→emulators migration without cloning this repository — **the goal, stated plainly (maintainer, 2026-09-08): a customer unpacks the zip, opens Claude Code in it, asks for a migration, and gets a complete one with no access to this repository's sources.** The same assembly leaves the tree unpacked at `zip-distro/target/unzipped/swingbridge-emulators-<version>/`, which is what the integration tests and the guide-loop skills read.

The kit's objective is not distribution for its own sake: **the maintainer migrates the testapps through the kit's own instructions, at the kit's own paths**, so the path a customer walks is the one that gets exercised on every release.

**Rationale.** Central gives a migrator coordinates. It does not give them a guide, a tool, a sample app and an agent prompt in one place, and until this landed the only way to get those was to clone the repo and build the whole reactor. The zip is the kit; Central is the plumbing under it. It is also the natural delivery vehicle for the on-premises local-LLM target — a self-contained bundle of docs + tool + app + prompt is the same bundle with the model swapped.

**Sub-decisions:**

- <a id="D_kit_no_jars"></a>**D_kit_no_jars** — superseded by [D_kit_tool_zip](#D_kit_tool_zip).
- <a id="D_kit_tools_pom"></a>**D_kit_tools_pom** — superseded by [D_kit_tool_zip](#D_kit_tool_zip).
- <a id="D_kit_tool_zip"></a>**D_kit_tool_zip — the tool ships as a zip of its own; the kit unpacks it into `tools/` and adds the table jars.** `:migration-tool` packages itself as `swingbridge-migration-tool-<v>-dist.zip` — `README.md`, `bin/{hazard-scan,import-swap}` + `.cmd` twins, `lib/` with the tool jar and its runtime dependencies — attached as the module's `dist` classifier, so it installs to `~/.m2` and publishes under `-Prelease` with no extra wiring, and built in the **default** build (it takes about a second). `:zip-distro` unpacks it into the kit's `tools/` and adds three jars to `tools/lib/`: `:emulators` and both add-ons. Invocation is `SWINGBRIDGE_HOME/tools/bin/<tool>` everywhere — one shape in the guide, both READMEs, the kit brief and the tool's own javadoc. `tools/pom.xml`, the tools' Maven wrapper and `exec:java@<id>` are gone.
    - **Engine here, tables there — and the reason is the one-way add-on direction, never zip size.** The tool zip carries **no emulators jar and no add-on jar**: the add-ons cannot be in it without core learning they exist (CLAUDE.md §Third-party add-ons), and keeping the emulators jar out keeps the module free of `:emulators`, its stated contract. So the rule is one sentence: *the tool ships the engine; whoever assembles a classpath drops table jars into `lib/`* — which `:zip-distro` then does on the migrator's behalf, so a kit user never assembles anything. `HazardScan` works out of the bare zip (its table is the tool's own resource); `ImportSwap` out of the bare zip fails loudly, which is what makes a tableless zip on Central safe. **A bigger `lib/` is not an argument against packaging more of it** (maintainer, 2026-09-08): download size is not a constraint here, so if bundling jars turns out easier for the migrator, we bundle them. What has to be answered first is *which module packages them* — pulling the emulators jar into the tool's own zip means `:migration-tool` depending on `:emulators`, which is the contract above, and the add-on jars cannot come from core at all. Both are `whether` questions for a brainstorm, not a size trade.
    - **The corrected premise.** `D_kit_tools_pom`, the retired `tools/pom.xml` and `KitSmokeIT`'s javadoc all said a tableless `ImportSwap` run *"rewrites nothing and reports success"*. It does not, and never did: `PortedTypes.load` throws `IOException("no META-INF/emul/ported-types.tsv found on the classpath and none given with --table. Put the swingbridge-emulators jar on the classpath, …")` and `main` exits 2. The failure is loud and already names the fix. That premise was the strongest argument for a pom (a classpath that could not be got wrong silently); with it corrected, the argument is only that a *partial* classpath — core rows, no add-on rows — is silent, which the report's per-source row counts make legible and which `KitSmokeIT` now asserts by counting three sources.
    - **Why the pom lost, argument by argument.** *"A launcher's manifest `Class-Path` has no home"* — true of a launcher **jar**, not of a `lib/` folder: the JVM's `*` classpath wildcard is the launcher, on Linux and in `cmd.exe` alike, and no manifest is involved. *"`lib/` duplicates `~/.m2` and Central"* — true, and not an objection: duplication is what makes the tools runnable with no Maven and no network, and download size is not a constraint we trade against (see *Accepted costs*). *"A development kit's SNAPSHOT jars go stale against `~/.m2`"* — dev-kit-only, and the same entry says nobody downloads a dev kit; the kit lives under `target/` and is regenerated by the very `clean install` that repopulates `~/.m2`, so the two diverge only after a `-pl` incremental install, which CLAUDE.md §Building forbids for exactly this class of hazard. **And what the pom cost, never weighed:** a customer without Maven downloaded the Maven distribution, `exec-maven-plugin` and its plugin tree before the four jars ("a first run downloads four files" was false); Phases 1–2 needed the **network**, which the air-gapped enterprise the kit names as first-class cannot give; two invocation shapes existed for one tool across the guide, the tool's README and the kit brief; the guide's no-kit variant hard-coded `0.1-SNAPSHOT` in shipped prose while the pom filtered its version; and `KitSmokeIT` had to hide behind `-Pkit` because resolution could fail. That last one reverses: the smoke test is in the default build now, and `-Pkit` adds only the invoker run.
    - **Why a zip built by `:migration-tool`, rather than `:zip-distro` assembling a `lib/` itself.** The zip is a Central-publishable artifact, which finally gives the guide's "without the kit" path a one-line answer — download the zip, `dependency:copy` the emulators jar into `lib/` — instead of `dependency:copy` × N into a folder the reader invents. The scripts and the classpath get tested where the tool lives (`DistZipIT`), on both platforms. And the kit consumes a finished thing rather than re-deriving one.
    - **Hand-written scripts, four files.** Each is five lines: resolve `$0`'s directory, honour `JAVA_HOME` if set, `exec java -cp "<dir>/../lib/*" <Main> "$@"`. Nothing is filtered into them — no version, no path — because the wildcard does the work. Rejected: **appassembler** (large opaque generated scripts for a five-line job; last release 2020) and a **Java dispatcher `Main`** with subcommands (adds code to save two files, and re-opens `M1D_hazard_scan_tool`'s `Q_entry_point`, which the second `main` already won).
    - **Rejected shapes, kept because they will be re-proposed:** the `tools/pom.xml` + `exec:java` shape (above); a **launcher jar** with a manifest `Class-Path` (the manifest cannot come from `:migration-tool`'s pom without breaking its no-`:emulators` contract, and `-jar` ignores `-cp`, so a user could not add a table jar at all); a **shaded/fat tool jar** (same `-jar` problem, and it would have to bundle the emulators jar's table, coupling the tool to one emulators version).
    - **The survivor from `D_kit_no_jars`, re-homed because the add-on poms and DEVELOPING.md cite it:** everything a migrated pom can be told to reference is resolvable by coordinate and publishes under `-Prelease` — a release kit pins a released version and Maven finds it on Central, a development kit pins `-SNAPSHOT` and Maven finds it in the `~/.m2` that the same `clean install` populated. **The kit still ships no library jar to build against.** The three jars in `tools/lib/` are swap-table sources for the tool, and nothing in any shipped pom points at that folder. The corollary that sets the CI shape survives too: a SNAPSHOT kit is only usable on the machine that built it, so the only kit worth handing out is a release build.
    - **Accepted costs.** For the record and not as a cost: `lib/` is **4.7 MB**, of which ArchUnit is 4.6 (the tool jar is 60 KB) — the guardrail engine's reader, per [M1D_static_sweep_tool](../migration/1-swing-to-emulators/decisions.md#M1D_static_sweep_tool) `Q_one_rule_engine`. `D_kit_no_jars`' *"`lib/` duplicates `~/.m2`"* argument was already weak; **the size half of it is now explicitly dead** — a one-off download beside a first testapp build that fetches Vaadin, and the maintainer's standing call is that a jar which saves the migrator a step earns its bytes. Trimming `lib/` is not a goal, and neither is holding it small. The real cost here is `KitSmokeIT` running on **Linux only**: it needs the whole reactor installed, and a full Windows reactor build is not worth its minutes for one more script run — the Windows CI job builds `-pl migration-tool -am` and lets `DistZipIT` drive the `.cmd` twins, which is the half no Linux run can execute.
- <a id="D_kit_mirrors_repo"></a>**D_kit_mirrors_repo — the kit mirrors the repository's geometry, and that is load-bearing.** Guides at `guides/1-swing-to-emulators/`, the worked example at `testapps/crud/`, the add-on addenda at `third-party/*/`. That is what lets every link in the shipped docs stay relative and keep resolving after the unzip. Both alternatives were rejected: a prettier `docs/` + `examples/` layout forces an assembly-time link rewrite, and rewriting a link to `emulators/decisions.md` into a GitHub URL turns a persona leak into a *working* persona leak, which hides it instead of fixing it. Examples ship **unpacked, not as nested zips**, for the same reason — a zip is opaque to a link. This is also why the migrator docs tree moved from `migration/out/` to a top-level `guides/`: a *kit-only* rename is impossible under mirrored geometry (the guide's `../../../testapps/crud` is written for a depth of three and would point above the kit root from a depth of two), and the sibling layout is better on its own, since the persona split becomes a top-level fact where `out` read as generated output for a hand-authored tree.
- <a id="D_kit_link_scope"></a>**D_kit_link_scope — a file under `guides/` may only link to what the kit ships, gated from both ends.** `:emulators`' `GuideLinkScopeTest` says a guide's relative links must resolve *and* must land inside the shipped set; `:zip-distro`'s `KitLayoutIT` says the shipped tree's links resolve inside the tree. The pair needs no shared list to agree — add a fileSet without allow-listing it, or the reverse, and one side reddens. The 17 out-links that existed when this landed were **fixed rather than rewritten**, in three kinds: 11 maintainer-doc pointers (`CLAUDE.md`, `D_*` / `M1D_*` entries, module READMEs) became in-place rationale, or an absolute GitHub URL under an explicit maintainer-facing "further reading" note; 3 worked-example pointers to `testapps/crud` stayed verbatim and only changed depth; the migrated app itself was never linked, which is right for prose. The same test carries the second clause: **every `SWINGBRIDGE_HOME` / `MIGRATED_APP_FOLDER` token must be declared in its own document's Conventions block**, each document being read standalone — an undeclared placeholder is a dead link without the brackets.
- <a id="D_kit_testapps_standalone"></a>**D_kit_testapps_standalone — the testapps leave the reactor and stay in place, each stage with a standalone pom and the Maven wrapper.** A testapp inside the reactor never exercises the path a migrator takes: measured 2026-09-07, `swingbridge-emulators-parent` silently supplied the stage-2 testapp poms the Vaadin BOM import, the vaadin-boot / slf4j / junit / annotations versions, the JDK-24 enforcer, `maven.compiler.release` and the surefire config — everything `vaadin-boot-scaffold.md` tells a real migrator to write, and which no round had ever had to write. The first finding the new arrangement produced, before anything was built: that document told the migrator to *"mirror the sibling `:sampler`"*, a subproject that exists only inside this reactor. Nothing is flattened or generated at assembly time — the pom the customer builds is the pom that is committed — which is why "does the generated standalone pom still build" is not a question anyone has to answer. **Two neighbouring shapes were rejected the same day:** *a separate repository for testapps + kit* — the docs cannot follow (they are authored here under `DecisionIdTest`, `HazardTableTest` and the add-ons' `MigrationDocTest`), two golden tests read the testapps off disk, and the stumble → fix emulators → re-run loop would become two checkouts and a version bump per iteration; reactor *membership* was the thing to sever, not repo location. *Each testapp packaging itself as a source zip* — the kit ships source trees, so a `fileSet` copy suffices; a nested zip is opaque to the guide's links; and the artifact route makes the build order circular, since a testapp can only build after the reactor is installed while `:zip-distro` is in the reactor. The duplication this costs — `swingbridge-emulators.version` and `vaadin.version` in three poms with no parent to inherit from — is guarded by `:migration-tool`'s `TestappStandalonePomTest`, which also asserts the absent `<parent>` and the wrapper's presence; without it a stale pin resolves fine against a `~/.m2` holding the old SNAPSHOT and fails first for a stranger who unzipped the kit. `testapps/inventory/1-emulators/pom.scaffold.xml` went with the move: a run now starts from a copy of `swing/`, so the pre-migration pom *is* `swing/pom.xml`, and writing the stage-2 pom from the scaffold guide became part of what a run has to do rather than something handed to it.
- <a id="D_kit_ci_invoker"></a>**D_kit_ci_invoker — `-Pkit` builds the shipped copies with `maven-invoker-plugin`; nothing builds `testapps/` directly.** The build that matters is the customer's: the shipped copy, at the kit's paths, resolving SB-Emulators by coordinate. So the invoker runs `verify` (not `install` — nothing consumes a testapp artifact) over `target/unzipped/.../testapps/*/*/pom.xml`, and CI's reactor command becomes `./mvnw -B -C -ntp install -Pkit`, since those builds resolve the reactor's SNAPSHOTs from `~/.m2`. Do **not** stage a private repository with `invoker:install`: it installs only the reactor's own artifacts, so Vaadin would re-download on every invocation. Assembly, unpacking and the layout/link/slot checks stay in the **default** build (seconds, and a round's residue needs the unpacked tree); the invoker run and the end-to-end smoke test sit behind the profile, so the local `clean install` CLAUDE.md §Building asks for before every migration round stays cheap. Rejected: a shell loop over `testapps/*/*/pom.xml` and an aggregator `testapps/pom.xml` — both build the *repo* copy rather than the shipped one, and the second is a reactor again.
- <a id="D_testapps_inplace_rebuild"></a>**D_testapps_inplace_rebuild — the root `clean install` also rebuilds every testapp stage in place.** Not instead of D_kit_ci_invoker's shipped-copy build, which still answers *"does the customer's copy build?"*; this one answers *"is the working tree's `target/` today's?"*, which nothing asked while the testapps sat outside the reactor. The miss was measured: `testapps/crud/1-emulators/target/classes` kept a `META-INF/services/com.vaadin.flow.server.VaadinServiceInitListener` from before crud moved to Spring Boot, so `SwingBridgeEmulatorsBootstrap` ran twice (ServiceLoader plus the auto-configuration's bean — R_no_spi_selfregister's "every per-UI step twice, silently"), `TabScope.setup` ran twice, and every F5 logged `Invalid state: uis doesn't contain given ui`, chased as the vaadin-blocking-dialogs switch's regression because a scratch-worktree run of `main` had no `target/` to be stale. A `maven-invoker-plugin` execution in `:zip-distro` runs `clean verify` over `testapps/*/*/pom.xml`, **bound to `install`**, since the stages resolve SB-Emulators by coordinate and are only worth building once this run has installed (~45 s for six stages). `-Dtestapps.skip` skips it for one run; the default stays on, and the property's comment carries the hunt so that nobody flips it to save the 45 s. The rejection above of "a shell loop over `testapps/*/*/pom.xml`" stands for what it rejected — a substitute for the shipped-copy build.
- <a id="D_kit_placeholders"></a>**D_kit_placeholders — an unfilled slot ships as `<intended-filename>.placeholder`, and exactly one of the pair may exist.** Where a slot's real artefact does not exist yet, the kit ships a plain-text file saying what would be there, why it is not, and where to get it meanwhile. This beats an empty directory because **the layout is final on day one** — the README, the guides and the prompt can name the path today, and filling the slot moves nothing else — and because it is honest *in-band*, at the moment the reader reaches for the thing, rather than in release notes they did not read. It is also the kit's `ideas/`: every placeholder is a promise, and `find . -name '*.placeholder'` is the open-items list. Two guards, or placeholders rot exactly as stale ideas do: slots are declared in `zip-distro/src/main/kit-slots.txt`, and `KitLayoutIT` fails when a slot has **both** the artefact and its placeholder or **neither** (and when a placeholder names no declared slot), while the same test writes the unfilled list to `target/placeholders.txt` so "still a placeholder in this release" reaches the release notes generated rather than remembered. v1 ships one: `tools/swing-mcp/swing-mcp-agent.jar` (no release train of its own yet — behavioural capture off the desktop app is a later slice). `testapps/inventory` was the second until the maintainer filled it (2026-09-08, below); its line in `kit-slots.txt` stays, which is what a slot graduating looks like.
- <a id="D_kit_what_ships"></a>**D_kit_what_ships — what travels, and why each absence is not an oversight.** *Crud ships both stages*: the finished `1-emulators/` is the answer key the guide's worked-example links land on, and the only reader who must not peek at it is this repository's own doc-quality probe. *jlawyer-shape ships stage 1 only* — honest mode: a second answer key buys nothing the first does not, and the question a demo answers is whether a stranger gets from Swing to browser on the guides alone. (Its README consequently *names* `1-emulators/` where it used to link it — a finding the kit's own link check produced.) *The inventory testapp ships stage 1 only, on its author's terms* — decided by the maintainer on 2026-09-08, and **on the grant's own wording, not on the relicense** that landed the same day: a zip is mere aggregation under GPLv2 §2, so the kit's licence never bore on what a third party's grant permits, and [D_gplv2_ce_relicense](#D_gplv2_ce_relicense) point 5 says as much. The grant ("feel free to use/modify … keep the class header or add reference to this GitHub repository") presupposes redistribution in its second limb, and the kit honours both limbs: the `@author` headers travel intact in the sources, and `testapps/inventory/PROVENANCE.md` travels *because* it is where the grant is reproduced verbatim and the upstream URL is named — the inverse of the add-ons' `PROVENANCE.md` rule two items down, whose files are maintainer records with no licence content. Its repository links became absolute for that reason. Withdrawing is one restored placeholder, since the slot stays declared. What was not done: shipping `1-emulators/` (round output, not an answer key the guide links — jlawyer-shape's argument applies) and adding a Vaadin header to any of its files (PROVENANCE.md § "Trees we do not touch": a header on a file Vaadin did not author is a false claim). *Sampler is not bundled and is not a slot*: a Vaadin-Boot zip would be the one binary in a source-and-docs archive, for an app that carries no commitment surface — the welcome README carries clone-and-run instead, and the "cloning and building the reactor is the barrier the kit exists to remove" objection is answered by D_kit_tool_zip, since building the migrated app needs Maven and the network regardless — which is now true of *only* the app, the tools having stopped needing either. *An add-on's `PROVENANCE.md` does not ship* — the BSD fork's `LICENSE` does, which is the actual obligation; provenance is a maintainer record of how the fork was made, and its links point into the decision logs. *A fully offline kit is out of scope*: Vaadin is not ours to bundle and `vaadin-maven-plugin`'s frontend build reaches the network anyway, which also makes a bundled `repo/` moot.
- <a id="D_guide_round_residue"></a>**D_guide_round_residue — the guide loop's migration step is a residue over the kit.** `/migrate-<app>-dryrun` shrinks to: `./mvnw -C clean install` (which installs the SNAPSHOTs *and* leaves the kit unpacked, and that folder is `SWINGBRIDGE_HOME`); open the kit's own `CLAUDE.md` and run `/migrate-testapp <app>` as a customer would; then two pieces of harness residue only — **copy back** the finished tree and its `STUMBLES.md` from `SWINGBRIDGE_HOME/work/<app>/` (which lives under `target/` and dies at the next `clean`) into `testapps/<app>/1-emulators/` as the committed baseline, and **a short deny-list**, since the probe still must not read the shipped answer keys or the inventory app's `PROVENANCE.md`. (A third item — spawning the migration as `subagent_type: migrator` — was residue for one day, on the reasoning that "a customer's default agent type is not ours to name"; D_kit_lsp_agent reversed that and moved the spawn line and the agent definition into the kit.) **Restructured 2026-09-08 (D_kit_lsp_preflight):** the residue is now layered as `/build-kit` → `/guide-migrateapp <app>` → `/migrate-<app>-dryrun`, the last holding only that app's deny-list, disclosures and extra report lines; the generic half drives the kit from a Claude Code session *rooted at the kit*, not from this repository's, and stages the app copy before that session starts. Anything general enough for two apps sits one layer down; anything a customer should know moved into the guides (`agent-prompt.md` took the phase-batching rule and the `## Not a doc gap` categories that had lived in the inventory residue). **Collapsed 2026-09-24:** the per-app layer is a file, not a skill — `/migrate-<app>-dryrun` became `.claude/skills/guide-migrateapp/<app>.md`, which `/guide-migrateapp <app>` reads as its step 0. `/guide-migrateapp` carries `disable-model-invocation` (a round rebuilds the reactor and needs the maintainer at a second terminal, so no model should start one), and the Claude Code harness began enforcing that flag on skill-to-skill calls too, so a per-app skill could no longer hand off to it. The residue was only ever data — a deny sentence, a restore step, extra report lines — so it moved to where the procedure reads it. The layering is unchanged, the maintainer still types one command, and a new testapp joins the loop by gaining a file rather than a skill. The three `/migrate-<app>-docfix` skills collapsed the same day into `/guide-docfix <app>` for symmetry rather than necessity (they called no other skill): two were one text with different paths, and the third was that text plus the adopted app's extra owners, which became `.claude/skills/guide-docfix/inventory.md`.
